The post New Abe Office Malware Bypasses Chrome App-Bound Encryption to Steal Browser Passwords and Cookies appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
A new remote-access trojan called Abe Office can steal browser passwords and cookies, even from Chrome’s App-Bound Encryption. It poses as an office helper tool and carries a valid code-signing certificate.

Researchers at Rogue Authority broke its weak protections and watched the operator at work in a sandbox.

Abe Office malware

The file is named AbeAgent.exe and calls itself the “Abe Office workstation helper.” No such product exists. The file is signed through SSL.com in the name of a private person, Kimberley Hankinson, in Pennsylvania. The certificate became valid on 26 October 2026 and the file was signed on 4 November.

A signature only shows who sealed a file and that nobody changed it afterward. It does not prove the file is safe. A brand-new certificate in a person’s name, used at once to sign a “company” product, is a pattern researchers see again and again in signed malware. The certificate has been reported to the CA and added to the CertGraveyard.

The name “Abe” most likely stands for App-Bound Encryption, the Chrome feature the malware is built to beat.

On first run, the program copies itself to the user’s profile folder and restarts from there. It removes the Mark of the Web tag, which is the hidden label Windows uses to warn about downloaded files.

It then adds a Run key named “Abe Office Sync” and a scheduled task, both starting it with the switch –autostart. It also tries to add a firewall rule called “Abe Office Agent.”

Three encrypted add-ons are written to disk. One is the main RAT, one runs the hidden desktop, and one is a small helper that runs inside the browser. Before loading them, the starter asks its server for a key. The goal is to hide the add-ons from anyone who has only the file.

According to technical research published by Rogue Authority, the lock does not hold. The file contains a default password, AbeOffice-ChangeMe, which can be used to work out every key. Researchers decrypted all three add-ons this way. The key sent by the live server matched the one they had computed offline.

The same password protects the network traffic. The AES key is just a hash of that password, so the whole captured conversation could be read. This is good news for defenders, since anyone holding a sample can unpack the kit.

The hidden desktop add-on creates an invisible Windows desktop and starts browsers on it. It first copies the victim’s Chrome and Edge profiles to C:\ProgramData\AbeOffice\SystemCache. In the sandbox it copied 287 profile files. A browser opened from those copies is already signed in to email, banking and shopping sites.

This lets the operator act as the victim without a password, and from the victim’s own PC. That helps get past “new device” checks. Hidden-desktop tools like this are growing in number, as shown by our earlier report on Shadow hVNC, which also steals cookies and reuses live sessions.

In a multi-day sandbox run, the operator connected three times over about a day and a half. The operator listed the browsers, opened Chrome and Edge on the hidden desktop, and went straight to the saved-password pages. The sandbox held no saved passwords, so nothing was taken.

Google added App-Bound Encryption in Chrome 127 in July 2024. A Windows service with system rights checks which app is asking before it gives up the key. Google said malware would now need system rights or code injection, which are noisier actions. Google’s security blog explains the design.

Abe Office takes the second route. It starts a browser off-screen at position -32000,-32000 and injects its helper DLL. The helper asks the browser’s own elevation service to decrypt the key. Because the request comes from the real browser, the service agrees.

The key is saved to C:\ProgramData\AbeOffice\abe_job\key.dat. The code also holds backup routes, including a browser extension named “Abe Crypto Bridge.”

Other stealers use similar tricks. SpyCloud found that families such as Lumma and Vidar claimed bypasses soon after launch. Phemedrone used Chrome’s remote debugging port. Our earlier story on infostealers bypassing Chrome’s cookie protection covers Elastic’s findings on these methods. A recent Marsalek malware report shows the same DLL injection idea.

The command server at 2.26.230[.]54 also hosts the operator’s control panel. Shodan data showed its Windows computer name matched the one that drove the hidden browsers. Its port 80 served an “Abe Update” page listing the kit’s files.

A second server, 87.199.195[.]141, served the same page. VirusTotal links 133 files to the two servers, first seen between mid-September and early November.

They include 10 other AbeAgent.exe files, 61 launcher-bootstrap-stub.exe files and 49 app.zip packages. Only this build uses a certificate from a real CA, so it may be the newest step. The delivery method is still unknown.

If you ran this file, treat your browser sessions as stolen. From a clean device, sign out of all sessions, change passwords for key accounts starting with email, and turn on two-factor authentication. Then clean or reinstall the PC.

Defenders should look for the AbeOffice folders, the “Abe Office Sync” Run value and any process started with –autostart. They should block outbound traffic to both servers on port 9090.

They should also flag browsers launched with –window-position=-32000,-32000 or with local remote debugging, and non-browser programs reading Login Data, Cookies and Local State files. A sign-in from the victim’s own PC should not be trusted by default either.

The post New Abe Office Malware Bypasses Chrome App-Bound Encryption to Steal Browser Passwords and Cookies appeared first on Cyber Security News.

articles.title: Notepad++ 8.9.9 Released With Fixes for 6 Vulnerabilities Allowing Plugin Command Execution
articles.description:
Notepad++ released version 8.9.9 on November 6, 2026, fixing six security flaws across Windows message handling, protected file saving, clipboard operations, and MIME Tools decoding. The update addresses flaws including conditional plugin command execution, memory exposure, and buffer overflow. The release notes list no assigned CVE identifiers for these issues. The command execution issue involves […]

The post Notepad++ 8.9.9 Released With Fixes for 6 Vulnerabilities Allowing Plugin Command Execution appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
Notepad++ released version 8.9.9 on November 6, 2026, fixing six security flaws across Windows message handling, protected file saving, clipboard operations, and MIME Tools decoding.

The update addresses flaws including conditional plugin command execution, memory exposure, and buffer overflow. The release notes list no assigned CVE identifiers for these issues.

The command execution issue involves WM_COPYDATA, a Windows message used to exchange data between applications. In Notepad++ 8.9.8, the sender checks whether a window handle supplied by the caller is trusted rather than proving which process sent the message. A local attacker could nominate a separate, legitimate Notepad++ window to pass those checks.

This could let an attacker pass plugin commands into an elevated editor. However, the demonstrated attack required the optional NppExec plugin to be installed and initialized, an already elevated target, and a second Notepad++ instance running from the same executable path. It is local privilege escalation under specific conditions, not network-based remote code execution.

The release separately lists a WM_COPYDATA sender authentication bypass and the plugin command execution flaw. Both highlight the danger of trusting caller-controlled message data across privilege levels.

The update follows earlier Notepad++ code execution fixes involving configuration files, although those earlier vulnerabilities have different causes.

Another flaw affects saves that require User Account Control approval. Notepad++ wrote document contents into a temporary file, closed it, and passed its path to an elevated helper.

A malicious process running as the same user could replace those contents before the helper copied them into the protected file selected by the user. User approval remained necessary.

Memory Flaws and Plugin Risks

The heap disclosure advisory describes an unchecked clipboard length in Paste Binary. A local process could supply a small text buffer alongside a larger claimed size, causing Notepad++ to copy adjacent process memory into a document. Testing recovered heap data beyond the supplied buffer.

The NPPM_MENUCOMMAND flaw used unchecked indexes when selecting stored commands. Testing showed out-of-bounds data reaching ShellExecute and blocking the interface, but attacker control over the resulting command was not demonstrated.

Separately, MIME Tools versions through 3.1 contain SAML Decode buffer overflows. Crafted input could crash the editor or potentially execute code when decoded. MIME Tools 3.2 fixes that issue.

Earlier Notepad++ plugin abuse involved replaced plugin files, a different attack path from these newly patched flaws. Users should install version 8.9.9 through the official download page and verify MIME Tools is updated.

The release also improves Find in Files performance, refreshes Scintilla and Lexilla, adds dialog font controls, and fixes clipboard history errors and memory leaks.

articles.title: GhostAction Hackers Compromise 500+ GitHub Accounts to Steal AWS, OpenAI, and Cloud Credentials
articles.description:
A new wave of the GhostAction campaign has hit more than 500 GitHub accounts. The attackers use those accounts to plant a fake security workflow in tens of thousands of repositories, and the workflow steals cloud, AI, and publishing keys. Security firm Socket reports that the accounts added the malicious file starting October 7, 2026, […]

The post GhostAction Hackers Compromise 500+ GitHub Accounts to Steal AWS, OpenAI, and Cloud Credentials appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
A new wave of the GhostAction campaign has hit more than 500 GitHub accounts. The attackers use those accounts to plant a fake security workflow in tens of thousands of repositories, and the workflow steals cloud, AI, and publishing keys.

Security firm Socket reports that the accounts added the malicious file starting October 7, 2026, and that some of the repositories belong to large organizations.

GhostAction GitHub account compromise

Socket studied a burst on October 8, 2026. Two hijacked accounts, henrywoo and kitao, pushed a file named security-audit.yml into 346 repositories.

The commit messages were “Add security audit workflow” and “Update security audit workflow.” Despite the name, the file does no security work. It collects secrets and sends them in plain text to the IP address 193.32.204[.]199.

The list of targets includes uber/athenadriver, which is owned by Uber, and kitao/pyxel, a popular Python game engine with more than 18,000 stars. The henrywoo account has write access to the Uber project because he is its original author.

This shows why one stolen maintainer account is so costly. The damage reaches every repository the account can edit, not just the owner’s own projects.

The attackers first get a working login for a maintainer account. Socket did not see how they did this. Next, they scan each repository for the secret names its workflows already use, and they write those names into the fake file.

Last, they commit the file straight to the default branch, where it runs on the next push. The same file went into hundreds of repositories within minutes, so Socket believes a tool did the work and not a person.

The timing supports that view. The henrywoo changes landed in a window of about 16 minutes, and the kitao changes landed in a four-minute window. Even repositories that had sat idle for a decade got the file.

You can read how this campaign grew in our earlier GhostAction coverage of the 772-repository wave, which tracked the same weak spot in GitHub Actions.

According to technical research published by Socket, earlier GhostAction waves only took secrets stored in GitHub Actions. GitGuardian first described that style in September 2025, when 327 users and 817 repositories lost 3,325 secrets.

The new version keeps that trick and adds a search through the repository files and the full git history.

This matters because many developers delete a key from the latest file and think the problem is gone. The old commit still holds the key.

The workflow uses a setting called fetch-depth: 0, which pulls every branch and tag so the script can read the whole past of the project.

The script looks for 13 types of keys. These include AWS access keys and session tokens, plus OpenAI, Anthropic, and OpenRouter API keys. It also looks for GitHub and GitLab tokens, Google and Firebase keys, Slack tokens, and SendGrid keys.

One detail shows the AWS focus. An AWS key ID alone cannot log in to anything. The secret half usually sits a line or two away in an .env file or a Terraform file.

So the script also copies two lines above and below each key ID. That lets the attacker rebuild a full, usable AWS key pair.

Stolen publishing tokens are just as risky. For Pyxel, the named secrets were tokens for PyPI and crates.io plus a GitHub personal access token. With those, an attacker could push a bad update of a package that many people trust.

As of October 9, 2026, the file was still on the default branch of the repositories Socket checked. The workflow had also run successfully, which means data could already have left.

Socket saw no bad package versions on PyPI or crates.io at the time of writing, but that does not prove the stolen keys went unused.

Forks add more risk. Socket counted 279 forks under the henrywoo name that carry the file, and Actions can run it on later pushes if they are enabled.

Machine learning projects such as henrywoo/pyllama and henrywoo/chatllama stand out, since their users often hold AWS and AI keys.

The campaign has kept growing. OpenSourceMalware counted 790 repositories with the workflow through October 9, 2026, which our team covered in a report on 790 hijacked GitHub repositories. AI tools can make exposed keys even more dangerous.

Microsoft says attackers used an AI framework called ARTEX to find GitHub secrets and reach Azure Key Vault in about five minutes, as shown in our ARTEX AI report.

Start by opening .github/workflows/security-audit.yml and checking which secret names it lists. Rotate every secret named there.

For a GitHub personal access token, revoke it and make a new one. Then review the Actions run history and treat every finished run as a successful theft.

Next, scan the full git history with git log -p –all and rotate every key you find, even if it no longer shows in the current files. For AWS keys, check CloudTrail for new IAM users, new access keys, and use in odd regions.

Treat the maintainer account as fully compromised. Revoke all sessions, tokens, OAuth grants, and SSH keys. Turn on phishing-resistant multi-factor login, then search the organization audit log for new workflow files.

Block 193.32.204[.]199 in egress logs, including self-hosted runners. Finally, turn on GitHub secret scanning with push protection and require approval for workflow runs from outside contributors.

The post GhostAction Hackers Compromise 500+ GitHub Accounts to Steal AWS, OpenAI, and Cloud Credentials appeared first on Cyber Security News.

articles.title: Anubis Ransomware Hackers Deploy New Lindnor Backdoor and 13 Security-Killing Tools in U.S. Attack
articles.description:
Attackers using Anubis ransomware broke into a U.S. organization in October 2026. They used a new custom backdoor called Lindnor and dropped at least 13 tools built to switch off security software. Symantec’s Protection Bulletin says the encryption payload was blocked before it could run. Anubis ransomware Lindnor backdoor Symantec tracks the developer of Anubis […]

The post Anubis Ransomware Hackers Deploy New Lindnor Backdoor and 13 Security-Killing Tools in U.S. Attack appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
Attackers using Anubis ransomware broke into a U.S. organization in October 2026. They used a new custom backdoor called Lindnor and dropped at least 13 tools built to switch off security software.

Symantec’s Protection Bulletin says the encryption payload was blocked before it could run.

Anubis ransomware Lindnor backdoor

Symantec tracks the developer of Anubis as Hawkmoth. The group runs a ransomware-as-a-service (RaaS) operation that appeared in December 2024 as a rebrand of the Sphinx ransomware. The payload looks mostly unchanged from Sphinx, and only the branding is new.

Because Hawkmoth lets affiliates carry out the attacks, the methods can change from one break-in to the next. Researchers at Barracuda have described the group’s mix of wiping, leaking and extortion. The group has claimed about 96 victims in the past 12 months, and 52% of them are in the United States.

The group is also persistent. In a July 2026 case, Symantec saw the attackers use four different tools to steal data: Megasync, WinSCP, Filezilla and S3browser. Using that many tools of one type in a single attack is unusual.

According to technical research published by Symantec, investigators did not learn how the attackers first got in. The first warning sign was the Lindnor backdoor, which sat on two machines. Those were the only two Microsoft SQL Servers among the affected systems.

The attackers named the backdoor healthcontroller64.exe on one machine and placed it in a folder made to look like a Chrome component directory. On the other machine it was svchelper.exe in a VMware folder. Both copies ran as a service.

Lindnor sends the process ID, Windows version, file path, computer name, user name, domain and logon server to its command-and-control server. It has a main server and a backup, and both use port 443, which blends in with normal web traffic.

Custom backdoors are rare in ransomware cases, since most crews use public or built-in tools. Symantec also saw Lindnor on two other unrelated networks, but no ransomware appeared there.

Within about an hour, the attackers dropped at least 13 executables meant to shut down security products. They leaned on a method called Bring Your Own Vulnerable Driver (BYOVD) and brought five signed but flawed drivers to get kernel-level control.

Two of the tools, gbbsym.exe and symgooq.exe, pretended to be Symantec software. Eleven of the 13 had not been published before, though all the drivers were already known.

Symantec blocked every dropped file except huntreagent.exe and s1.exe. Those two have the same size but different hashes, so they may be two builds of one tool. The pattern looks like trial and error, with the attackers trying one tool after another until something worked.

BYOVD works because Windows trusts signed drivers. Symantec’s Lights Out whitepaper says hundreds of vulnerable drivers are in circulation and that BYOVD tools now come bundled with RaaS kits.

Our earlier report on EDR killer tactics beyond vulnerable drivers shows how common these tools have become.

The attackers installed the real AnyDesk remote tool, then created a new local user and added it to a local group. They also ran safemode.exe, which sets AnyDesk to keep working when Windows starts in Safe Mode with Networking.

This matters because most security software does not fully run in Safe Mode. That gives attackers a quiet window to load drivers and turn off protection. The trick is not new, but it is rarely seen.

The Anubis encryptor was named iservice.exe. It adds the .anubis extension to files and leaves ransom notes called restore files.txt and restore files.html. The notes say data was stolen and will be published if talks fail.

Anubis also has an optional wiper mode that empties file contents. Our earlier coverage of Anubis wipe mode explains why paying may not bring files back. In this case, Symantec blocked the payload before encryption began.

The attackers came ready for security tools to get in their way, but the last step still failed. Symantec says few ransomware crews build their own backdoors.

Defenders should watch for the file names and hashes Symantec listed, including the domains msrcontrib[.]com and cfgsync-relay.eastus.cloudapp.azure[.]com. The key Lindnor hash is fc200686175559f4544a5de826905f09a68476d889690a3be40ac32356790cb8.

Teams should also block known vulnerable drivers, limit admin rights and alert on new services that mimic Chrome or VMware files.

Watch SQL Servers closely, because both Lindnor infections were found there. Finally, review any AnyDesk install and any odd Safe Mode registry change.

The post Anubis Ransomware Hackers Deploy New Lindnor Backdoor and 13 Security-Killing Tools in U.S. Attack appeared first on Cyber Security News.

articles.title: Jailbroken DeepSeek AI Agent Breaches European Telecom and Accesses Millions of Patient Records
articles.description:
A jailbroken DeepSeek AI agent spent more than two weeks breaking into a European telecom provider and 13 companies hosted on its systems. It reportedly reached millions of healthcare records along the way. Researchers at Malbear Labs call the campaign “Operation Snowball.” They found it after a routine sweep turned up an open directory holding […]

The post Jailbroken DeepSeek AI Agent Breaches European Telecom and Accesses Millions of Patient Records appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
A jailbroken DeepSeek AI agent spent more than two weeks breaking into a European telecom provider and 13 companies hosted on its systems. It reportedly reached millions of healthcare records along the way.

Researchers at Malbear Labs call the campaign “Operation Snowball.” They found it after a routine sweep turned up an open directory holding the attacker’s full workspace.

Jailbroken DeepSeek AI agent Breach

According to technical research published by Malbear Labs, the open directory needed no password. Inside were about 70 session transcripts, scan results for hundreds of hosts, stolen credentials and database dumps. Everything the operator typed and every report the agents wrote back was in Chinese.

The researchers did not publish the server’s IP address, which protects the victims. They also warn that the operator’s language does not prove nationality or any link to a government.

The setup was a custom agent framework built on DeepSeek Flash, a model with a one-million-token context window. That window let the main agent keep every host, password and failed attempt in memory for days. A human attacker has to re-read notes after each break. This agent did not.

DeepSeek normally refuses to write webshells or guess passwords. The operator got around this with a 78,000-character system prompt. It began with a public jailbreak template called “Little Code Sauce,” which spread through a plugin community on a Chinese forum.

The operator removed its roleplay tricks and added about 400 lines of attack instructions. The prompt told the model that a refusal was a malfunction and gave it a list of refusal phrases to avoid in English and Chinese.

This matches what other teams have seen. Palo Alto’s Unit 42 reported that a hacker named BUGSTER used a jailbroken DeepSeek V4 with the Hermes Agent framework.

That actor stole more than 5,200 records from an Indian university, and the jailbreak was only a simple system-prompt override. You can read our earlier coverage of that case for the full timeline.

The agent ran tasks from scouting to data theft with very little help. It scanned networks, tested passwords, deployed webshells and moved between systems. When defenses blocked it, it changed course.

Reports say it wrote its own replacement tunneling tool and rebuilt an exploit chain against a locked-down Liferay server.

The operator’s messages were very short. One was “Go on,” and another told the agent to close up the latest high-risk hole. The agent chose the target, the flaw and the method. A person running this does not need to understand the techniques.

The harness also scored every break-in, like a game. A pivot into a separate internal network segment earned far more points than a single server shell. Security tools such as firewall consoles also scored high.

At the time of recovery the total was 3,725 points. The scoring shows the operator cared most about the systems that watch and divide a network.

The most worrying finding involves healthcare data. Default login details reportedly gave the agent full database admin access to a TrakCare system running on an old Oracle 9i database.

That exposed millions of records across patient, vaccination and appointment tables. The agent also pulled thousands of rows of subscriber billing and device data and took cryptographic keys from the telecom.

One caution applies. A summary of the report notes that these outcomes were not independently verified in the material available. Treat the exact scale as the researchers’ claim for now.

Even so, the root cause is basic, because an unchanged default password opened the door.

This campaign is not a one-off. CrowdStrike reported that the China-linked group VAPOR PANDA ran the ARTEX framework, mostly on DeepSeek, against more than 200 organizations in at least 14 countries over 11 days starting October 17.

It confirmed access at nine organizations, where the group planted the BLOODALCHEMY backdoor. Telecom providers in the US, Belgium and the Philippines were also hit.

Speed is a big change here. CrowdStrike’s Adam Meyers said human intruders usually run up to 40 commands an hour, while ARTEX activity passed 1,500. Our own report on how ARTEX automates enterprise attacks explains the framework in more detail.

Because no human sits at the keyboard, hunting for working-hours patterns or slow, careful sessions will not help. The agent’s activity is loud and repetitive, so watch endpoint and network logs for fast scanning, bursts of failed logins and unusual tunnels.

Start with the basics:

  • Change every default password, especially on old database systems.
  • Keep internal network segments truly separate.
  • Place endpoint sensors on servers that seem unreachable from the internet.
  • Keep an eye on open directories and exposed storage.

The lesson is simple. AI did not invent new weaknesses. It found the old ones faster than any team can patch them.

The post Jailbroken DeepSeek AI Agent Breaches European Telecom and Accesses Millions of Patient Records appeared first on Cyber Security News.

articles.title: Hackers Used Default admin:admin Credentials to Exploit ForgeRock RCE and Remotely Unlock Cars
articles.description:
Researchers used default admin:admin credentials as part of a vulnerability chain that let them run code on two automakers’ production ForgeRock servers and remotely unlock connected cars. Found in early 2026 and disclosed on November 7, the flaws also exposed vehicle locations and supported remote engine commands. The findings came from controlled security research, not […]

The post Hackers Used Default admin:admin Credentials to Exploit ForgeRock RCE and Remotely Unlock Cars appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
Researchers used default admin:admin credentials as part of a vulnerability chain that let them run code on two automakers’ production ForgeRock servers and remotely unlock connected cars.

Found in early 2026 and disclosed on November 7, the flaws also exposed vehicle locations and supported remote engine commands.

The findings came from controlled security research, not a reported criminal campaign. Both unnamed automakers fixed the issue within about two hours of receiving the report and rotated affected credentials. Their identity systems served multiple regions, but the researchers tested the complete account takeover and vehicle access chain only with US accounts and vehicles.

ForgeRock Attack Chain

The investigation began with the Android apps used by vehicle owners. Both apps relied on ForgeRock Access Management for login sessions and OpenIDM for customer records. Tracing an email validation request led the researchers toward administrative services, including the Apache Felix Web Console running alongside OpenIDM.

A web application firewall blocked direct requests to those services. However, specially encoded paths made requests appear to target static files while Jetty, the backend web server, interpreted them as console requests. This mismatch in URL handling exposed the hidden management interface, where the documented default username and password still worked.

Access to Felix’s ConfigMgr interface allowed the researchers to create an OpenIDM scheduled task that ran Groovy code. They used it to install a small Java component inside the running service, giving them a controlled command endpoint. This confirmed remote code execution within the production identity process rather than inside the cars themselves.

From Server Access to Vehicle Commands

According to the researchers’ technical report, server access exposed administrative credentials that allowed local requests to customer records. The team changed a test account’s email and password, received its verification codes, and completed the normal login process. They then exchanged the session for tokens accepted by the vehicle APIs.

Those tokens exposed the account’s vehicles, location, status, and supported remote controls. With the owner beside the test vehicle, Shah confirmed unlocking, engine start, engine stop, and locking.

Restoring the original email did not cancel the new tokens. The findings follow earlier Kia remote access research and Subaru STARLINK security flaws.

Ping Identity’s production hardening guide already advises removing or protecting the Felix console and changing its default credentials. It also warns that console authentication is separate from IDM authentication. The case shows why blocking administrative URLs at a firewall cannot replace securing the service behind it, especially when that service controls customer identity and access to connected vehicles.

Give your SOC the alert context to stops incidents quickly. Integrate Threat Intel from 16K SOCs.

articles.description:

Sonatype Research Labs confirmed the finding on November 4, 2026, and tracks it as sonatype-2026-010515, with a high severity score of 8.7. PolinRider malware The hijacked packages […]

The post Hackers Hijack 10 npm Packages to Spread PolinRider Malware Using Ethereum Blockchain appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
Attackers have taken over 10 npm packages and slipped hidden code into 12 releases. The code uses the Ethereum blockchain to find a server and download more malware.

Sonatype Research Labs confirmed the finding on November 4, 2026, and tracks it as sonatype-2026-010515, with a high severity score of 8.7.

PolinRider malware

The hijacked packages do very different jobs. Some help with Redux, health APIs and browser activity tracking. Others offer utilities and server examples.

The packages are @adminide-stack/client-redux, @adminide-stack/health-api-server, @adminide-stack/user-activity-browser, @adminide-stack/utils, server-hemera-mongo, cdeops, @adminide-stack/forms-core, @adminide-stack/yantra-help-browser, @cdmbase/wiki-browser and @pubngo-stack/help-browser.

Six releases hide the loader with Base64 and eval(atob(...)). The other six use a character-permutation trick and the JavaScript Function constructor. Sonatype’s full technical write-up lists every affected version. For example, @adminide-stack/utils has two bad builds, 0.0.16-129 and 0.0.16-130, and cdeops has 13.5.31.

According to technical research published by Sonatype Research Labs, each loader asks public Ethereum RPC servers for a transaction sent by one fixed wallet, 0x1eef0849eda15d87f64e51c73c8442cf3c8bcef3. If those servers fail, it falls back to the Blockscout API. The loader reads the first four bytes of the transaction’s recipient address as one IPv4 address and the next four as a backup address.

The malware then pulls XOR-encoded JavaScript from the first address over plain HTTP on port 443. It uses the paths /0x/cls and /0x/ls. The code from /0x/cls runs inside the app with eval and also in a detached node -i process. The code from /0x/ls runs only in the detached process, so it can keep going after the app closes.

This design works like a digital dead drop. The attacker can post a new transaction with a new server address and never touch the npm packages again. Blocking one server does not stop the malware from finding the next one.

Most npm malware runs through a preinstall or postinstall hook, and many teams now turn those off. These packages have no such hooks. The bad code runs when the app loads the package. For server-hemera-mongo, it runs when the service starts, because the code sits in dist/main.js.

Turning off install scripts therefore gives no protection here. A similar trick showed up in earlier PolinRider activity that hid JavaScript loaders in open-source projects, where the loaders also used blockchain services to fetch a second stage. Teams need to ask a simple question: did the package code actually run on a developer laptop, a build server or a live service?

Sonatype found the same wallet in all 12 releases. GitGuardian’s GhostAction and PolinRider report from October 27, 2026 names this exact wallet as the Ethereum resolver in PolinRider loaders found in hacked GitHub repositories. Those older loaders also pulled /0x/cls and /0x/ls on port 443.

The server data points the same way. Greenflagged’s analysis of the npm releases decoded the wallet’s transactions and saw 95.135.181.151 as the advertised server on November 3. GitGuardian had already listed that IP as a fallback server in a PolinRider persistence script.

Researchers still urge care on attribution. Sonatype says the link does not prove PolinRider and GhostAction share one operator. GitGuardian’s working view is that GhostAction’s operator copied a public PolinRider launcher. The GhostAction campaign has hit tens of thousands of GitHub repositories, so the two groups may share many victims.

PolinRider is also older than it first looked. OpenSourceMalware traced PolinRider code to npm packages from May 2025, months before the first known victims in January 2026. That payload included a remote access tool and a Python stealer that went after browsers, wallets, Git and cloud storage.

A report from the Sonatype-linked community write-up says later stages install a Node remote access trojan that persists through startup files for tools such as VS Code, Cursor, Discord and GitHub Desktop.

Start by searching for the 12 bad releases in package-lock.json, yarn.lock, pnpm-lock.yaml, internal mirrors, caches and build records. Remove them and stop mirrors from serving them. Keep a copy for the investigation and move to versions you have checked yourself.

A lockfile entry alone does not prove the code ran. Check which entry point the app loaded, and match it with process and network logs. An import error does not prove safety either, because the bad code may have run before the failure.

If the code ran, treat the host as compromised. Look for detached node -i processes started by another Node process, and for plain HTTP requests to port 443 that use /0x/cls or /0x/ls. Payload requests carry a Sec-V header. It reads A10-npm_inject in the six Base64 releases, A10-II in utils 0.0.16-130 and A10-E in cdeops 13.5.31.

Last, rotate any secrets the affected process could reach. That includes npm publishing tokens, source repository access, cloud keys and CI secrets. The attacker can change the remote JavaScript at any time, so logs, not package lists alone, show what really happened. The Sonatype Guide security event offers further detection help.

articles.title: Google Gemini Safety Bypass Lets Users Download AI-Generated Images That Its Own Filters Blocked
articles.description:
Google Gemini allowed users to download AI-generated images that its safety filters had refused to display, according to research published by Fog Security on November 5, 2026. The bypass did not require a jailbreak. Instead, the download feature sometimes delivered a rejected image while the conversation showed a different, allowed picture. Gemini Image Safety Filter […]

The post Google Gemini Safety Bypass Lets Users Download AI-Generated Images That Its Own Filters Blocked appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
Google Gemini allowed users to download AI-generated images that its safety filters had refused to display, according to research published by Fog Security on November 5, 2026.

The bypass did not require a jailbreak. Instead, the download feature sometimes delivered a rejected image while the conversation showed a different, allowed picture.

Gemini Image Safety Filter Bypass

Fog Security reported the issue to Google in June 2026. By October 22, researchers could no longer reproduce it across 12 new attempts, and older conversations downloaded the correct images.

Google attributed the change to routine maintenance rather than a fix linked to the report. A Gemini web app flaw allowed blocked images to bypass safety refusals through the full-size download path, despite remaining restricted in chat.

Researchers first submitted an image request that triggered a refusal, then requested a different, permitted image. Although the allowed picture appeared onscreen, its download button sometimes retrieved the rejected output.

Results ranged from blurry, unfinished files to complete images, with successful tests across multiple days and sessions. Both image URLs used lh3.googleusercontent.com and required the signed-in user’s session. Inline links ended in =s1024-rj, while download links ended in =s0-d-I.

Researchers suspected a state-management error involving image generation, safety checks, and cleanup. That explanation remains unconfirmed.

A December 2025 Google community report also described downloads returning older images instead of the displayed preview. However, that complaint did not establish a safety bypass.

Unlike prompt injection targeting Gemini’s memory, this issue did not rely on hidden instructions changing the assistant’s behavior.

It also differed from AI jailbreaks using assistant prefill, which push models toward prohibited answers. Here, the refusal remained intact while file delivery failed to enforce it.

Fog Security tested copyrighted characters, a synthetic person, and the researcher’s own likeness. It did not test child safety content or images involving other real people. No access to another user’s data or privilege escalation was reported.

Google initially marked the June 25 report out of scope, then reviewed it after researchers stressed the infrastructure issue. It declined to track an abuse bug on September 30. On October 23, Google said no internal ticket had been filed and closed the report.

Fog Security recommends binding each download to its approved preview and removing files from refused or failed generations. The finding shows why AI safety testing must cover stored files and download links, not only chatbot replies. A refusal protects users only when every delivery path follows the same decision.

CISA added the vulnerability on November 6, 2026, and set a November 20 remediation deadline. Its entry lists ransomware use as unknown and does not require forensic […]

The post CISA Warns of SonicWall SonicOS SSLVPN Vulnerability Exploited in Attacks appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
CISA added a SonicWall SonicOS SSLVPN vulnerability, CVE-2026-19868, to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog, warning that valid-credential users can bypass SAML authentication controls and potentially evade multi-factor authentication.

CISA added the vulnerability on November 6, 2026, and set a November 20 remediation deadline. Its entry lists ransomware use as unknown and does not require forensic triage under Binding Operational Directive 26-04. Organizations should still assess their exposure and follow the required vendor guidance.

SonicWall SonicOS SSLVPN Vulnerability Exploited

The vulnerability affects authentication enforcement in SonicOS SSLVPN. According to the CVE record, someone with valid credentials for an alternate authentication method may bypass the controls applied through SAML. Successful exploitation may also bypass MFA enforced through that SAML login process.

SAML allows an organization to manage sign-ins through a central identity provider. The risk here is that another authentication route may allow access without completing the expected checks. This is not described as a password-free attack. Valid credentials for an alternate method remain required.

The flaw is classified as CWE-308, or use of single-factor authentication. This weakness occurs when a system accepts one authentication factor, such as a password, when it should require additional checks. The result can undermine protection even when administrators believe MFA covers remote access.

The CVE record identifies affected Gen7 and Gen8 platforms running SonicOS 7.3.3-7015 and earlier, and 8.2.2-8015 and earlier, respectively. Cybersecurity News’ earlier SonicWall SSLVPN vulnerability report lists fixed releases as 7.3.4-7013 for Gen7 and 8.2.3-8015 for Gen8, or later supported versions. The reported CVSS score is 7.1.

SonicWall’s warning initially described a report of potential exploitation. CISA’s subsequent catalog entry raises the urgency for defenders.

However, the available information does not identify the attackers, affected organizations, or the number of confirmed incidents. Ransomware involvement should not be presented as established.

Previous SonicWall authentication bypass attacks involved CVE-2024-53704, a separate flaw that allowed session hijacking without authentication. Those attack details should not be applied to this vulnerability, which has different access requirements.

Administrators should check appliance models, firmware versions, SAML settings, and internet exposure before applying the matching update. The SonicWall security advisory should guide deployment decisions. Published coverage lists no workaround, making the firmware upgrade the main remediation step.

Security teams should also review enabled login methods and VPN activity for unexpected access. An MFA setting alone should not be treated as proof that every authentication route enforces the same checks. Confirming those controls after patching helps ensure the intended remote access policy is actually applied.

articles.title: Researchers Uncover NotC2 AI-Powered C2 Framework That Hides Malicious Commands Inside AWS Services
articles.description:
Varonis Threat Labs has built NotC2, a proof-of-concept command-and-control (C2) framework. It runs entirely on native AWS services and uses Amazon Bedrock to turn plain English into cloud commands. It is service abuse, not a flaw in Bedrock, and it only works after an attacker already holds AWS credentials . NotC2 AI-powered C2 framework Classic […]

The post Researchers Uncover NotC2 AI-Powered C2 Framework That Hides Malicious Commands Inside AWS Services appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
Varonis Threat Labs has built NotC2, a proof-of-concept command-and-control (C2) framework. It runs entirely on native AWS services and uses Amazon Bedrock to turn plain English into cloud commands.

It is service abuse, not a flaw in Bedrock, and it only works after an attacker already holds AWS credentials .

NotC2 AI-powered C2 framework

Classic C2 depends on custom servers and protocols that security tools can spot and block. Attackers have long moved away from that model by using trusted platforms such as Telegram, Discord, Slack, Pastebin, GitHub Gists and Google Sheets. Few companies can block these domains without hurting daily work.

Cloud storage follows the same idea. Amazon S3, Google Drive, OneDrive and Azure Blob Storage can all carry commands and stolen data. Cybersecurity News recently reported that attackers are hiding C2 traffic across AWS, Google Cloud, Cloudflare, Microsoft and GitHub.

Much of that traffic travels over port 443, so reputation-based blocking loses its value .

NotC2 did not appear from nothing. Researcher Dhiraj Mishra built XRayC2, which hides commands in AWS X-Ray trace annotations while infected hosts poll the same monitoring API the application already uses. We covered how hackers weaponize AWS X-Ray as a covert command channel in an earlier report .

Rhino Security Labs also showed Cobalt Strike beacons that use S3 objects as the channel. The beacon polls a bucket for task objects and writes results back as response objects. Rhino noted two weak spots in that design. The beacon needs API keys, and constant polling adds delay .

Each of these methods used one AWS service. Varonis asked what would happen if the whole C2 loop ran inside AWS, including the skill normally supplied by a human operator.

According to technical research published by Varonis Threat Labs, the name stands for “notification,” after the service that sends results back, plus “C2.” The loop uses four AWS services, and each one has a clear job.

Amazon SQS is the command input. The attacker’s external server drops messages into a queue, and there is no constant connection to spot. AWS Lambda is the engine.

An event source mapping runs the function for each new message, using the function’s execution role. Each run lasts at most 15 minutes and leaves no lasting process, though it can still appear in cloud logs.

Amazon SNS carries results out. The function publishes output to a topic, and SNS delivers it to the attacker’s HTTPS endpoint once the subscription is confirmed. The Lambda function never contacts the attacker directly.

Amazon Bedrock is the AI interpreter. It reads a request such as “list all running EC2 instances with their IPs” and builds the matching AWS API call .

Normally an operator must know the exact CLI syntax, such as a long aws ec2 describe-instances command with filters and queries. With NotC2, the attacker types a short prompt starting with “ai:” and the model does the rest.

A single generic tool, called execute_aws_operation, accepts a service, an operation and its parameters.

The model can also adapt. If an API call returns an error, the loop feeds it back, and the model can fix the request or suggest a next step. Reconnaissance turns into a chat, with questions like “show me what I have access to.”

The model cannot grant new permissions, but it makes existing access much easier to use. Varonis demonstrated listing EC2 instances, DynamoDB tables, databases and Lambda functions. With enough permissions, an attacker could also delete S3 buckets or EC2 instances.

The whole chain depends on the permissions of the stolen credentials. To deploy, an identity needs sqs:CreateQueue, lambda:CreateFunction, lambda:CreateEventSourceMapping and iam:PassRole for an existing Lambda role. If no suitable role exists, the attacker also needs IAM role and policy rights.

At runtime, the Lambda role needs rights to read and delete queue messages, manage and publish to the SNS topic, subscribe the external endpoint, and call bedrock:InvokeModel. It also needs rights to the target services themselves. Attackers often hunt for these paths with open-source tools such as Pacu, an AWS testing framework from Rhino Security Labs .

Real attackers are already moving this way. A recent LLMjacking case showed stolen cloud keys being used to run up huge model bills . Another report showed attackers targeting AI gateways linked to Amazon Bedrock .

The network signals mostly disappear. There are no odd domains, unknown IPs or custom protocols. The clues sit in the victim’s own cloud logs, including CloudTrail, Lambda logs, SNS delivery logs and Bedrock invocation logs.

CloudTrail records management events by default, but data events need extra setup. CloudTrail also hides SQS and SNS message content, and prompt-level Bedrock detail needs model invocation logging.

Defenders should watch for three signs:

  • An SNS subscription created by a Lambda role that points to an outside HTTP or HTTPS address.
  • A sudden rise in Converse or InvokeModel calls from a role that never used Bedrock.
  • A tight sequence of an SQS message, a Lambda run, Bedrock calls and an SNS publish to an outside subscriber.

Least privilege is the strongest control. Limit who can create queues and functions, set up event source mappings, pass powerful roles to Lambda, call Bedrock and create external SNS subscriptions. Blocking Lambda internet access helps, but it will not stop NotC2 alone, because SNS handles the outside delivery.

Teams should also restrict SNS subscriptions to approved destinations.

NotC2 shows that perimeter-focused security breaks down in serverless setups. With no C2 server to block, defenders must focus on workload identities, service links and unusual behavior. Block any one required step, and the chain fails.

The post Researchers Uncover NotC2 AI-Powered C2 Framework That Hides Malicious Commands Inside AWS Services appeared first on Cyber Security News.

Plex2Shell links four flaws, tracked as CVE-2026-96652, CVE-2026-96654, CVE-2026-96655 and CVE-2026-96656. Together, […]

The post Hackers Exploit Plex2Shell Flaws to Take Over Plex Media Servers and Deploy Crypto Miners appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
Hackers are now using a public exploit chain called Plex2Shell to break into unpatched Plex Media Server systems and install cryptocurrency miners and proxy software. According to SecurityWeek, the attacks began one day after the exploit code went public on October 16, 2026.

Plex2Shell links four flaws, tracked as CVE-2026-96652, CVE-2026-96654, CVE-2026-96655 and CVE-2026-96656. Together, they let a remote user run code on a server without a password.

The code runs with the same rights as the Plex service. Security researcher Zach Main found the bugs and reported them to Plex on July 27. Plex confirmed the report and paid a bounty on August 4.

Hackers Exploit Plex2Shell Flaws

Plex Media Server often listens on port 32400, and many people leave it open to the internet so they can stream from anywhere. That makes it an easy target for anyone scanning for it.

The first flaw is a server-side request forgery bug in the /player/timeline endpoint. The server only checks that a token exists, not that it is valid, so even a fake token works. An attacker can then slip a full web address into the protocol field and trick Plex into sending a request to itself.

That request appears to come from the machine itself, which Plex trusts more. It opens a plugin interface that normally needs no token for local traffic. A broken check in the plugin code lets the attacker call other plugin functions.

The attacker then uses a TVDB plugin function and a web address that starts with 127.0.0.1 but points to a server the attacker controls. Plex sees the local prefix and adds the owner’s admin token to the request. The token goes straight to the attacker.

With the admin token, the attacker changes a transcoder setting so Plex writes a malicious file into its codec folder. The file is hidden inside a video. The next time Plex transcodes a video, it loads that file and runs it. The researcher’s write-up and proof-of-concept code are public on GitHub.

A researcher running a honeypot, a decoy server used to watch attacks, saw the first real exploitation on October 17. The attackers dropped an XMRig-based Monero miner and a Linux proxy tool called “myawesomeproxy.” The Hacker News reports that the miner pointed to a domain tied to the AISURU botnet. The attacks fetched payloads from 217.60.194[.]116.

Cybersecurity News also covered the first exploitation reports. It noted that the evidence did not show how many real servers were hit. The attack is not limited to home servers.

QNAP says some NAS users have been breached, and BleepingComputer reports that CISA added all four flaws to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities list on October 20.

Update to Plex Media Server 1.43.3.10861 or newer, and check the version the server actually reports. Updating will not remove a payload that is already installed. QNAP advises treating an exposed server as compromised, checking for signs of infection, doing a clean reinstall, and resetting credentials.

Stop forwarding port 32400 if you do not need remote access. If you do need it, use a VPN. Also check the Plex process for strange child processes, unknown downloads, and high CPU use. Miners often show up first as a slow, hot server. For another example of how exposed services get turned into miners, see this Redis cryptojacking campaign.

The agency released advisory ICSA-26-307-01 on November 3, 2026. CISA credited Chinmay Patel of Digital Boundary Group and Subnet Solutions with reporting the vulnerabilities. The Canadian vendor […]

The post CISA Warns Two Critical 9.0 Flaws in PowerSYSTEM Center Allow Unauthorized Access and SQL Injection appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
CISA warned that two critical PowerSYSTEM Center flaws (CVSS 9.0) could let authenticated users access administrator resources or execute unauthorized database commands, affecting energy and manufacturing sectors worldwide.

The agency released advisory ICSA-26-307-01 on November 3, 2026. CISA credited Chinmay Patel of Digital Boundary Group and Subnet Solutions with reporting the vulnerabilities.

The Canadian vendor has provided upgrade guidance and temporary measures for organizations that cannot immediately update affected systems.

The first flaw, CVE-2026-63017, involves incorrect authorization, tracked as CWE-863. A user with limited permissions can access resources normally reserved for administrators. In simple terms, signing in with a basic account does not keep the user within the access limits intended for that account.

CISA Warns Critical Flaws in PowerSYSTEM Center

The second flaw, CVE-2026-63774, is an SQL injection vulnerability tracked as CWE-89. Insufficient input checks in the report designer allow an authenticated user to execute unauthorized SQL commands. The disclosed impact concerns database commands, not confirmed operating system code execution.

Both CVSS vectors describe low attack complexity, low privileges, and no required user interaction. They specify an adjacent attack vector rather than unrestricted network access.

CISA states that these vulnerabilities are not remotely exploitable and that no known public exploitation had been reported when the advisory was released.

CVE-2026-63017 affects PowerSYSTEM Center 2020 versions through 5.29.x, PowerSYSTEM Center 2024 versions 6.0.x through 6.2.x, and PowerSYSTEM Center 2026 versions 7.0.x through 7.1.x. CVE-2026-63774 affects the listed 2024 and 2026 ranges. The advisory does not list the 2020 branch as affected by SQL injection.

Subnet Solutions recommends PowerSYSTEM Center 2020 Update 30 for affected 2020 installations. Organizations running the 2024 branch should upgrade to PowerSYSTEM Center 2026 Update 1.1. Existing 2026 installations should also update to Update 1.1, according to CISA’s machine-readable advisory.

Checking installed versions is therefore essential before planning upgrades. Cybersecurity News previously covered CISA’s OT asset inventory guidance, which explains how accurate device and software records support vulnerability management across industrial environments.

For organizations unable to update, Subnet recommends monitoring user activity records and restricting Client Access Server users’ access to browser F12 Developer Tools to reduce authorization-related risk.

For the SQL injection issue, the vendor recommends restricting user access to the report designer. These are interim measures, not replacements for the recommended updates.

CISA also advises keeping control systems off the public internet, placing them behind firewalls, and separating them from business networks.

Where remote access is necessary, organizations should use updated VPNs and assess connected devices. Related secure OT connectivity guidance explains the value of limited exposure and controlled connections.

Before applying changes, operators should assess operational impact and risk. Operators should follow internal response procedures for suspected malicious activity and report it to CISA.

Two GitHub advisories published by maintainer airween on September 30 describe flaws allowing malicious file uploads and server crashes that could lead to remote code execution. ModSecurity inspects web traffic and blocks requests that look […]

The post ModSecurity Patches Two High-Severity Flaws Allowing WAF Bypass and Potential Remote Code Execution appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
Two high-severity flaws have been disclosed in ModSecurity, the open-source web application firewall (WAF) used with Apache, IIS, and Nginx.

Two GitHub advisories published by maintainer airween on September 30 describe flaws allowing malicious file uploads and server crashes that could lead to remote code execution.

ModSecurity inspects web traffic and blocks requests that look harmful. Many sites depend on it, so any gap in how it reads a request matters.

CVE-2026-104269 (GHSA-5pww-8rfg-9crf) affects ModSecurity 3.0.0 and later, allowing unauthenticated network attacks that bypass file checks and compromise integrity no patched version is available.

ModSecurity Patches High-Severity Flaws

The problem is a mismatch in how the firewall and the app read an upload. ModSecurity’s multipart parser does not support RFC 2231, a standard for encoded values in headers. Many app frameworks do. When a request holds both a plain filename and an encoded filename*, those frameworks prefer the encoded one.

An attacker can use this by sending filename=”safe.jpg” together with filename*=UTF-8”shell.php. The OWASP Core Rule Set sees a harmless JPG and lets it through. A Go backend reads the name as shell.php and may save it to disk. If the web server serves that folder, the attacker can run code on it.

The advisory says Go, Python (Flask and FastAPI), Node.js, and Java Spring parsers behave this way. PHP’s native upload handling reads only filename=, so it is not affected. Researchers 0xkalawy and ZeyadZonkorany found the issue, and B0YK4 coordinated the report.

The second flaw is CVE-2026-73857 (GHSA-jx3r-phvx-2jmj), reported by researcher Tobias Klein. A single crafted request from an unauthenticated remote user can make a worker process use an uninitialized pointer. That lets the request write a fixed value to an address the sender picks.

The result can be a crash, a memory leak, or a redirect of program flow, which could lead to remote code execution. The weaknesses are listed as CWE-787 (out-of-bounds write) and CWE-824 (access of uninitialized pointer). Its CVSS vector rates the impact as high for availability only, which my calculation puts near 7.5.

The risk is narrower than it sounds. The bug can be reached only when the SecParseXmlIntoArgs setting is On or OnlyArgs. It is Off by default. The code path was added in version 3.0.15, so 3.0.15, 3.0.16, and the current v3 master are affected. Earlier 3.0.x releases and ModSecurity v2 are not.

There is one point to check. The advisory lists 3.0.17 as the patched version, but its text also says a fix is “not yet” available and will come in the next release. Admins should confirm the release on the official project page before assuming they are safe.

For the XML flaw, make sure SecParseXmlIntoArgs is Off, which is the workaround the advisory gives. Then upgrade once you confirm the fixed release.

For the filename flaw, no patch is listed, so do not rely on the WAF alone to judge uploads. Apps should ignore the name sent by the client and create their own safe name. They should also block script extensions such as .php and store uploads outside the web root. These steps are general good practice and are not part of the advisory.

ModSecurity has had other bypass problems recently. Cyber Security News has covered earlier ModSecurity firewall bypass bugs and multiple ModSecurity rule bypass flaws.

articles.description:
Microsoft says threat actors are using an AI tool called ARTEX to find secrets in public GitHub code and use them against cloud accounts. In one case, the AI agent went from searching GitHub to pulling data from Azure Key Vault in only five minutes. ARTEX AI Azure Key Vault secrets Searching public code for […]

The post Hackers Use ARTEX AI to Steal Azure Key Vault Secrets Just 5 Minutes After Scanning GitHub appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
Microsoft says threat actors are using an AI tool called ARTEX to find secrets in public GitHub code and use them against cloud accounts.

In one case, the AI agent went from searching GitHub to pulling data from Azure Key Vault in only five minutes.

ARTEX AI Azure Key Vault secrets

Searching public code for passwords and keys is an old trick. It was slow because a person had to find the repositories, read the code and test each secret by hand. Microsoft Threat Intelligence now reports that agentic AI tools remove much of that delay.

The agents scan many repositories at once, read the results and carry on with the next steps without a human at the keyboard.

Starting in August 2026, the threat actors sent large numbers of search queries to GitHub. The queries often held the name of a target company, a word linked to secrets, a cloud service term, or the name of another AI provider. The goal was to find application credentials, cloud keys and AI API keys that developers had left in code.

ARTEX is the framework behind much of this work. It was built as a penetration testing tool, but criminals and state-linked groups have picked it up.

Our earlier report on how ARTEX automates enterprise intrusions at machine speed explains how its AI agents plan tasks, run tools and decide what to do next.

According to technical research published by Microsoft, the second stage began as early as October 28, 2026. Microsoft saw successful service principal sign-ins from the IP address 199.19.77[.]84 across several application IDs.

A service principal is the identity an app uses to sign in, so a stolen app secret lets an intruder act as that app. In some cases, a vendor-owned multitenant app was compromised and then used to reach many downstream customers.

Once inside, the agents listed subscriptions, resource groups, permissions and AI model deployments. They went after operations that return credentials, such as storage account keys, App Service settings, connection strings and Kubernetes user credentials.

Some compromised apps also reached SharePoint and OneDrive, downloaded files and searched content through Microsoft Graph.

The agents also seemed to learn from their mistakes. When a cloud request failed with an HTTP 400 error, the tool changed the API version or method and tried again. One Key Vault request was rerun about 28 seconds after it failed, and the retry worked.

The agents also used the Azure Run Command feature to run scripts on virtual machines, which can expose stored credentials or give the intruder a way to stay in.

Microsoft says its findings overlap with work from security firm Todyl. Todyl’s investigation found about 45 app registrations at roughly 18 organizations. It says the actor reached 27 organizations, including clients of managed service providers.

It also reports 81 downloaded files and about 2,279 mailbox items accessed, and says these numbers are a minimum.

Todyl also saw scripted sign-ins in bursts of up to 24 in 10 seconds. Microsoft named two more IP addresses. The address 65.87.223[.]26 showed shell commands hidden in a user agent and attempts to get App Service tokens.

The address 157.22.126[.]128 scouted AI workloads on Azure AI services. Microsoft also listed 199.19.77[.]18 as a Tor exit node that may bring unrelated noise.

Our coverage of stolen Entra ID and Azure DevOps credentials gives more background on the MSP side of this campaign. The agents showed a clear interest in AI service keys and in apps with access to Foundry Tools. Todyl noted that one partner saw thousands of dollars in AI usage charges in about 10 minutes.

The first rule is simple. A secret that was ever public must be treated as stolen. Microsoft stresses that deleting the code does not fix the problem, because old copies can remain in edit history, caches and archives. Rotate the key at once and check how it was used.

GitHub secret scanning checks full Git history and can warn you when a key leaks. Its public monitoring option also watches for secrets leaked by your staff in public repositories outside your own. Teams on Azure DevOps can turn on secret scanning and push protection to block secrets before they are pushed.

Microsoft also advises moving apps away from client secrets and toward managed identities, which remove the risk of secrets sitting in code. Other steps include least privilege for service principals and Defender for Cloud plans for Key Vault, Storage and Resource Manager.

Teams can also use Conditional Access for workload identities and block 199.19.77[.]84/32 as a named location. Block that exact address and not the whole network range.

Defenders should check Entra service principal and non-interactive sign-in logs for 199.19.77[.]84 and 199.19.77[.]18. Error codes AADSTS7000215 and AADSTS7000222 mean someone holds a credential for your app, and a failure followed by a success is urgent. Look back to at least October 28 and as far as log retention allows.

Because the agents change IP addresses and user agents fast, behavior is a better clue. Watch for one address signing in to three or more service principals, or one app asking for tokens across Resource Manager, Key Vault, Storage and Graph within minutes.

Microsoft also suggests honeypots and decoys to pull AI agents toward worthless targets. Our report on ARTEX-linked ConnectWise tenant targeting shows how fast these tools can move across many tenants.

The post Hackers Use ARTEX AI to Steal Azure Key Vault Secrets Just 5 Minutes After Scanning GitHub appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
Hackers are spreading a Python-based malware kit called ArmorSteal through fake software download pages. The kit steals passwords, crypto wallets and Discord accounts, and it also mines Monero in the background.

Seqrite Labs found a newer build of the kit on an infected Windows machine and rebuilt its full logic.

ArmorSteal malware

ArmorSteal reaches victims through search results. Zscaler ThreatLabz reported on 22 October 2026 that the operators built fake sites posing as the Chocolatey package manager and the Microsoft Activation Scripts tool.

People who search for install steps land on lookalike domains such as choclatey[.]org and massgravel[.]net. The page tells them to paste a PowerShell command.

The command does install the real tool, so everything seems normal. In the background, it also drops the malware into C:\Windows\SystemHealth\Update, a name picked to look like a normal Windows folder.

This tactic is not new. Cyber Security News recently covered how fake software downloads quietly hijack Windows PCs and turn them into a source of income for attackers.

According to technical research published by Seqrite Labs, the team noticed three scheduled tasks named SysCheck2, SysCheckX and SysHeal, all pointing at that folder. The kit ships with its own copy of Python 3.11, so it runs on any Windows machine.

Every script is protected with the trial version of PyArmor, which leaves nothing readable on disk. The trial runtime carries its decryption key, so researchers could unpack every script with the open-source Pyarmor-Static-Unpack-1shot tool.

SysCheck2 starts the main controller, SysMon.py, at every logon through a hidden console. SysCheckX launches the miner manager, xm_handler.py, as SYSTEM 45 seconds after boot.

SysHeal is new in this build and ran the controller once as SYSTEM on 27 September 2026. Each part holds its own list of command servers, so killing one process does not stop the others.

The controller builds a victim ID from the motherboard serial number. It then tries 11 domains in order, including pymons[.]is, workerstats[.]net and datamons[.]org.

The domain seen on the infected machine was only seventh in the list, so blocking it alone does very little. Zscaler’s build had only four domains, which shows the operators keep growing the setup.

Before it does anything visible, the malware checks its network owner through ipinfo.io. If the owner is Google, Amazon, Microsoft or Azure, it shows a fake “Memory is insufficient” error and quits.

Many sandboxes run on those clouds, so they never see the payloads. The malware also runs code from the server only if it carries a valid signature from the attacker’s RSA-2048 key. Nobody else can take over the botnet, even if they seize a domain.

The miner manager downloads xmrig-v4-3333.zip, checks its SHA-256 hash and unpacks it. Seqrite could not see the coin or wallet because the zip was gone, but the older build mined Monero. Every minute, the script adds C:\Windows as a Defender exclusion, which hides the whole kit from scanning. That exclusion stays behind even after cleanup.

The best trick is how the miner avoids notice. Once a second, it looks for 20 monitoring tools, including Task Manager, Process Explorer, Process Hacker and Wireshark. If one is open, the miner shuts down at once, so a user checking why the fan is loud sees a quiet machine.

Mining restarts about a second after the tool closes. If xmrig.exe is removed, the script waits longer before each reinstall, from 2 minutes up to 6 hours, to avoid repeated alerts. On the infected machine, only the WinRing0x64.sys driver was left behind.

A similar driver showed up in a registry-hidden XMRig campaign we covered in September.

The spy module, basrq.py, logs every key along with the window title, so each password can be matched to a site. It checks the clipboard twice a second and swaps copied crypto addresses for the attacker’s.

Nine address types are covered, including Bitcoin, Ethereum, Solana and Monero. It also takes in-memory screenshots when chosen keywords appear. Extra scripts show fake Exodus, MetaMask and Phantom alerts, such as “You received 18.2 SOL”, to push victims into unlocking their wallets while the keylogger runs.

The stealer, got.py, takes Discord tokens from four Discord apps and 18 Chromium-based browsers. A token lets an attacker sign in without the password or 2FA. It copies data from about 20 wallet extensions and 13 desktop wallets.

It also scans every drive for BIP-39 seed phrases and zips matches as seeds.zip. To get around Chrome’s App-Bound Encryption, it downloads the public ChromElevator tool, which the author says exists for research.

It also hunts for vaults from KeePass, 1Password, Bitwarden, Dashlane, RoboForm and Enpass. This browser-protection bypass is spreading, as in the Marsalek malware hidden in fake game cheats.

When Seqrite checked on 31 October 2026, only pymons[.]is and datamons[.]org still resolved. Datamons[.]org shows a bland decoy page for “SPC Data Services.”

File hashes are a weak signal, because each PyArmor rebuild changes them. Look for behavior instead, such as Python running from under C:\Windows, launched by scheduled tasks, adding Defender exclusions and starting a miner.

Defenders should hunt for the SysCheck2, SysCheckX and SysHeal tasks and the SystemHealth\Update folder. They should also remove any Defender exclusion for C:\Windows and block all 11 domains, not just one.

Users should never paste PowerShell commands from search results and should type official URLs by hand. Anyone who ran such a command should treat their passwords, tokens and wallet seeds as stolen and change them from a clean device.

The post Hackers Deploy ArmorSteal Malware Through Fake Software Downloads to Steal Credentials and Mine Crypto appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
Veeam warned that a critical Linux kernel flaw with a CVSS score of 9.8, could cause denial of service or memory corruption across backup and recovery products.

Veeam’s November 6 impact statement identified a Linux kernel use-after-free vulnerability (CVE-2026-98432) in TCP/IPv4 connection setup and outlined update paths for affected systems.

Its security advisory does not report active exploitation or confirm remote code execution. The stated risks could interrupt backup and restore work if an affected appliance becomes unavailable.

Affected products include Veeam Software Appliance 13.1 and Veeam Infrastructure Appliance 13.1. Infrastructure roles include backup proxies, hardened repositories, mount servers, gateways, and Cloud Connect components. Workers deployed through Veeam hypervisor plug-ins also need the updated kernel.

Veeam Warns Critical Linux Kernel Flaw

Windows-based Veeam Backup & Replication installations also require attention because they deploy Linux helper appliances. These support file recovery, virtual labs, and cloud restores. The advisory lists affected helper appliances in versions 13.1 and 12.3, rather than identifying the Windows kernel as vulnerable.

The disclosure follows separate Veeam authorization bypass fixes and earlier Backup & Replication security updates. Those issues have different causes and patch requirements, so administrators should not assume earlier product updates resolve this kernel flaw.

Veeam says a patched kernel has been available for Software Appliance and Infrastructure Appliance 13.1 since November 2. The fixed package is 5.14.0-570.60.1+27.2.el9_6_ciq, delivered through Veeam Updater.

Administrators can install available updates from the Veeam Host Management console without waiting for the automatic schedule. A restart may be required.

The updater checks repositories every 12 hours. Under default settings, mandatory updates install on the nearest Sunday at 14:00 in the backup server’s time zone.

Teams should check update history to confirm installation. Systems using a local repository mirror receive the package only after that mirror synchronizes.

For Windows deployments, the 13.1 private fix requires Backup & Replication 13.1.2.57. Repacked 13.1.2 installation media includes the fix.

Veeam’s November 6 advisory says the private fix for version 12.3 will become available soon. Temporary helper appliances receive updated images when deployed again.

At the same time, persistent virtual labs and Microsoft Azure helper appliances must be redeployed. Replace recovery media created before the update. Hypervisor plug-in workers receive the updated kernel on their next launch.

AWS, Azure, and Google Cloud plug-in appliances receive Ubuntu kernel updates through Veeam Updater. Administrators should install available updates and review the Ubuntu CVE tracker for package status.

Veeam Kasten container images do not include a kernel, but their Kubernetes nodes still need vendor checks. Customer-managed Linux proxies, repositories, and gateways also require distribution updates. Completing these separate checks helps teams avoid leaving recovery components unpatched after updating the main appliance itself.

The post U.S. Agencies Warn of Hackers Targeting Industrial Refrigeration to Disrupt Food and Medicine Storage appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
CISA, FBI, HHS, USDA, and DOT have warned that hackers are targeting industrial refrigeration and cold chain monitoring systems worldwide, putting food, medicine, and other temperature-sensitive goods at risk.

The November 5, 2026, warning urges operators to secure exposed controllers before attackers can change temperatures, damage equipment, or disrupt storage operations.

The joint federal fact sheet also includes the Department of Health and Human Services, the Department of Agriculture, and the Department of Transportation. It covers systems widely used in healthcare, chemicals, food production, agriculture, and transport, including refrigerated delivery services.

The agencies identified malicious activity targeting electronic temperature controllers and commercial refrigeration controllers in grocery stores and cold storage facilities.

Attackers may exploit unpatched software, weak settings, or internet-accessible devices to gain remote access and change how cooling equipment operates. The fact sheet describes three possible entry points, including authentication bypass, arbitrary code injection, and weak configurations.

CISA, FBI Warn of Refrigeration System Threats

Authentication bypass lets attackers bypass login checks, while code injection can let them run commands on affected systems. The warning does not name specific attackers, affected vendors, or individual CVEs.

After gaining access, hackers could force refrigeration units into continuous heating or defrost cycles. The resulting temperature changes could ruin stored goods, shorten equipment life, and create fire hazards.

Consumers could also face harm if products reach them after unsafe storage. These are potential effects, not confirmed outcomes across every targeted facility.

Attackers could also cause a denial-of-view condition, leaving operators unable to see current temperatures. This creates a separate risk because staff may lose the information needed to judge whether stored products remain safe.

The warning follows reported supermarket refrigeration attacks across Europe, where altered temperature controls forced retailers to remove chilled and frozen food from sale. However, the federal fact sheet does not explicitly connect its findings to those incidents.

Earlier research into Copeland refrigeration controller flaws also showed how compromised equipment could affect cooling and temperature readings. That research concerns specific products and should not be treated as proof of the entry points used in the current activity.

The agencies recommend removing refrigeration control systems from direct internet access. Where remote access is essential, operators should protect it behind a firewall or edge device and keep that equipment updated.

Dedicated operational technology networks should separate refrigeration devices from business systems. Operators should replace default passwords, enforce strong credentials, and use phishing-resistant multifactor authentication wherever possible.

Firmware updates remain essential, alongside plans to retire equipment that no longer receives vendor support. Limit access to approved devices and IP addresses. Facilities should maintain tested offline backups, review logs, and collect network traffic where controller logs are unavailable.

Safe temperature limits and alerts for unexpected changes can help staff detect dangerous conditions. U.S. organizations should report suspicious activity to CISA, their local FBI office, or the FBI’s Internet Crime Complaint Center.
