articles.description:
Google has released its November 2026 Android security update, addressing more than 200 vulnerabilities across the operating system, kernel, and hardware components. Published on November 2, the bulletin includes critical remote code execution flaws that require no user interaction. Devices with security patch level 2026-11-05 or later receive all applicable fixes. The most serious Framework […]

The post Google Patches Over 200 Android Vulnerabilities, Including Critical Zero-Click RCE Flaws appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
Google has released its November 2026 Android security update, addressing more than 200 vulnerabilities across the operating system, kernel, and hardware components.

Published on November 2, the bulletin includes critical remote code execution flaws that require no user interaction. Devices with security patch level 2026-11-05 or later receive all applicable fixes.

The most serious Framework issue, CVE-2026-58868, could allow remote code execution without additional execution privileges. Google lists fixes for Android 14, 15, 16, 16 QPR2, and 17. The lack of required user interaction makes this a zero-click threat, removing the need to persuade someone to open malicious content.

Two other critical remote code execution vulnerabilities, CVE-2026-58876 and CVE-2026-58936, affect the System component across those same Android releases.

Google describes the most severe System issue as requiring neither additional privileges nor user interaction. However, the bulletin does not provide enough technical detail to establish the precise delivery method for each flaw.

These findings follow earlier Android updates addressing remote attack risks, including the September 2026 Android security update. The November bulletin does not state that its newly listed flaws are being exploited. A zero-click vulnerability describes the interaction required for an attack, not proof that attackers have already used it against users.

The update also covers high-severity information disclosure, privilege escalation, and denial-of-service bugs. Android runtime flaw CVE-2026-58988 could expose information locally without additional execution privileges or user interaction.

Other Framework and System entries could allow attackers to gain greater access, expose protected data, or interrupt services, depending on the specific vulnerability.

Android 0-Click Remote Code Execution Flaws

According to Google’s November Android Security Bulletin, the kernel fixes include critical issues affecting Bluetooth, Human Interface Device support, and protected Kernel-based Virtual Machine components.

Google says the most severe kernel vulnerability could enable remote privilege escalation without additional privileges or user interaction, making these fixes important alongside the platform patches.

Hardware coverage extends to Arm, Imagination Technologies, MediaTek, Unisoc, and Qualcomm components. MediaTek’s entries include eight critical modem vulnerabilities, while Qualcomm’s closed-source section contains another critical issue. These findings do not mean every Android phone contains every affected component. Exposure depends on the device’s hardware, software version, and the fixes supplied by its manufacturer.

The bulletin separates fixes into November 1 and November 5 patch levels. The earlier level covers the listed platform issues, while November 5 includes all applicable fixes from both groups and previous bulletins.

Cybersecurity News’ Android security patch guide explains why checking the patch date matters more than simply checking the Android version.

Users should install available manufacturer updates and check Google Play system updates separately. Google lists several affected Mainline components, including Media Codecs, MediaProvider, Telephonycore, and WiFi. Google’s update guidance explains how Pixel owners can check for software updates. Availability varies by device and carrier, so publication does not guarantee immediate delivery to every supported phone.

Google Play Protect remains useful, particularly for detecting harmful apps, but it does not replace operating system patches. Google’s severity ratings also assume platform protections are disabled or successfully bypassed, rather than guaranteeing exploitation on every device. For administrators, the practical priority is confirming supported devices receive the complete applicable November security update.

articles.title: Ransomware Gangs Claim 30% More Victims, but Researchers Warn Some Breaches May Be Fake
articles.description:
The number of organizations named on ransomware leak sites rose 30% in the third quarter of 2026. Researchers say that does not mean attacks rose by the same amount. Most of the growth came from new, unproven groups, and some of their claims may be false. Leak sites are where ransomware gangs post the names […]

The post Ransomware Gangs Claim 30% More Victims, but Researchers Warn Some Breaches May Be Fake appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
The number of organizations named on ransomware leak sites rose 30% in the third quarter of 2026. Researchers say that does not mean attacks rose by the same amount. Most of the growth came from new, unproven groups, and some of their claims may be false.

Leak sites are where ransomware gangs post the names of victims to pressure them into paying. Defenders have long used these posts to count attacks.

Fake or recycled claims are not new, and a past case of fake extortion demands showed that old data can be passed off as a fresh breach. This quarter the problem looks larger.

Analysts at ReliaQuest noted that 43 groups that had never posted before Q3 drove 93% of the increase. Groups active in both Q2 and Q3 added only 1% more named organizations.

The team said it is realistic that some claimed attacks are false allegations. It also said the listings likely mix new attacks, rebrands, recycled data and claims with no proof behind them.

Ransomware Gangs Claim 30% More Victims

The posting patterns of the new groups differ a lot. Some post steadily every week. Others dump dozens of names at once.

A group called “Global Secret Group” listed 48 victims, 28 of them on one day. Another, “crpx0,” listed 47 victims, 41 on a single day, and has not posted since August.

Researchers say bulk releases do not prove the claims are fake. They fit better with data collected in advance than with many separate break-ins.

Other new groups look more like real operations. “Storm” listed 71 victims over 20 days, more than established names like DragonForce (69) and LockBit (62).

But Storm first posted about five weeks after a similarly named group, “Stormous,” made its last post. That timing makes a rebrand possible, though it is unconfirmed.

The clearest example of a doubtful claim is “ExfilSquad,” first seen in July 2026. It released data samples with employee names, email addresses, phone numbers and work locations, plus empty fields and basic customer relationship details.

ReliaQuest says this is low-risk personal data. It does not prove a network breach. The group likely scans GitHub for exposed credentials and takes only what those accounts can reach.

It then uses a ransomware-style leak site to make that limited access look like a major breach. It also posted payment deadlines it did not follow through on, and it listed some targets with no data samples.

The likely real harm is targeted phishing against the named employees, plus the cost of investigating the claim. That is why researchers advise treating each post as an unverified claim.

Recent cases show the same caution, such as the Emperador ransomware group claim against AB InBev, which stayed unverified with no company confirmation.

What Defenders Should Do When Named

When a new group lists your organization, check three things. Was the organization really compromised? Does the evidence match how the group says it got the data? Is the name a distinct group, a rebrand, an affiliate or an opportunistic poster? Paying on a false claim wastes money and funds crime.

Ignoring a real claim can leave exposed data open to phishing and account takeover. ReliaQuest advises teams to review internal logs, access records and any posted samples. If the evidence shows an intrusion, start incident response.

If it does not, keep the claim marked unverified while looking for other sources of exposure. Teams should also record overlaps in tools and infrastructure with known groups, which can point to a rebrand.

Because new names have no history or public indicators, detection should focus on shared behavior. That means abuse of remote services, stolen identities, lateral movement and data theft.

Established groups like Qilin and The Gentlemen show why. Both exploited internet-facing systems, used vulnerable drivers to disable endpoint security tools, and changed Group Policy settings to spread ransomware.

Together they drove about a quarter of listed manufacturing victims. Our earlier look at The Gentlemen ransomware group covers how this affiliate-driven crew grew so fast.

Defenders can block much of this activity. They should patch and monitor edge devices, enforce Microsoft’s vulnerable driver block list, and alert on unexpected Group Policy changes.

The GentleKiller vulnerable driver tool shows how attackers use signed but flawed drivers to shut down security software.

Teams should also audit GitHub and other code repositories for exposed keys and passwords, rotate any they find, and review customer system logs for unusual bulk downloads.

The data also shows ransomware spreading beyond the US. US listings grew 9%, and about 85% of the added victims were elsewhere.

The US share of all listed victims fell from 55% in Q1 to 49% in Q2 and 41% in Q3. Manufacturing victims rose 70%, but professional, scientific and technical services stayed the top sector for the sixth quarter in a row. A lower ranking does not mean lower risk.

articles.title: CISA Warns of WordPress Core Vulnerability Exploited in Attacks to Execute Malicious Code
articles.description:
The U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency has warned that attackers are exploiting a WordPress Core vulnerability that can allow malicious code to run on website servers. CISA added the flaw to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on November 3, 2026, confirming evidence of active exploitation and raising the need for prompt patching. Tracked as […]

The post CISA Warns of WordPress Core Vulnerability Exploited in Attacks to Execute Malicious Code appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
The U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency has warned that attackers are exploiting a WordPress Core vulnerability that can allow malicious code to run on website servers.

CISA added the flaw to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on November 3, 2026, confirming evidence of active exploitation and raising the need for prompt patching.

Tracked as CVE-2026-119977, the vulnerability affects WordPress Core versions 4.7 through 7.1.3 and carries a high severity CVSS score of 8.1. Attackers do not need a valid account or user interaction. However, exploitation requires precise timing during a full WordPress Core upgrade, rather than simply visiting any website running an affected version.

The weakness involves predictable temporary folders created during updates. When WordPress extracts a complete upgrade package, it places files in a staging directory beneath wp-content/upgrade. On affected setups, those files can be reached through the web while the server is still completing the update, briefly exposing a separate copy of the WordPress installer.

An attacker who reaches that installer before cleanup finishes could use it to connect the staged installation to a database they control, creating a path toward server code execution. This is a time-of-check, time-of-use race condition, commonly called TOCTOU. The attack depends on reaching temporary files before WordPress removes them.

The brief opening does not make the flaw harmless. Cybersecuritynews.com’s report on WordPress remote code execution attacks described more than 18,500 requests targeting staged installer paths during the first 21 hours of monitoring. Repeated requests can help attackers catch the short upgrade window, although those requests alone do not prove a successful breach.

WordPress Core Vulnerability Exploited

The official CISA alert confirms exploitation but does not identify the attackers or disclose how many websites were compromised. Its catalog entry gives defenders a stronger reason to prioritize the issue beyond its severity score. CISA also urges organizations outside government to address known exploited vulnerabilities through risk-based patching.

A separate Cybersecuritynews.com report covering more than 60,000 WordPress attack attempts cited 60,471 blocked attempts over 24 hours. That figure measures firewall activity, not unique victims or confirmed infections. Keeping these categories separate is important when judging the scale of a campaign and explaining what monitoring data actually shows.

WordPress released version 7.1.4 on October 28, 2026, to fix the upgrade weakness and other security issues. The official security announcement credits researcher Umut Bayram with reporting the flaw and recommends immediate updates. WordPress also announced backports for eligible older branches, while noting that only its latest release remains actively supported.

Administrators should open the Dashboard, select Updates, and verify that the security release has finished installing. Sites relying on automatic background updates still need that check. Until patching is complete, restricting public web access to the upgrade directory can reduce exposure. A firewall should remain an extra layer of protection, not a replacement for fixing WordPress Core.

Defenders should review server logs for unusual requests to PHP files under wp-content/upgrade and investigate unfamiliar administrator accounts, plugins, or file changes. These checks help identify signs that need further investigation, without treating every blocked request as proof of compromise.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
Every SOC believes its controls work; BAS is the machine that checks. By safely running real attacker techniques against production defenses continuously, not annually these platforms convert “we should be covered” into pass/fail evidence per technique, per control.

The 2026 field spans safe-simulation purists, autonomous-pentest crossovers, and validation suites grading entire kill chains.

Cymulate takes 1; AttackIQ and SafeBreach complete the podium.

Key Takeaways

• 1 overall: Cymulate the broadest usable validation platform from phishing surface to full kill chain.

• Podium: Cymulate (breadth+usability), AttackIQ (ATT&CK-anchored rigor), SafeBreach (attack-playbook depth).

• Category drift: BAS (safe simulation) and autonomous pentesting (Pentera’s real exploitation) are converging into exposure validation know which risk posture you’re buying.

• 2026 theme: validation feeds CTEM BAS results now flow into exposure-management prioritization rather than standalone scorecards.

How We Scored (Methodology)

Research-based evaluation; no lab testing, no paid placement; editorial scores excluded from structured data.

Criteria: technique realism/coverage, production safety, control-integration depth (what it grades and tunes), remediation guidance quality, continuous-operation ergonomics, and pricing accessibility.

Weights: realism/coverage 25%, control integration 20%, remediation value 20%, safety 20%, ergonomics 15%.

The 2026 BAS Power Rankings

*Editorial research-based scores, not lab results.

1. Cymulate — Best Breadth-to-Usability Ratio

Snapshot: Module-based SaaS | Full-kill-chain simulation modules | Exposure-management convergence

Why it earns 1: Cymulate covers the attack surface most platforms sample: email gateway, web gateway, WAF, endpoint, lateral movement, data exfiltration, and full APT kill-chain scenarios, each runnable by a lean team without an offensive-ops background.

Scoring is readable by executives without insulting operators, and results now feed its exposure-management layer validation as an always-on posture gauge rather than a quarterly report.

Pros: Module breadth; operator-friendly ergonomics; kill-chain scenarios; exec-grade reporting.

Cons: Deep custom tradecraft belongs to the playbook specialists.

Bottom line: The most validation per analyst-hour in the category.

2. AttackIQ — Best ATT&CK-Anchored Validation

Snapshot: Platform subscription | MITRE-aligned scenario library | Anatomic/Flex delivery options

Why it ranks here: AttackIQ made ATT&CK the operating system of validation: scenarios mapped tightly to the framework, alignment with MITRE’s own research ecosystem, and reporting that tells you precisely which techniques your EDR missed and which detection gaps to file. Flexible delivery (self-serve to managed) widens who can run it.

Pros: Framework rigor; detection-gap precision; MITRE-ecosystem alignment.

Cons: Framework-first lens suits mature programs best.

Bottom line: ATT&CK coverage, graded honestly.

3. SafeBreach — Best Attack-Playbook Depth

Snapshot: Platform subscription | Largest curated playbook library claim | Breach-studio customization

Why it ranks here: SafeBreach’s moat is its playbook corpus thousands of attack methods curated over a decade, including rapid operationalization of headline threats (new ransomware TTPs simulated within days).

Custom attack composition lets red-minded teams extend it. Where the leaders compete on usability, SafeBreach competes on depth of arsenal.

Pros: Playbook depth; fast new-threat simulation; customization studio.

Cons: Arsenal breadth rewards teams who exploit it.

Bottom line: The deepest safe-attack library on the board.

4. Pentera — Best Real-Exploitation Validation

Snapshot: Per-scope licensing | Autonomous pentesting real exploits, safely orchestrated | Credential/AD attack depth

Why it ranks here: Pentera crosses the line BAS drew: not simulated attacks, but actual exploitation credential theft, relay attacks, AD compromise executed autonomously with production guardrails.

The evidence is unarguable (“we obtained domain admin via this chain”), which transforms remediation meetings. The posture question is whether your change-control culture accepts live exploitation.

Pros: Proof-grade findings; AD/credential depth; automation scale.

Cons: Live-exploitation governance; scope discipline required.

Bottom line: Not simulation the real thing, leashed.

5. Picus Security — Best Detection-Content Remediation

Snapshot: Platform subscription | Simulation + mitigation-content library | SIEM/EDR rule suggestions

Why it ranks here: Picus closes the loop others leave open: every failed simulation ships with vendor-specific remediation the exact signature, rule, or policy to add to your firewall, SIEM, or EDR.

Validation becomes a tuning engine, not a grading exercise. For teams whose bottleneck is “what do we change,” the mitigation library is the product.

Pros: Actionable per-vendor fixes; tuning-loop design; accessible operation.

Cons: Kill-chain scenario depth trails the top three.

Bottom line: The validation platform that hands you the patch.

6. XM Cyber — Best Attack-Path-Centric Validation

Snapshot: SaaS platform | Continuous attack-path modeling | Choke-point remediation math

Why it ranks here: XM Cyber validates by graph: continuously computing how an attacker chains misconfigurations, credentials, and exposures from breach point to crown jewels, then ranking the choke-point fixes that sever the most paths.

It’s exposure validation through the attacker’s route map a different and complementary lens to technique-by-technique BAS.

Pros: Path-chaining insight; choke-point economics; hybrid/cloud coverage.

Cons: Technique-level control grading is the classic-BAS lane.

Bottom line: Validates the routes, not just the walls.

7. Google (Mandiant Validation) — Best Intel-Driven Validation

Snapshot: Platform + intel pairing | Mandiant frontline TTPs as test content | Security-validation lineage (Verodin)

Why it ranks here: The Verodin lineage under Mandiant answers validation’s content question with provenance: test against what Mandiant’s responders saw on breach floors this quarter.

Control validation driven by live adversary intel is the pitch; the platform’s reach is strongest for estates already inside the Google/Mandiant ecosystem.

Pros: Frontline-intel test content; actor-specific validation; ecosystem fusion.

Cons: Standalone-platform momentum versus pure-plays.

Bottom line: Validate against what responders met last month.

8. Keysight — Best Network-Layer Validation

Snapshot: Platform licensing | Threat Simulator + network-test heritage | Traffic-realism depth

Why it ranks here: Keysight validates where its heritage lives the wire: realistic malicious traffic against network controls, IPS/NGFW/sandbox grading, and the packet-level realism a network-equipment-testing lineage buys.

For network-security-heavy estates (carriers, industrials), it’s the specialist layer in a validation stack.

Pros: Traffic realism; network-control depth; test-engineering pedigree.

Cons: Endpoint/identity lanes are others’ home turf.

Bottom line: The wire’s validation specialist.

9. IBM (Randori Lineage) — Best ASM-Fused Offensive Validation

Snapshot: Suite integration | Attack-surface recon + continuous red teaming | IBM security-stack ties

Why it ranks here: The Randori lineage pairs attacker’s-eye attack-surface discovery with continuous automated red teaming
against what it finds validation that starts from your real external exposure rather than a scenario menu.

Now woven into IBM’s portfolio, its edge is the recon-to-attack pipeline; brand-standalone momentum is the honest question.

Pros: ASM-to-attack pipeline; external-exposure realism; IBM integration.

Cons: Portfolio-era roadmap clarity.

Bottom line: Validation that begins where attackers actually start.

10. FourCore — Best Accessible Challenger

Snapshot: Accessible SaaS tiers | ATT&CK-mapped simulations | Lean-team ergonomics

Why it ranks here: FourCore brings BAS economics down-market: ATT&CK-mapped attack simulation, detection grading, and remediation hints at tiers a mid-market budget clears. Library depth and scenario sophistication trail the established arsenal but the alternative at this budget is no validation at all, which this beats decisively.

Pros: Entry economics; ATT&CK mapping; quick setup.

Cons: Arsenal depth versus incumbents.

Bottom line: First validation platform for lean budgets.

Buying Advice: Validate the Validator First

A BAS purchase succeeds when the first ninety days produce fixed controls, not pretty heat maps so structure the pilot as a remediation test.

Run each finalist against the same three control sets (EDR, email gateway, egress filtering), count not the failures found but the failures fixed within thirty days using the platform’s guidance, and grade the guidance’s specificity: “tune your EDR” is marketing, “add this rule” (the Picus pattern) is product.

Decide the simulation-versus-exploitation posture deliberately Pentera-class proof plays politically stronger but needs change-control blessing; safe simulation runs weekly without a meeting.

Check content velocity (days from headline TTP to runnable scenario the SafeBreach race), wire results into your exposure-management or ticketing flow so findings age visibly, and keep one metric sacred: control-failure half-life, the median days a validated gap stays open. That number falling is the entire business case.

FAQs

What are the best BAS tools in 2026? Cymulate for breadth and usability, AttackIQ for ATT&CK rigor, SafeBreach for playbook depth, Pentera for real-exploitation evidence, Picus for actionable fixes, with XM Cyber, Mandiant Validation, Keysight, IBM/Randori, and FourCore by lane.

BAS versus penetration testing? Complementary: pentests bring human creativity annually; BAS brings machine consistency continuously mature programs run both, with BAS catching the drift between tests.

Is it safe to run attack simulations in production? Classic BAS is engineered production-safe (benign payloads, simulated actions); exploitation-class tools (Pentera, Randori lineage) execute real techniques under guardrails and deserve change-control governance.

How often should simulations run? Continuously for core controls (weekly scheduled), plus event-driven runs after every control change and headline threat the value is trend lines, not snapshots.

What’s the key BAS metric? Control-failure half-life: median days from validated gap to confirmed fix falling half-life proves the program works.

Verdict

Ten platforms, one conversion: assumptions into evidence. Cymulate for the broadest usable sweep, AttackIQ for framework truth, SafeBreach for arsenal depth, Pentera for proof nobody argues with, Picus for the fix in hand, XM Cyber for the routes, Mandiant for frontline content, Keysight for the wire, Randori’s lineage for the attacker’s start line, FourCore for the first budget run them against your real controls, fix what fails, and watch the half-life fall.

articles.description:
Hackers are expanding information theft beyond saved passwords, targeting authentication tokens and session data stored by ChatGPT, Claude, Codex, and other AI tools. Two Windows malware families, WardenStealer and Aoki, collect credentials that may remain usable after a password reset, leaving victims exposed even after they believe their accounts are secured. The post Hackers Use New Infostealer Malware to Steal ChatGPT, Claude, and Codex Tokens That Survive Password Resets appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
Hackers are expanding information theft beyond saved passwords, targeting authentication tokens and session data stored by ChatGPT, Claude, Codex, and other AI tools.

Two Windows malware families, WardenStealer and Aoki, collect credentials that may remain usable after a password reset, leaving victims exposed even after they believe their accounts are secured.

The danger extends beyond unauthorized chatbot access. Developers often connect AI assistants to source repositories, cloud services, and build pipelines.

Stolen credentials and configuration files can expose those connections, while valid sessions let criminals act as authenticated users without repeating the normal login process or facing a fresh multifactor authentication challenge.

Researchers from SpyCloud identified this activity by examining recovered infection logs, rather than relying only on malware advertisements or code analysis.

In its October 30 research report, the company reported more than 130,000 unique WardenStealer infections since first observing the family on August 3, 2026.

Hackers Use New Infostealer Malware

WardenStealer is a Rust-based Windows infostealer sold through a malware-as-a-service model. Alongside browser passwords, cookies, messaging data, and cryptocurrency information, it collects files belonging to locally installed AI applications.

Earlier reporting on Warden Stealer distribution methods described ClickFix lures, malicious advertisements, cracked software, and fake game cheats used to spread the malware.

SpyCloud found Claude Code credentials containing OAuth access tokens, refresh tokens, and authentication material for connected Model Context Protocol servers.

Other stolen files included account identifiers and standing instructions used by the assistant. Codex authentication data contained an OpenAI API key alongside access and refresh tokens, while Claude Desktop yielded configuration and usage information.

These items serve different purposes. Access tokens authorize requests, refresh tokens can obtain replacement access tokens, and API keys allow software to use paid services.

Changing a password does not necessarily invalidate every credential already issued. The practical response therefore requires revocation, not simply another password change; validity depends on the provider, token type, and account controls.

Aoki takes a more clearly organized approach, placing stolen AI material in a dedicated collection category. SpyCloud observed data associated with ChatGPT, Claude Code, Claude Desktop, Codex, GitHub Copilot, and Cursor.

Previous coverage of Aoki AI credential theft likewise described its growing interest in locally stored AI authentication files and session data. Some recovered files contained cookies for authenticated desktop application sessions.

Reusing a valid cookie can let an attacker resume an existing session without entering the password or completing the MFA check required for a new login. This is endpoint credential theft, not evidence that ChatGPT, Claude, or Codex suffered a service-side breach.

Stolen AI Access Creates Financial and Enterprise Risks

The stolen material already has buyers. SpyCloud observed underground offers advertising AI subscriptions and API credit at steep discounts, including $100 of claimed Codex or Claude API credit for $8.94.

Researchers cautioned that they could not establish whether every advertised credential came from malware rather than phishing, exposed secrets, or fraudulent registrations.

This market supports LLMjacking, where criminals consume AI services using someone else’s account.

Reporting on AI token jacking risks explains how compromised keys can feed illicit proxy services and leave victims facing unexpected charges. SpyCloud also observed wholesale services offering suppliers commissions when uploaded keys generated billable usage.

For businesses, configuration theft adds another concern: attackers can learn which services an assistant reaches and how the developer works.

Earlier research into AI coding agent theft highlighted how saved connections, prompt histories, and project context can reveal internal systems. Exposure depends on what files were collected and which associated credentials remain valid.

Incident responders should include AI credentials in every developer-device infostealer investigation. Revoke active sessions, rotate exposed API keys and tokens, and review unusual API consumption.

Check connected services as well: replacing an AI account password does not automatically resolve every secret or authorization copied from the infected endpoint.

articles.title: Hackers Use Fake Software Downloads to Secretly Hijack Windows PCs and Monetize Their Resources
articles.description:
Hackers are using fake software downloads to quietly turn Windows computers into revenue sources, installing programs that share internet bandwidth, run computing workloads, or deliver unwanted utilities. The campaign targets people searching for cracked commercial software, free games, activation tools, plugins, and unofficial applications, hiding extra installations behind what appears to be an ordinary setup […]

The post Hackers Use Fake Software Downloads to Secretly Hijack Windows PCs and Monetize Their Resources appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
Hackers are using fake software downloads to quietly turn Windows computers into revenue sources, installing programs that share internet bandwidth, run computing workloads, or deliver unwanted utilities.

The campaign targets people searching for cracked commercial software, free games, activation tools, plugins, and unofficial applications, hiding extra installations behind what appears to be an ordinary setup process.

Rather than delivering one payload, the installers can attempt several installations during the same session. Each component becomes a separate opportunity to monetize the device.

The approach reflects a wider problem seen in fake software installer campaigns, where familiar installation screens can conceal background activity that users never knowingly approved.

Microsoft researchers identified the evolving campaign and documented three confirmed installation branches in their November 3 technical analysis.

These delivered WorldProxyPool proxy software, CharityEngine and BOINC distributed-computing components, and Advanced Windows Manager utilities.

Microsoft stressed that legitimate software can create security and privacy risks when installed through deceptive bundles without informed consent.

Hackers Use Fake Software Downloads

The attack begins when someone launches a download advertised as a game, cracked application, audio plugin, or utility.

Observed lures included Echo Client, FabFilter Total Bundle, Navicat Premium cracks, Roblox executors, and mobile-unlock tools. These names describe the campaign’s disguises, not evidence that the genuine products were compromised.

The installer then launches temporary processes through an Inno Setup-style wrapper and starts numbered payload stages.

Previous reporting on abuse of Inno Setup shows how attackers can exploit a familiar installation framework to hide additional execution. Here, the wrapper coordinates multiple downstream packages instead of simply installing the application the user expected.

The delivery system calls these packages “offers.” It contacts changing internet infrastructure to select payloads and report installation outcomes, using session and affiliate-related values to connect events.

Crucially, each offer can succeed or fail independently. A blocked component therefore does not prove that the entire installation chain stopped or that the computer remained unaffected.

WorldProxyPool provides the bandwidth-monetization branch, routing third-party internet traffic through affected devices. Its installation creates three scheduled tasks running as SYSTEM: one starts the agent at boot, another runs a hidden PowerShell watchdog every five minutes, and a third checks for updates hourly.

Similar fake downloads installing proxyware illustrate why unauthorized network sharing deserves attention alongside more familiar malware threats.

The computing branch installs CharityEngine, BOINC, and supporting components, including VirtualBox. Microsoft observed computing workloads, capability checks, and communication with CharityEngine infrastructure.

This is resource hijacking, but the report does not establish cryptocurrency mining. Separately, the utility branch installs Advanced Windows Manager and updater-style software through the same delivery system, extending the bundle beyond network and computing-resource abuse.

Detecting Resource Hijacking and Blocking Unwanted Installations

The strongest detection approach connects installation activity, outbound requests, new software, and persistence changes rather than relying on a single filename or domain.

Microsoft noted that callback domains rotate frequently, while the broader execution pattern remains consistent. Analysts should examine the complete installer session because reporting requests may occur after, or around the time, child payloads start.

Defenders should review unexpected scheduled tasks, especially those running as SYSTEM, and investigate software that users did not intentionally install.

Earlier research into malware delivering BOINC clients provides useful context, although Microsoft’s report does not establish a connection between those operations.

A legitimate component’s presence alone is not proof of compromise; its installation history and surrounding behavior matter.

Microsoft recommends avoiding cracked software and unofficial download sources, enabling potentially unwanted application protection, and keeping cloud-delivered antivirus, tamper protection, and reputation-based checks active.

Organizations can also evaluate attack surface reduction rules that restrict untrusted executables. These controls address the central weakness exploited here: users approving an apparently useful download without understanding the additional software it installs.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
Hackers are abusing stolen Microsoft Entra ID application credentials and Azure DevOps identities to access Microsoft 365 and Azure environments, reaching at least 27 organizations.

Todyl’s latest investigation update describes an ongoing campaign targeting managed service providers (MSPs) and their customers since November 1, 2026.

The operator targeted about 45 app registrations across roughly 18 organizations, with more than 33 authenticating successfully. Downstream access expanded the victim count to government, energy, agriculture, transportation, construction, legal, education, and nonprofit organizations. These figures cover only environments sending logs to Todyl, so the actual reach could be wider.

Investigators recorded searches across about 25 tenants, downloads of 81 files, and access to approximately 2,279 mailbox items. The latest reported attempt, at 21:31 UTC on November 3, was blocked. No Microsoft vulnerability was involved. Instead, the attacker used valid credentials to act as trusted applications.

This distinction matters because application identities operate without a user signing in. Their existing permissions can allow access without an MFA prompt, while user-focused Conditional Access policies do not govern app-only authentication. Cybersecurity News previously covered how stolen credentials and excessive permissions can turn limited access into broader exposure.

The attacker also used an Azure DevOps federated workload identity and replayed user session tokens. How the attacker stole the original credentials remains unknown. Todyl found no evidence that a vendor platform was compromised, even though credentials belonging to trusted security integrations were among those abused.

Attack Moves Through Cloud Environments

According to Todyl’s investigation, the operator typically requests an Azure Resource Manager token, followed by tokens for Key Vault, Microsoft Graph, and Storage. This sequence gives investigators a useful pattern to hunt, particularly when previously unused applications begin authenticating shortly afterward.

The latest update describes 29 wildcard Microsoft Graph searches followed by SharePoint downloads at roughly one file per second. Collected material included password lists, private keys, VPN profiles, backup credentials, and remote access settings. Such files could enable further attacks beyond Microsoft 365, where Todyl’s cloud logs provide limited visibility.

MSP relationships increased the damage. One multi-tenant application reached 15 customer tenants in repeated loops of about 10 seconds. The broader risk resembles earlier reporting on compromised accounts reaching Azure DevOps and cloud resources, although that case involved a different intrusion.

Scripted clients accounted for 95% of observed sign-ins, with bursts reaching 24 attempts in 10 seconds. However, long pauses and changing browser signatures suggest human control.

Todyl describes automation, not confirmed self-spreading malware. AI involvement remains a low-confidence possibility, and the operator has not been identified.

Defenders should review service-principal sign-ins and non-interactive user logs for 199.19.77.84, the confirmed source address. Failed attempts matter alongside successful ones. Todyl recommends blocking the exact address rather than its entire hosting network, where unrelated activity exists.

Response should include disabling affected applications where needed, removing compromised credentials, revoking user sessions, and rotating secrets in accessible vaults and documents.

Workload-specific Conditional Access has licensing and coverage limits, so user policies alone are insufficient. MSPs should also review delegated customer access, preserve audit logs, and notify affected clients.

articles.title: Hackers Use OpenAI Codex Jailbreak Toolkit That Secretly Injects Ads Into AI Responses
articles.description:
A jailbreak toolkit targeting OpenAI Codex is doing more than trying to bypass AI safety rules. The Chinese-language package, called Haiou, changes the coding agent’s trusted instructions so that ordinary greetings trigger advertisements for a third-party AI gateway. Researchers describe the behavior as prompt adware because it persists through written instructions rather than a conventional […]

The post Hackers Use OpenAI Codex Jailbreak Toolkit That Secretly Injects Ads Into AI Responses appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
A jailbreak toolkit targeting OpenAI Codex is doing more than trying to bypass AI safety rules. The Chinese-language package, called Haiou, changes the coding agent’s trusted instructions so that ordinary greetings trigger advertisements for a third-party AI gateway.

Researchers describe the behavior as prompt adware because it persists through written instructions rather than a conventional executable advertising payload.

The discovery shows how installing an unofficial AI enhancement can change future responses without requiring a flaw in the underlying model.

Haiou combines security-focused capabilities with promotional instructions, turning a tool marketed for unrestricted technical work into a distribution channel for its creator’s service.

Its presence alongside hacking tools also shows that such packages have entered real cybercrime workflows. Check Point researchers identified the adware behavior while investigating a threat actor’s misconfigured webserver.

Their November 3 technical report describes an exposed Cobalt Strike server whose logs showed compromises of private computers belonging to Chinese-speaking individuals.

The server also hosted Ladon, VulnClaw, and Haiou. Researchers found no evidence connecting the jailbreak’s author to cybercrime, an important distinction between observed use and proven intent.

Hackers Use OpenAI Codex Jailbreak Toolkit

Check Point analyzed Haiou version 4.5.0, distributed through GitHub as a local Codex enhancement. Instead of exposing readable prompts throughout the repository, the package ships encrypted content.

Its Windows, Linux, and macOS launchers verify Ed25519 signatures and SHA-256 hashes, then decrypt the payload using an embedded AES-256-GCM key before extracting a ZIP archive.

That packaging makes casual inspection harder, although encryption alone does not prove malicious intent. The extracted material contains modular prompts and six security-related skills covering penetration testing, reverse engineering, license cracking, memory analysis, and game security.

Like other prompt injection attack techniques affecting AI agents, Haiou relies on written instructions to redirect model behavior rather than exploiting a memory corruption vulnerability.

Its jailbreak modules use role-playing, refusal suppression, and requests framed as educational capture-the-flag exercises. Other instructions discourage asking for authorization or setting boundaries before acting.

These are attempts to weaken safeguards; the report does not establish that every technique reliably bypasses every model or security restriction.

The advertising rule sits inside the identity prompt module. When users enter specified greetings or activation words, the agent is told to return only a fixed promotional message.

This resembles trigger activated prompt injection methods in which planted rules remain inactive until a matching condition appears, making a harmless greeting the entry point for an unwanted response.

Another module labels the promoted gateway “protected infrastructure” and forbids offensive testing against it, even when users claim authorization.

The package also includes an uninstaller that restores original configurations and removes the advertisement. These details show that persistence depends on installed agent instructions rather than an irreversible model change.

AI Gateway Risks and Investigation Indicators

The advertised service is an OpenAI-compatible gateway positioned between applications and model providers. Check Point found no indication that this particular gateway was malicious.

Its assessment instead suggests that the freely available jailbreak likely helps attract customers to a paid service. The report does not establish credential theft, data theft, or malicious tool execution by this gateway.

The wider concern is trust. Coverage of malicious AI marketplace skills has documented how agent extensions can influence recommendations and abuse trusted sessions.

Haiou demonstrates a narrower outcome: persistent advertising through global instructions. Developers should therefore review prompt changes, installed skills, and gateway settings before trusting enhancement bundles, rather than treating readable instructions as harmless configuration.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
Hackers are stealing access to corporate large language models and reselling it, leaving victims with cloud bills reaching $1 million. Mandiant investigated multiple incidents during 2026 where unauthorized AI use generated more than $100,000 in charges in a single day, showing how quickly stolen credentials can become a major financial loss.

Google Threat Intelligence Group (GTIG) detailed the activity in research published November 2. The attacks affected financial services, retail, technology, and transportation organizations across North America, South America, and Asia Pacific. Known as LLMJacking, the technique targets paid AI resources rather than using stolen computing power to mine cryptocurrency.

The main entry point was exposed or stolen cloud credentials, including service account keys, GitHub personal access tokens, and active session tokens. Previous Cybersecurity News reporting on LLMjacking through a leaked AWS key describes a similar path from stolen access to unauthorized model use.

Attackers also collected corporate LLM API keys from public GitHub repositories. To check whether keys worked without creating obvious traffic spikes, one group sent tiny requests using max_tokens=1. These low-volume tests stayed below the victim’s security alert thresholds before larger abuse began.

One tracked group, UNC6993, used a misconfigured service account key to reach cloud resources. It also operated a fake membership portal that persuaded users to paste session data containing active access tokens. Reusing those tokens allowed access without completing a fresh password or multifactor authentication check.

Stolen AI Access Becomes a Resale Business

According to Mandiant’s investigation, attackers increasingly split responsibilities. Some groups break into enterprise environments, while others run “LLM Mixers,” routing services that combine stolen credentials and sell unauthorized model access to paying subscribers. The victim receives the bill while the operators collect revenue.

In one incident, an attacker made more than 500,000 LLM API calls in under eight hours using stolen third-party keys. The activity powered Jet Night, a token-routing service that passed nearly $1 million in costs to one organization. GTIG believes its unusually cheap plans depend on stolen access.

Credential theft is not the only concern. Attackers also searched private repositories, databases, and secret managers for additional passwords and keys. The risk mirrors concerns raised in Cybersecurity News coverage of the Northflank security incident, although that separate investigation has not established a link to these operations.

Some intruders created administrator accounts, added SSH keys, and disguised backdoor service accounts as billing tools. In another case, Mandiant reported exploitation of LiteLLM flaw CVE-2026-40217 through /key/regenerate, allowing ordinary virtual keys to gain PROXY_ADMIN privileges and giving attackers lasting gateway control.

The GTIG guidance urges defenders to treat unexpected activation of AI services as a critical warning. Several victims had not enabled LLM services before the intrusion. Teams should investigate new access keys, rapid account creation and deletion, unusual model requests, and attempts to disable logging.

Organizations should rotate exposed secrets, restrict permissions, scan repositories for keys, patch gateways, and enforce model-specific quotas. Monitoring must include tiny validation requests, not just spending spikes. Revoking the first stolen key is insufficient when attackers have already created replacement accounts or other persistent access.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
Hackers reportedly changed temperature settings on refrigeration equipment used by the French Blood Establishment, EFS, from around −30°C to 110°C after targeting its cooling service provider, Coolworld. The incident occurred overnight between November 1 and 2, 2026, raising concerns about frozen plasma stored for patient transfusions.

According to reporting published by Cyberattaque citing Le Canard enchaîné, facilities in Bourgogne-Franche-Comté were among those concerned. France’s Health Ministry said staff detected the abnormal temperatures in time and that the incident caused no operational consequences.

Coolworld supplies temperature-controlled equipment and maintenance services, including refrigerated containers used in medical settings. An on-call technician reportedly noticed temperatures rising during the night, allowing teams to respond before the disruption affected operations.

Initial information concerned donor samples retained for blood safety monitoring. EFS later told Le Canard enchaîné that frozen plasma intended for transfusions was also involved. However, the available reports do not confirm destroyed plasma, disrupted transfusions, or harm to patients.

The number of affected units, the length of the disruption, and the temperatures actually reached inside stored products remain undisclosed. No public technical findings identify the attackers or explain how they entered Coolworld’s systems, Cyberattaque reported.

French Blood Plasma Freezers Hijacked

The reported 110°C figure describes a setpoint, meaning the temperature requested through a control system. It does not establish that freezer interiors, blood samples, or plasma bags reached that temperature. Controller settings, measured air temperatures, and temperatures inside stored products are separate readings.

This distinction matters because the risk depends on actual storage conditions and how long products remained outside approved limits. Reporting on the incident notes that fresh frozen plasma requires storage at −25°C or below. A prolonged temperature rise could make affected supplies unsuitable for transfusion.

Investigators have not publicly identified a controller model, exploited vulnerability, or stolen maintenance account. Claims that a specific Danfoss flaw caused this incident would therefore go beyond the available evidence.

The incident follows earlier attacks against supermarket refrigeration systems, where attackers reportedly changed settings to force continuous defrosting. Similar behavior does not prove that the same attackers, equipment, or entry method were involved at Coolworld.

An October 12 CERT-FR security alert confirmed numerous compromises involving Danfoss AK-SM and AK-SC controllers, alongside Copeland and Dixell XWEB systems. The agency warned operators against exposing management interfaces directly to the internet.

Cybersecurity News also documented internet-facing Danfoss systems, while noting that search results alone do not establish whether individual devices are vulnerable or compromised. No public evidence connects those exposed systems to the EFS incident.

CERT-FR recommends removing public internet access, reviewing full device configurations, checking defrost schedules, and restoring remote access only through secure VPNs or protected networks. Supported equipment should receive firmware updates, default passwords must be changed, and applicable security settings should be enabled.

For healthcare providers, the reported incident highlights risks extending beyond stolen records. A supplier compromise can affect equipment that preserves essential medical products.

Independent temperature monitoring and prompt staff response were important safeguards here, although the full technical cause remains unknown. Available reporting contains no confirmed theft of donor information.

articles.description:
OpenAI has built Pando, a new Git backend, with Codex agents in just 10 weeks, replacing the system behind its main shared code repository without stopping engineering work. The company says agents now run around the clock to red-team both Git and Pando, testing the software that supports its growing AI-driven development workload. In its […]

The post OpenAI Builds Pando Git Infrastructure Using AI Agents and Deploys Continuous Security Testing appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
OpenAI has built Pando, a new Git backend, with Codex agents in just 10 weeks, replacing the system behind its main shared code repository without stopping engineering work.

The company says agents now run around the clock to red-team both Git and Pando, testing the software that supports its growing AI-driven development workload.

In its November 2 technical report, OpenAI said one engineer designed Pando’s core, teams of agents implemented it, and a small group of engineers deployed it. Production traffic began flowing through the system in April 2026. Pando now supports all development in OpenAI’s monorepo, where teams keep code together.

Codex increased the number of branches, pushes, merges, and downloads hitting OpenAI’s source control systems. One engineer could prepare several changes at once, with each push triggering multiple automated jobs that fetched the same code. The previous setup struggled, with slow transfers, failed merges, and reliability sometimes dropping below 90%.

Pando keeps the Git protocol and familiar workflows while changing how servers store and deliver data. OpenAI reports that median push latency fell by nearly 80%.

The system delivers nearly a petabyte of Git data daily and has served more than 57 terabytes of compressed Git packs in one hour. These are company-reported production figures, not independent benchmarks.

OpenAI Builds Git Infrastructure

Pando manages updates to each branch separately, letting unrelated pushes proceed in parallel. It stores incoming packfiles, Git’s compressed bundles of objects, in blob storage and records branch versions and their dependencies in a separate metadata store. This avoids making every branch update compete through one repository-wide coordination point.

The trade-off is important. Updates remain ordered within an individual branch, but readers fetching several branches may see versions from different moments. Pando therefore does not promise a single, point-in-time view of every branch across the repository.

For downloads, Pando reuses stored packs instead of building a custom response for every client. Its Express delivery service uses regional caches, with reported cache hit rates above 99%. OpenAI says tests on standard cloud virtual machines saturated 10 Gbps links. Related client improvements are available through OpenAI’s public Git repository.

Continuous Red-Team Testing and Security Checks

OpenAI implemented Pando in Rust without legacy dependencies. Engineers built tests that compare its behavior with standard Git, alongside repeatable simulations that check system rules and expose race conditions. These checks targeted bugs in transfer negotiation and the selection of packs needed to reconstruct repository history.

Agents also used Lean and TLA+, tools for expressing and checking system properties, to help find implementation bugs. Some continuous testing sessions lasted hundreds of hours. Separately, OpenAI says agents using Daybreak-capable models continuously red-team Git and Pando. The report does not provide a vulnerability count or detailed findings from that work.

This approach connects with Codex Security’s vulnerability validation workflow and OpenAI’s broader Defense Factory security model, both focused on investigating flaws and preparing fixes.

Pando’s rollout began as a proxy to the old backend, allowing gradual migration without downtime. For security teams, the account illustrates how faster AI-assisted development can be paired with continuous testing, while retaining human design and deployment roles. It does not establish that agent-built infrastructure is free from vulnerabilities.

articles.description:
North Korean hackers used a fake job interview, a poisoned coding task, and a hijacked internal AI tool to reach Binance’s wallet systems. The FBI says the North Korean group it calls “TraderTraitor” stole more than $6 billion in digital assets on 29 October 2026. Binance puts the impacted value at about USD 6.34 billion. […]

The post North Korean Hackers Abuse Internal AI Tool and Fake Job Interviews in $6.34 Billion Binance Heist appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
North Korean hackers used a fake job interview, a poisoned coding task, and a hijacked internal AI tool to reach Binance’s wallet systems. The FBI says the North Korean group it calls “TraderTraitor” stole more than $6 billion in digital assets on 29 October 2026. Binance puts the impacted value at about USD 6.34 billion.

Binance says this was a multi-stage campaign and not a simple phishing case. In June 2026, a wallet DevOps engineer searched online for an AI coding tool and installed a tampered Homebrew package.

Binance replaced the device and rotated credentials, but the attacker had already learned who worked on wallet infrastructure. A similar fake Homebrew ad pushed MacSync Stealer earlier this year, according to the SANS Internet Storm Center.

In September, a second engineer was approached on a job platform by a fake “Project Director.” Two interviews followed, one with a fake HR person and one with a fake CEO. The first included personal social media content to build trust. Near the end of the second, the engineer was told to download an “assignment” onto his work computer.

Malware and the AI Tool

The code ran during setup. It swapped a real pyenv file for a malicious copy, made a new symlink, and started a zsh shell. Binance says the zero-day malware slipped past endpoint tools and wiped its own traces.

On 20 October, the attacker used that computer and an internal AI tool to take over two more engineers. One of them held a container deployment token. Between 17:15 and 19:56 UTC on 29 October, the attacker logged on to the third engineer’s computer. Using the stolen token, they deployed a container and ran a malicious script.

This fits a pattern. Our earlier report on WaterPlum described fake recruiters infecting more than 30,000 devices. Our TraderTraitor Terraform story showed the same group using fake DevOps tests.

Using the wallet signing service, the attacker moved funds outside the normal withdrawal process. Between 20:05 and 20:09 UTC, five hot wallets sent 233.46 million XRP out. Later transfers included about 970,500 SOL, 44.2 million OP and 18,270 BTC.

The attacker then used Ethereum’s EIP-7702 feature. It lets an account hand some execution rights to a smart contract without revealing the private key. The attacker sent 50 signing transactions to match the wallet’s changing nonce, which is a transaction counter. One worked, and the wallet pointed to the attacker’s code.

Stopping withdrawals did not remove that delegation, because it lived on-chain. Binance’s wallet used Multi-Party Computation (MPC), so no single key could undo it quickly.

The team built a special procedure instead. At 00:10 UTC on 30 October, it cleared the delegation by authorizing the zero address. Researchers note this removes the attacker’s code but does not replace the signing key.

About USD 2.85 billion was frozen or intercepted. Binance says it will absorb the loss and that 98% of impacted tokens were replaced by 31 October, which users can check on its Proof of Reserves page.

According to reports, the funds came from the SAFU reserve, an insurance fund, and company money. The FBI says the actors are converting stolen funds mainly into Ethereum and expects more laundering through DeFi and swap services.

Binance rebuilt the wallet system and the AI tool, replaced devices, and removed engineers’ credentials. It also scanned all employee devices and added AI-based anomaly detection. An independent review is underway.

Treat job offers that ask you to run code on a work computer as a threat. Use separate devices for interviews. Limit what internal AI tools can reach. Keep deployment tokens off laptops.

Track changes to account permissions, not just transfers. Finally, plan to both revoke access and rotate keys during an incident, since they are separate steps.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
Password manager mSecure has urged current and former customers to immediately protect passwords and other confidential information stored in its application after its maker, mSeven Software, detected suspicious activity.

The warning also covers two-factor authentication methods and existing passkeys, making it broader than a routine password reset notice.

In its customer email, mSeven said it had “recently learned of suspicious activity” linked to mSecure. The company launched an investigation, took steps to reduce the risk, and brought in external cybersecurity experts.

However, the notice does not explain what happened, how many users are affected, or whether anyone accessed customer vaults.

mSecure Security Notice

The notice reproduced on mSecure’s support forum recommends changing passwords, resetting or re-enrolling two-factor authentication methods, and removing existing passkeys. Its wording calls for immediate action but does not identify particular accounts, app versions, or storage options at risk.

That distinction matters. Suspicious activity does not, by itself, confirm that attackers stole or decrypted stored credentials. The information released so far leaves the cause, scope, and possible exposure unclear. Customers should therefore avoid treating claims of a confirmed vault theft as established fact.

Forum users have asked whether their master passwords, stored logins, or encryption keys are affected. Others questioned whether saving replacement credentials in mSecure would be safe. These comments show the practical gaps in the warning, rather than evidence that any specific attack occurred.

The incident follows a separate review reported in December 2025 by Germany’s Federal Office for Information Security, known as BSI.

That earlier finding does not prove how the current incident happened. It does, however, make a clear explanation of data protection especially important. Related reporting on VaultJacking and synced password vaults illustrates why access to one credential store can have wider consequences, although no connection to mSecure has been established.

The priority is protection. mSecure’s existing unauthorized sign-in guidance explains that changing the manager’s password alone does not secure credentials already copied elsewhere. Users must change affected account passwords through the services’ official websites or apps, prioritizing sensitive accounts such as financial services.

The notice also calls for reviewing stored authentication methods. Separate research on passkey implementation risks provides useful background, but does not establish passkey theft here. Customers still need mSeven to clarify which data was exposed, what safeguards failed, and whether remediation is complete. Those answers remain central to assessing the incident’s actual impact.

articles.title: Hackers Use AI Agents to Launch 3AM Ransomware Attacks Against UK School Networks
articles.description:
A ransomware affiliate has hit a group of UK schools with a mix of human control and AI-style automation. The attackers used built-in Windows tools, stolen backup passwords and fake admin accounts to spread across the school network, then encrypted about 37 machines. The group behind the encryptor is 3AM, also written ThreeAM. It sells […]

The post Hackers Use AI Agents to Launch 3AM Ransomware Attacks Against UK School Networks appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
A ransomware affiliate has hit a group of UK schools with a mix of human control and AI-style automation. The attackers used built-in Windows tools, stolen backup passwords and fake admin accounts to spread across the school network, then encrypted about 37 machines.

The group behind the encryptor is 3AM, also written ThreeAM. It sells its Rust-based ransomware to affiliates, who do the break-ins and share the profit.

Readers who followed earlier ThreeAM ransomware reports will know the group usually targets small and mid-sized victims.

Researchers at Bitdefender noted the malware and the unusual behavior behind it. They call it a hybrid operation: a person picks the goals, while a language model appears to handle repetitive work such as retrying failed commands.

They also say they could not prove which model was used, or whether a person was pasting results back and forth.

Hackers Use AI Agents

The victim was a UK school estate with 47 systems. These included about 21 servers, eight of them domain controllers, and ten workstations still running Windows 10.

The network began as several separate Active Directory domains that did not connect to each other. Bitdefender could not tell how the attackers got in.

Their first recorded move, on 10 and 11 September, was to steal passwords from three backup servers using a modified public Veeam script. Defenders who track Veeam backup security fixes will see why backup software is such a popular target.

The attackers then ran Mimikatz, renamed sysmon64.exe, and created two domain admin accounts named “library” and “svc_bkpmon”. The names were chosen to blend into a school’s account list.

On 15 September they moved 40 finance files through the Windows registry and sent them to a server they controlled. The clearest sign of AI use came on 13 September.

The attacker ran a command, ran it again unchanged 41 seconds later, changed one call 49 seconds after that, and then switched to a different tool 47 seconds later.

Retries across the attack came every 40 to 101 seconds, while moving to a new task took minutes. That pattern fits a person choosing the goals and a model handling the retries.

The commands also contained mistakes a model would make when writing from memory. One call to Veeam used the wrong port and login method.

Bash-style escape characters appeared inside Windows commands on three different days. The attackers also left behind test files with names like “psexec-ok” and “da_proof.txt”, plus numbered script versions such as av_remove, av_remove2 and av_remove3.

On 18 September, the attackers joined three domains with two-way trusts, using the built-in netdom and dnscmd tools.

They also searched shared folders for the names and networks of other schools. This kind of fiddly setup work, where an error message points to the fix, suits a model well.

On 19 September, the attackers tried to remove security software from the file server, but anti-tampering controls blocked it. They then ran the ThreeAM encryptor, host.exe, between 05:07 and 05:33 UTC at 12 to 13 seconds per machine. It deleted system-state backups as it went.

What Defenders Should Take From This Case

Bitdefender is careful to say this is one case and not a trend. The toolkit was old, the encryptor was a standard build, and no step needed new skills. The company expects hybrid attacks like this to become more common in 2027.

The same research stresses that AI-run intrusions are noisy. A loop that retries every minute leaves repeated commands, probe files and numbered scripts behind.

This matches other cases the site has covered, such as AI agents running ransomware in the JadePuffer campaign, where a model planned and carried out an extortion operation.

The attack also fits a wider pattern of Cursor-driven Aur0ra ransomware cases, where AI coding agents handled most of the network work.

Bitdefender advises to keep admin accounts for separate domains apart, alert on any new domain trust or on netdom use, protect backup servers and keep copies that no domain account can delete, limit WMI, remote registry and ADMIN$ access to known management hosts, put an endpoint agent on every machine.

The attacks, reported on Monday, November 2, have raised concerns about the security of connected equipment across Europe’s food supply chain. The post Hackers Target Supermarket Refrigeration Systems Across Europe, Raising Freezer Temperatures to 50°C appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
Hackers have targeted supermarket refrigeration systems across at least 10 European countries, forcing retailers to remove chilled and frozen food from sale after temperature controls were changed.

The attacks, reported on Monday, November 2, have raised concerns about the security of connected equipment across Europe’s food supply chain. Some stores reported settings or temperatures reaching 50°C, equivalent to 122°F.

According to the BBC’s report, disruptions were reported in Belgium, Estonia, Finland, Ireland, Italy, Luxembourg, the Netherlands, Portugal, Germany and Sweden.

European Union officials warned that the incidents could represent a deliberate effort to disrupt food supplies. No group has claimed responsibility, and investigators have not publicly identified the attackers.

The impact varied between countries and retailers. In Ireland, Musgrave Group said 13 SuperValu stores were affected, with chilled and frozen products removed from sale. Restocking was underway by Monday. In Portugal, the Mosqueteiros group linked incidents at seven Intermarché stores to an attack involving an outside refrigeration service provider.

Swedish retailers ICA and Coop also reported refrigeration problems. Reuters reported that one Swedish store said attackers had set its refrigerators and freezers to 50°C. That distinction matters because a changed temperature setting does not prove every affected freezer, or the food inside it, reached that temperature.

Belgian federal prosecutors opened an investigation after refrigeration failures affected numerous stores. In Estonia, a refrigeration contractor said hackers accessed a customer’s control system and raised temperatures to 50°C.

Dutch supplier reports identified at least 17 affected businesses, including smaller food retailers and butcher shops, showing that the disruption extended beyond major supermarket chains.

Refrigeration Controls Became a Prime Target

These attacks concern operational technology, the equipment and software that control physical processes. Supermarket refrigeration controllers manage cooling systems and allow service teams to check temperatures remotely. That access helps maintenance staff respond to faults, but poorly protected connections can also give attackers a route to settings that directly affect food storage.

Danfoss equipment has been linked to several incidents. An ICA spokesperson told AFP that affected stores used an external refrigeration control system supplied by the Danish manufacturer.

Danfoss also confirmed that its products were involved in the latest attacks. However, the available reporting does not establish one entry point or a single software flaw across every affected store.

Reports about earlier attacks describe changes that kept equipment in defrost mode, preventing normal cooling. Cyber Security News covered this method in its report on hacked supermarket refrigeration systems in France. The same physical outcome can follow different changes to controller settings, so investigators must examine device logs and configurations rather than assume every incident used an identical method.

The new incidents follow attacks in France roughly three weeks earlier that reportedly affected around 700 grocery stores. Retailers suffered major food losses after attackers interfered with refrigeration controls.

The BBC put estimated losses in the tens of millions of euros, highlighting how quickly interference with cooling equipment can become a costly business disruption.

Cyber Security News also documented the latest Swedish reports in its coverage of supermarket fridge attacks. That report noted that French investigations involved Danfoss AK-SM and AK-SC controllers, alongside Copeland and Dixell XWEB systems. Those findings concern the French incidents and should not be treated as a confirmed equipment list for every country in the latest wave.

The timing and similar effects have raised questions about a wider campaign. Still, neither a shared attacker nor state involvement has been publicly established.

EU agriculture commissioner Christophe Hansen warned about further disruption, while European Commission spokesman Thomas Regnier said the incidents showed how cyberattacks can interfere with essential services and daily life.

The immediate priority is to reduce access to exposed refrigeration controls. Guidance described in the French response recommends removing management interfaces from the public internet, updating firmware, changing default passwords, and using protected remote connections. Retailers should also check temperature settings and defrost schedules for changes that could continue affecting equipment after access is restored.

Older controllers need particular attention because some affected products reportedly no longer receive security updates. The UK’s National Cyber Security Center has urged retailers to update refrigeration control software and warned that vulnerable equipment exists across the food supply chain. These incidents show why keeping food cold now depends partly on keeping remote control systems secure.

The post Hackers Hijack Emergency Alert Apps in Ukraine and Russia to Send Fake Nuclear Attack Warnings appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
Hackers targeted emergency alert apps in Ukraine and Russia late on November 1 and into November 2, sending false warnings about radiation, chemical threats, and nuclear strikes.

The incidents disrupted trusted public safety channels during wartime. However, officials said the app breaches did not disable their wider warning systems. No independent report has linked either attack to a named hacking group.

Ukraine’s Air Alert app began sending false notifications late Sunday, including warnings of dangerous radiation levels in Kyiv. Other messages claimed chemical threats and street fighting.

Some appeared in English with spelling and grammar errors. In contrast, others mixed Russian and Ukrainian, according to Associated Press reporting published by ITV News.

Hackers Hijack Emergency Alert Apps

Ukraine’s Air Force told residents there was no radiation threat. The app’s operators said unauthorized parties had interfered with the service, prompting them to turn off push notifications and temporarily suspend operations. Officials warned users not to open links in suspicious notifications and directed them toward other official information channels.

The app, developed through cooperation between Ukraine’s Digital Transformation Ministry and security company Ajax Systems, delivers warnings that help civilians seek shelter.

Officials said service was restored overnight. Air Force spokesman Yurii Ihnat stressed that the breach did not affect military operations because the app is separate from military command systems.

Hours later, Russia’s Emergencies Ministry reported a “massive cyberattack” against its mobile application. Attackers used the access to distribute false public warnings.

The Kyiv Independent reported that messages claimed nuclear warheads had been launched across Russia and urged people to shelter in basements and gather food for three weeks.

According to Euronews, Russian officials are working to fix the vulnerability and restore app services, while confirming that other warning channels, including SMS, broadcasts, sirens and loudspeakers, remain operational. The ministry did not identify the attackers.

Public reports establish that attackers could send unauthorized messages, but they do not explain how they gained access. The cited reporting disclosed no confirmed entry point, affected software version, or vulnerability identifier. Claims involving stolen passwords, malware or a specific software flaw would therefore be premature.

Ukraine’s Center for Strategic Communications blamed Russia for the Ukrainian incident, but that claim has not been independently confirmed. The close timing also does not prove the Russian app breach was retaliation or that both attacks shared an operator.

The incidents follow earlier threats to Ukrainian services. Cybersecurity News previously covered Russian hackers inside Kyivstar’s network and charges against six Russian nationals over attacks on Ukrainian government networks. Neither report establishes a connection to these app breaches.

For residents, the immediate concern was trust in urgent warnings. Ukrainian authorities urged people to monitor official emergency channels and physical alerts while recovery continued. The response underscored the importance of maintaining multiple ways to deliver life-saving information when one digital service is compromised.
