articles.title: Hackers Use ARTEX AI to Automate Enterprise Attacks at Machine Speed – Insights for Defenders
articles.description:
AI-powered offensive frameworks are helping attackers move from stolen credentials to cloud privilege escalation, lateral movement, and data theft in minutes. Recent ARTEX campaigns show why organizations must rethink how they detect and stop automated intrusions. Cybercriminals and state-linked hacking groups are increasingly using an artificial intelligence-powered framework called ARTEX to automate complex attacks against […]

The post Hackers Use ARTEX AI to Automate Enterprise Attacks at Machine Speed – Insights for Defenders appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
AI-powered offensive frameworks are helping attackers move from stolen credentials to cloud privilege escalation, lateral movement, and data theft in minutes. Recent ARTEX campaigns show why organizations must rethink how they detect and stop automated intrusions.

Cybercriminals and state-linked hacking groups are increasingly using an artificial intelligence-powered framework called ARTEX to automate complex attacks against enterprise networks, cloud platforms, and identity systems.

Unlike traditional attack tools that require operators to manually select and execute each step, ARTEX uses multiple AI agents to investigate targets, run security tools, interpret results, and determine what to do next.

The framework has already appeared in real-world intrusions involving government agencies, financial institutions, technology companies, and critical industries.

Research published by Google Threat Intelligence Group and Mandiant on October 30, 2026, identified ARTEX being used for Active Directory attacks, privilege escalation, cloud infrastructure reconnaissance, lateral movement, and preparation for data exfiltration.

Microsoft separately linked ARTEX to Storm-0940, a China-state-aligned threat actor that used the framework to accelerate attacks involving compromised ConnectWise application credentials and Microsoft 365 environments.

In another campaign, CrowdStrike identified the China-nexus group VAPOR PANDA using ARTEX to target more than 200 organizations worldwide.

These investigations show a significant change in offensive operations. Attackers are no longer limited to using AI to generate scripts or explain vulnerabilities. They are increasingly connecting AI models directly to tools capable of performing actions inside targeted environments.

For defenders, the biggest concern is not necessarily a new exploitation technique. It is how quickly existing weaknesses can be discovered, combined, and abused.

What Is ARTEX AI?

ARTEX is an AI-powered penetration-testing and offensive security framework designed to automate different stages of a security assessment.

Originally released publicly on GitHub in July 2026, it was developed as a multi-agent system capable of coordinating reconnaissance, vulnerability assessment, exploitation, and post-compromise activities.

The framework is written in Go and includes a web-based management interface built with Next.js. Its architecture combines large language models (LLMs) with specialized agents responsible for planning and carrying out tasks.

Rather than acting as a simple chatbot, ARTEX can use available tools, examine their output, and adjust subsequent actions based on what it discovers.

A typical workflow involves an operator defining a target and objective. The system then divides that objective into smaller tasks, delegates them to specialized agents, and records discovered assets, credentials, vulnerabilities, and other findings in a shared graph.

This shared information allows agents to build on previous discoveries instead of repeatedly starting from scratch. According to Google, the framework supports six specialized sub-agents and can work with different AI models.

The original repository was taken down by its creator in October 2026 following reports of malicious use. However, copies and modified versions continue circulating through community forks and commercial variations.

ARTEX itself is a dual-use security framework, not a vulnerability or a malware family. Authorized penetration testers can use similar automation to assess security weaknesses. The danger emerges when threat actors direct these capabilities against organizations without permission.

ARTEX Automate Enterprise Attacks

A conventional enterprise intrusion often requires a human attacker to spend considerable time investigating the environment.

The attacker must identify available systems, understand access permissions, test credentials, examine errors, and determine which weaknesses can lead to additional privileges. Some of these activities require different skills or specialized tools. ARTEX can automate substantial portions of that process.

For example, after obtaining access to a compromised application or cloud account, an agent may examine available permissions and identify accessible services.

It may then test whether those permissions allow access to additional infrastructure, data repositories, or administrative functions. If one approach fails, the framework can analyze the response and attempt an alternative.

Google’s investigation found individual ARTEX execution bursts lasting approximately 2 to 25 seconds. In one observed operation, the framework generated 27 events in 23 seconds while testing AWS permissions.

These measurements describe individual sequences of automated activity, not the total time needed to compromise an organization. The distinction matters because the overall intrusion may still involve pauses, failed attempts, or human intervention.

Nevertheless, even a short burst can be enough to enumerate permissions, modify cloud resources, or trigger additional attack steps before an analyst investigates the first alert.

ARTEX also creates a different operational challenge. Multiple agents can work through separate tasks, producing large amounts of activity across different security systems.

An attack that initially appears to be ordinary scanning can rapidly progress into credential abuse, privileged access, and data collection.

The underlying security failures are familiar. These include stolen passwords, excessive permissions, vulnerable applications, poorly protected administrative interfaces, and exposed credentials.

What ARTEX changes is the speed at which these weaknesses can be connected. A vulnerable public-facing application might expose a credential. That credential could provide access to a database or cloud storage account. Additional secrets discovered there might grant access to administrative systems.

An automated agent can investigate this chain with far less manual effort than a human operator. This is particularly dangerous in organizations where applications, cloud resources, and identity systems are highly interconnected. A weakness that appears limited to one workload can become the starting point for a much wider intrusion.

Real-World ARTEX Attacks Targeting Organizations

Security researchers have documented several campaigns involving ARTEX. These investigations matter because they show different ways the same framework can be misused.

Not all the reported activities belong to the same threat actor, and attempts to access systems should not be confused with confirmed compromises.

Storm-0940 Uses ARTEX in Microsoft 365 and ConnectWise Attacks

On October 21, 2026, Microsoft Threat Intelligence reported that Storm-0940 had been using ARTEX since at least September to automate attacks against organizations across multiple industries.

The campaign included aerospace, defense, energy, financial services, government, manufacturing, and technology organizations. In several ARTEX-driven intrusions, Microsoft observed the attackers obtain privileged cloud access in less than three hours after initial targeting.

One especially significant incident involved unauthorized access to application credentials associated with ConnectWise Cloud Backup, formerly known as SkyKick.

These applications had already been authorized to operate in customer Microsoft 365 environments. After obtaining control of affected application identities, the attackers attempted to authenticate to more than 2,250 Microsoft 365 tenants.

Rather than requiring an employee to enter a password, the attackers abused existing application trust and permissions. This allowed application-only authentication without the normal interactive sign-in process.

In some environments, Microsoft observed follow-on Microsoft Graph activity involving cloud reconnaissance, application credential modifications, and attempts to change privileged access.

Such changes can be especially dangerous because newly added credentials or permissions may survive even after the initially compromised application is disabled.

Microsoft also documented a related password-spraying operation between October 10 and 14. During that activity, infrastructure associated with Storm-0940 generated more than 151,000 failed authentication events while targeting 327 accounts across eight organizations.

The activity peaked at approximately 2,900 failed attempts per minute. Microsoft did not observe successful authentication in that specific password-spraying dataset. The separate ConnectWise application-credential activity did result in unauthorized sign-ins and additional actions in some environments.

The 2,250-tenant figure represents attempted access, not 2,250 confirmed breaches. Successful application authentication also does not, by itself, prove that customer information was stolen.

The incident demonstrates the risk of granting extensive permissions to trusted third-party applications. Once those application credentials are compromised, attackers may be able to reuse existing access without exploiting a vulnerability in the cloud provider itself.

ARTEX Targets Enterprise Identity Providers and Software Vendors

Researchers at Wiz identified ARTEX-associated attacks against software and IT companies during October 2026. The activity overlapped with the campaign Microsoft tracks as Storm-0940.

Investigators observed attempts to map web applications, enumerate exposed API functionality, probe authentication mechanisms, and access resources belonging to other customers.

The attacks involved identity platforms including Microsoft Entra ID, Okta, and Amazon Cognito. In several cases, the agent examined publicly accessible JavaScript files, configuration resources, and API documentation to learn how an application operated.

It then attempted to interact with authentication endpoints, password-recovery features, and application functions.

Wiz observed password-spraying activity occurring in coordinated bursts, with a median gap of approximately one second between attempts.

Some bursts continued for 20 to 60 minutes. Other activity lasted much longer. Researchers documented sessions extending for 24 to 30 hours.

When an IP address was blocked, subsequent activity sometimes appeared from another address within minutes. The attackers also varied user-agent strings and repeatedly tested different endpoints. Importantly, most observed attempts were unsuccessful.

However, the automation shows why a single blocked request or a temporary rate limit is not always enough to stop an attacker who can continually test alternative paths.

VAPOR PANDA Uses ARTEX to Target More Than 200 Organizations

A separate investigation published by CrowdStrike on October 29, 2026 documented ARTEX use by VAPOR PANDA, a China-nexus espionage group.

This operation was distinct from the Storm-0940 campaign. Beginning October 17, the attackers used ARTEX against more than 200 organizations across government, telecommunications, defense, semiconductor, pharmaceutical, and other industries.

The targeting extended across at least 14 countries during an 11-day period. CrowdStrike confirmed post-exploitation activity at nine organizations.

The attackers used ARTEX for multiple concurrent intrusions, with a human operator providing directions while AI agents performed tasks. The group combined ARTEX with DeepSeek and another commercial AI model.

Its activities included investigating cloud configurations, exploiting weaknesses in applications, gathering credentials, and moving through compromised environments.

CrowdStrike also observed the deployment of the BLOODALCHEMY backdoor, which supported continued malicious access. In some operations, attackers instructed the agents to identify Windows systems without endpoint security coverage.

This finding highlights another risk: automated attackers can potentially use information about defensive coverage to select less-protected systems.

The VAPOR PANDA case demonstrates that ARTEX is not restricted to opportunistic scanning. It can also support targeted espionage operations directed by experienced attackers.

What ARTEX Can Do After Initial Access

Google’s investigation provides some of the clearest examples of how ARTEX behaves after attackers gain a foothold.In multiple incidents, the attackers provided the framework with already-compromised credentials. ARTEX then performed additional reconnaissance and attempted to expand access.

Active Directory Reconnaissance and Privilege Escalation

Google observed ARTEX running automated PowerShell reconnaissance against Windows domain infrastructure. The activity included identifying accounts, examining managed service accounts, reviewing Active Directory Certificate Services configurations, and mapping relationships across trusted domains.

Some operations used Kerberoasting techniques to obtain service tickets associated with domain accounts. Kerberoasting is a technique that can expose service account passwords when weak credentials are used.

Researchers also observed DCSync activity aimed at obtaining sensitive domain authentication material. Successful abuse of domain replication privileges can expose credentials needed to compromise additional accounts and systems.

ARTEX attempted lateral movement through techniques involving existing authentication material and Windows remote administration capabilities.

In one case, endpoint defenses blocked part of the activity before defenders disconnected the affected server. The findings demonstrate why protecting domain controllers, service accounts, and privileged credentials remains important even when the attack is AI-assisted.

Further technical details are covered in our report on ARTEX-assisted Active Directory attacks and lateral movement.

Cloud Permission Discovery and Credential Abuse

ARTEX has also been observed investigating Azure and AWS environments. Instead of assuming that a discovered credential has administrative access, the framework can test what actions the identity is permitted to perform.

This can include identifying accessible cloud resources, examining storage permissions, and evaluating management capabilities.

Google observed rapid permission checks and short sequences of cloud resource operations. Such behavior can help an attacker determine which credentials are useful for moving deeper into an environment.

Overly privileged service principals, static cloud access keys, and unrestricted workload identities can therefore become attractive targets.

Exploiting Legitimate Application Features

Another concerning finding is that ARTEX does not always need to deploy a traditional malware payload to cause harm. Google documented activity involving legitimate application functions being used in unintended ways.

In one incident, the framework attempted to cross from database access into operating-system execution. The process generated approximately 240 log events as the agents repeatedly adjusted their approach.

In another case, the framework abused an application’s notification capabilities to trigger messages to more than 1,300 internal users.

This demonstrates that legitimate features can become useful attack tools when access controls are weak or application permissions are excessive. A practical defense strategy begins with understanding where automated activity leaves evidence.

The following table summarizes observed behaviors and the logs defenders should prioritize.

These behaviors are not exclusive to ARTEX. Legitimate scanners and administrative automation may produce similar events. The strongest detections depend on correlating multiple activities and comparing them against approved behavior.

How Defenders Can Detect ARTEX-Driven Attacks

1. Monitor Non-Human Identities and OAuth Applications

The ConnectWise incident showed that an attacker may not need to compromise a normal employee account. An application identity with broad permissions can provide access to valuable resources without interactive user authentication.

Organizations should maintain an inventory of service principals, OAuth applications, API credentials, and other workload identities. For each identity, security teams should understand its owner, permissions, normal authentication sources, and expected operations.

Defenders should investigate unfamiliar application sign-ins, especially when followed by credential additions, new permissions, or privileged directory changes.

Microsoft recommends using the OAuthAppInfo, EntraIdSpnSignInEvents, and GraphAPIAuditEvents tables in Defender XDR to investigate affected applications and their subsequent activity.

The Microsoft technical report provides ready-to-run hunting queries that can be adapted to an organization’s environment.

2. Detect High-Speed Sequences, Not Just Individual Events

Traditional detection rules frequently evaluate individual events. An authentication failure might be treated as low risk. A cloud resource listing might be normal. A configuration query may not trigger an alert.

However, those activities become more concerning when they appear together within seconds. For example, a suspicious sequence might involve an unfamiliar application authentication, immediate resource enumeration, a credential change, and access to sensitive storage.

The correlation between those events may reveal an intrusion that would otherwise be missed. Security teams should build detections around unusual event velocity, unexpected sequences, and changes in an identity’s established behavior.

Alerts involving access to privileged systems or sensitive data should receive higher priority.

3. Monitor Active Directory and Internal Movement

Organizations should watch for unusual directory enumeration, unexpected service ticket requests, and suspicious authentication activity involving privileged accounts.

Kerberoasting attempts may be visible through Windows security event 4769 when appropriate auditing is enabled. Potential DCSync activity can be investigated through directory replication-related events, including event 4662, where the required audit settings are configured.

Defenders should also monitor unusual WinRM, SMB, and remote service activity between systems that do not normally communicate. Pay particular attention to domain controllers, identity servers, certificate services, and administrative workstations.

4. Watch for Abnormal Cloud API Activity

Cloud environments generate valuable evidence of automated attacks. Security teams should monitor rapid permission testing, unusual resource enumeration, repeated authorization failures, and unexpected changes to IAM roles.

Additional high-value detections include bulk access to cloud secrets, sudden increases in storage reads, and management API calls from unfamiliar infrastructure.

Cloud access should be evaluated in context. A build server accessing a known storage bucket during deployment may be normal. The same identity suddenly accessing unrelated production secrets from an unfamiliar network should trigger investigation.

5. Look for Automation Artifacts Without Relying on Them Exclusively

Researchers have identified ARTEX-related artifacts such as artex-probe-* filenames and other distinctive naming patterns. CrowdStrike has also documented campaign-specific identifiers involving artx or artex strings.

These indicators can help investigators identify known activity. However, attackers can change filenames, infrastructure, and user-agent strings.

A defender who searches only for the ARTEX name may miss the actual attack. Behavior-based detection remains essential because malicious agents can carry out activities using ordinary administrative tools and legitimate credentials.

Indicators of Compromise Associated With Storm-0940

The following IP addresses were published in connection with the Microsoft 365 and ConnectWise campaign.

Security teams investigating the ConnectWise incident should also identify the following legitimate application IDs.

These application identifiers belong to legitimate integrations and are not malicious indicators by themselves. Organizations should consult the full vendor advisory for additional affected identities and investigation instructions.

Similarly, an IP address match or a common Python user-agent string should be treated as investigative evidence rather than automatic proof of compromise.

Incident Response Checklist for Suspected ARTEX Activity

Organizations investigating potential ARTEX or Storm-0940 activity should prioritize the following actions.

  1. Determine exposure. Inventory affected applications, service principals, credentials, and systems. Review both current and previously authorized integrations.
  2. Preserve evidence. Collect authentication records, cloud audit logs, application changes, endpoint telemetry, and relevant network activity before making irreversible changes.
  3. Reconstruct the timeline. Correlate the first suspicious access with subsequent API calls, permission modifications, administrative activity, and data access.
  4. Contain confirmed access. Disable compromised identities or connections, revoke unauthorized permissions, and rotate affected credentials through an approved incident response process.
  5. Search for secondary persistence. Investigate new application secrets, administrator accounts, role assignments, mailbox changes, scheduled tasks, and other access paths the attacker may have created.
  6. Validate recovery. Confirm that unauthorized access has ended, essential services are functioning, and enhanced monitoring remains in place.

For organizations affected by the ConnectWise incident, Microsoft recommends reviewing activity from at least October 15, 2026, and extending service-principal investigations to October 1 where logs are available.

According to ConnectWise’s October 30 advisory, restoration of Cloud Backup is underway through a new, security-hardened application. Backup and restore capabilities have resumed for re-authorized Microsoft 365 tenants.

Partners should follow ConnectWise’s official re-authorization instructions, verify that new backup snapshots are being created, and avoid re-enabling previously disabled application connections unless specifically instructed.

Re-authorizing an application does not replace the need to investigate possible unauthorized access or remove attacker-created credentials.

A security researcher has found a way to run any command with root rights on the navigation unit in a 2014 Renault Latitude. The unit is a TomTom Carminat LIVE head unit that runs a custom system built on Linux 2.6.28.10. The research was published on November 2, 2026, and it shows how old in-car […]

The post Renault Car’s 15-Year-Old Linux Navigation Software Hacked to Execute Arbitrary Root Commands appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
A security researcher has found a way to run any command with root rights on the navigation unit in a 2014 Renault Latitude.

The unit is a TomTom Carminat LIVE head unit that runs a custom system built on Linux 2.6.28.10. The research was published on November 2, 2026, and it shows how old in-car software can still hide serious weaknesses.

The researcher is Rasmus Moorats. He did not start out to hack anything. He only wanted to fix the clock after daylight saving time ended in Estonia.

The “Set time” option was missing, and the settings menu would not open without a genuine map SD card. Analysts at NNS.ee noted that the problem comes from the way the unit reads a script file from the SD card.

They described a chain of small flaws that, when joined, give full control of the device. Cars like this are common, and many hold years of phone contacts and location data. Newer cars face similar risks, as shown in the PerfektBlue Bluetooth flaws that put millions of vehicles at risk.

Renault Car’s 15-Year-Old Linux Navigation Software Hacked

The unit has more protection than you would expect from 2011 software. Most partitions are read-only, “noexec” (which blocks programs from running), or both.

The system also checks SD cards with DRM, so a blank card or a copied card is rejected. Update images carry a signature too, so the researcher could not simply flash a changed system image.

To study the unit safely, he built an emulator with QEMU. The emulator showed him which files the unit reads from the SD card at boot. One of them is master.script, a small script that automates screen actions. A program called ttn parses it, and ttn runs as root.

Two commands in that script proved useful. SHEX runs a program from the system, but it accepts only one word, so no arguments can be passed.

The LOG command writes one line of plain text to a file, and it has a path traversal bug. Adding “../” to the log file path lets the writer reach outside the intended folder. Because ttn is root, every write is also made as root.

Neither bug was enough alone. The root file system was read-only, and the SD card could not run programs. The researcher then borrowed a trick from kernel exploits.

He used the LOG command to write into /proc/sys/kernel/core_pattern, the setting that tells Linux what to do when a program crashes.

He wrote a pipe command there that makes the kernel start /bin/sh with a script from the SD card. The kernel then ran the script as root.

To trigger a crash, he used SHEX to start /bin/dbus-monitor, which aborts when it cannot find the system bus. The final script was only three lines long.

His first proof was simple: the payload rebooted the unit. He then used the access to back up the internal storage with dd. He found the time setting in /mnt/flash/settings.dat and changed the offset from UTC+3 to UTC+2.

Why Old Car Software Is Still a Risk

This case was a research project done with physical access to the car, so it is not a remote threat. A criminal would need to insert a prepared SD card, and the driver would have to answer “Yes” to the “Execute master.script?” prompt.

That limits the risk, but it does not remove it. A shared car, a rental, or a repair shop visit could give someone that chance. The deeper issue is design. The unit trusts a script from removable media, runs the parser as root, and does not clean file paths.

These are common mistakes in embedded devices, and they last for as long as the car stays on the road. A car can be driven for 15 years or more, and head units rarely get patches.

Researchers keep finding the same pattern in newer vehicles. A Nissan Leaf infotainment flaw showed how a weak Bluetooth component could lead to control of doors, mirrors, and steering. That unit ran Linux 3.14, which dates from 2013.

Head units are also a target for criminals who want to make money. A recent report on Android car screen malware described a multi-stage downloader that used the built-in update path to join infected screens to an ad fraud and proxy botnet.

Even in that case, the report did not show control of steering or braking. Old Linux gadgets are also exposed in other ways. The Kairos botnet, for example, takes over Linux devices that allow passwordless Telnet root logins.

Owners of older cars have few options. They should keep unknown SD cards and USB sticks out of the head unit and buy map cards only from trusted sellers. They should also ask the dealer whether any security update exists.

articles.title: Microsoft Reveals 78% of Exploited Vulnerabilities Enable System Takeover and Privilege Escalation
articles.description:
Microsoft’s new research shows that attackers pick flaws that give them control of a system. About 78% of vulnerabilities exploited in real attacks let an attacker take over a system or raise their privileges. The finding comes from a data study published on November 2, 2026, by Microsoft Security Research. Software flaws keep piling up. […]

The post Microsoft Reveals 78% of Exploited Vulnerabilities Enable System Takeover and Privilege Escalation appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
Microsoft’s new research shows that attackers pick flaws that give them control of a system. About 78% of vulnerabilities exploited in real attacks let an attacker take over a system or raise their privileges.

The finding comes from a data study published on November 2, 2026, by Microsoft Security Research. Software flaws keep piling up. From 1999 through September 2026, about 383,000 vulnerabilities were disclosed.

Only about 2,000 of them, roughly 0.5%, were linked to real-world exploitation. Fewer than 1 in 200 flaws ever reach a real attack, so defenders gain a lot by knowing which ones matter.

Microsoft researchers Yair Tsarfaty and Or Begam noted that attackers go after remote code execution, privilege escalation and authentication bypass bugs far more than other types.

The analysts also warned that AI-assisted bug hunting and exploit writing could shrink the time defenders have to react. That follows a trend already seen when attackers exploit flaws within hours of disclosure.

Microsoft Reveals 78% of Exploited Vulnerabilities

The team studied each CVE in two ways: by impact and by affected platform. Impact means the best result an attacker could get. For example, if a bug bypasses login and then allows remote code execution, Microsoft counts it as remote code execution.

Platforms included Windows, Linux and Unix, mobile, network appliances, IoT and OT, virtualization hosts, and developer packages.

The full CVE pool looks very different from the exploited pool. Across all published CVEs, about 77% sit in application code and 23% in operating system code.

Among exploited bugs, operating system flaws jump to 41%. Server-side remote code execution rises from 20% of all CVEs to 37% of exploited ones. Local privilege escalation climbs from 11% to 18%, and client-side remote code execution from 4% to 13%.

Low-value bug types fall sharply. Cross-site scripting drops from 15% to 4%, and denial of service from 16% to 7%.

Microsoft explained that a crash or a small script run gives an attacker little to build on, while code execution and higher privileges give a foothold for later steps.

A good example is the Windows privilege escalation flaw in the CLFS driver, which let local users reach SYSTEM access.

Microsoft also cautioned that a bug’s label does not always match real results. Some flaws described as remote code execution may only cause a crash in real conditions. So teams should check what an attacker can actually do before they rank a fix.

Why Slow Patching Helps Attackers

The second finding is about speed. Microsoft’s 2026 exposure data shows the median fix takes about two weeks on Windows workstations.

On Windows Servers it takes more than a month. Linux servers and macOS applications take over 10 weeks, and network appliances take more than a year. That gap is the window attackers use, and it is widest on the systems that matter most.

Exploitation moves much faster. VulnCheck reported that 29% of exploits in 2025 were launched within one day of CVE publication. CISA data shows the mean time from CVE publication to the KEV catalog fell from 89 days in 2024 to 57 days in 2025.

In 2026, through September, the mean is 20 days and the median is only 3 days. Microsoft says two things decide a flaw’s value to an attacker: impact and exposure. Servers often run service accounts or cloud identities with more permissions than they need.

Taking over one gives access to data, admin rights and trusted network paths. Microsoft calls this the blast radius. Public exploit code makes this worse, as seen when the MiniPlasma Windows zero-day gave SYSTEM access on patched machines.

Microsoft said defenders should fix takeover flaws first. Stopping them breaks an intrusion early, before it spreads. The second tier includes denial of service on systems where uptime is critical, and leaked credentials that feed privileged identity paths.

The same pattern shows in the Cloud Files driver zero-day, where attackers used a local flaw to gain SYSTEM rights. Patching is still key, but some old or unsupported systems cannot be patched.

Microsoft suggests finding all internet-facing assets, including shadow IT and third-party dependencies, with Defender External Attack Surface Management.

Defender Vulnerability Management then ranks weaknesses beyond CVSS scores, using exploit signals, internet exposure and asset value.

Attack Path Analysis shows how an exposed server could lead through a privileged identity to sensitive data, so teams can cut that route. Microsoft also shares more detail in its original research post.

articles.description:
Hackers are distributing Yoba malware through fake ChatGPT and Claude downloads, pairing legitimate, digitally signed applications with malicious libraries. The campaign uses trusted software and GitHub hosting to make dangerous installers appear credible, ultimately deploying a cryptocurrency miner on compromised Windows computers. The attack does not require compromising OpenAI or Anthropic. Instead, criminals place malicious […]

The post Hackers Abuse Signed ChatGPT and Claude Applications to Deploy Yoba Malware and Evade Detection appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
Hackers are distributing Yoba malware through fake ChatGPT and Claude downloads, pairing legitimate, digitally signed applications with malicious libraries.

The campaign uses trusted software and GitHub hosting to make dangerous installers appear credible, ultimately deploying a cryptocurrency miner on compromised Windows computers.

The attack does not require compromising OpenAI or Anthropic. Instead, criminals place malicious files beside authentic executables and exploit how those programs load supporting libraries.

A valid signature protects the signed executable’s integrity, but it does not guarantee that neighboring files are safe.

Analysts from PolySwarm noted in their November 2 threat report that Yoba combines signed application abuse, environmental checks, and layered payload delivery.

Their assessment draws on Check Point Research’s investigation, which tracked fraudulent AI repositories for approximately two months.

Hackers Abuse Signed ChatGPT and Claude Applications

Attackers created GitHub repositories and GitHub Pages websites advertising supposed desktop applications named GPT-5.6 Sol, GPT-6 Astra, and Claude Opus.

Visitors were directed to ZIP archives distributed through GitHub releases. Earlier reporting on fake GitHub AI downloads describes the same campaign’s use of familiar branding to encourage installation.

Researchers traced repositories to July 2026, with malicious releases appearing in late August and early September. Some projects ranked prominently in Google searches despite showing no artificially inflated stars or forks.

Check Point assessed that search visibility likely involved SEO poisoning, rather than confirming how rankings were manipulated. Inside the archives, a genuine signed installer loads YobaDropper through DLL sideloading.

The malicious library exposes 180 functions to resemble a Windows multimedia component, but its harmful logic runs from its entry point. Related signed software sideloading attacks show how this technique extends beyond AI-themed lures.

Before continuing, YobaDropper checks its host executable’s name. A mismatch triggers 200,000 sleep cycles lasting 5.5 seconds each, delaying execution beyond many automated analysis windows.

It also filters keyboard layouts, excluding Russian, Belarusian, Armenian, Azerbaijani, Kazakh, and other language environments while explicitly exempting Ukrainian. Administrator privileges are required to proceed.

The dropper then copies a legitimate Windows Media Player component into a ProgramData directory and decrypts another malicious library.

A scheduled task running as Local System launches the copied executable after a three-minute startup delay. Microsoft-themed task details help disguise this second sideloading stage, which activates YobaLoader.

Telegram Tasking, XMRig Mining, and Detection Priorities

YobaLoader retrieves a Telegram channel’s profile image and feeds its final 50 bytes into a domain generation algorithm. Changing that image changes the generated domain, allowing operators to redirect the infection chain without rebuilding the malware.

The loader queries Google’s DNS-over-HTTPS service for a TXT record, validates returned instructions using Ed25519 signatures, and decrypts them using AES in ECB mode.

It then downloads an encrypted payload from hosting services such as Catbox. Separately documented hidden XMRig mining campaigns illustrate how DNS records and image content can support concealed delivery chains.

Researchers observed XMRig 6.26.0 injected into a Windows service process. Mining traffic passed through a local Tor SOCKS5 proxy, while activity monitoring paused mining during computer use.

YobaLoader also supports executable and hidden PowerShell payloads, although information theft and ransomware deployment were not documented.

Defenders should investigate unexpected DLL loads, Microsoft-themed scheduled tasks, and Windows executables running from unusual directories. Reviewing complete execution chains matters more than trusting signatures alone; the observed miner is only one payload this loader can deliver.

articles.title: NCSC Warns AI Could Accelerate Ransomware Attacks on Critical Infrastructure
articles.description:
The UK’s National Cyber Security Center handled 80 nationally significant cyber incidents during its latest reporting year, warning that artificial intelligence is making attacks faster, cheaper and easier to carry out. Its 2026 Annual Review records 1,831 attack reports, with 337 incidents requiring support from its Incident Management Team. The review covers 1 September 2025 […]

The post NCSC Warns AI Could Accelerate Ransomware Attacks on Critical Infrastructure appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
The UK’s National Cyber Security Center handled 80 nationally significant cyber incidents during its latest reporting year, warning that artificial intelligence is making attacks faster, cheaper and easier to carry out. Its 2026 Annual Review records 1,831 attack reports, with 337 incidents requiring support from its Incident Management Team.

The review covers 1 September 2025 to 31 August 2026, marking the NCSC’s tenth year as part of GCHQ. Published on November 3, the NCSC Annual Review 2026 warns that AI is increasing pressure on organizations still struggling to fix known security weaknesses.

The 80 nationally significant incidents represent a subset of the 337 cases that needed NCSC support, not the total number of cyber attacks across the UK. Alongside its response work, the agency notified 8,500 organizations of events indicating suspected system compromise through its Early Warning service.

The NCSC cautions against reading incident totals as a simple measure of whether threats are rising or falling. Reporting levels vary, major incidents can influence annual figures, and early alerts may prevent smaller compromises from developing into cases requiring national support. Response complexity also differs widely between incidents.

That context matters when comparing this review with earlier reporting on nationally significant UK cyber attacks. A lower incident count does not, by itself, prove that organizations face less risk or that the impact of individual attacks has decreased.

AI Could Accelerate Ransomware

The report’s central finding is not that attackers have abandoned established techniques. Instead, AI is helping them research targets, produce convincing social engineering messages, discover software flaws, and develop exploit code more efficiently. Skilled operators currently gain the greatest benefit because they can check results and correct mistakes.

The agency’s incident management findings draw an important line between observed activity and future risks. Its responders have begun seeing attackers use AI tools, but none of those observed uses enabled a new class of attack. Existing security controls therefore remain directly relevant.

Across the large organizations covered by its incident data, 88% of incidents involved four initial access routes: public-facing applications, phishing, valid accounts and external remote services. These findings show why exposed software, stolen login details and poorly protected remote access remain immediate concerns, even as AI capabilities improve.

Human involvement also remains important. The NCSC assesses that attackers will continue using AI mainly to improve existing operations rather than routinely handing complete attacks to autonomous systems. Operators still need to direct tools, validate findings and adapt when an approach fails.

The review warns that AI-powered malware is highly likely to feature in a ransomware attack against UK critical national infrastructure between now and 2028. This is a forecast, not confirmation that such an incident has already happened.

Its assessment of threats to the UK also expects China, Russia and other states to routinely use AI cyber capabilities by 2028. The likely result is an increase in the speed and scale of sophisticated operations against UK targets.

Businesses face risks from their own AI adoption too. The report warns that employees using unapproved AI services can expose sensitive company information and leave employers unable to track how that data is handled. Earlier coverage of CISA and NCSC secure AI development guidance explains why security must be considered throughout an AI system’s life.

For defenders, AI-assisted flaw discovery could create a growing workload of security updates. The NCSC urges organisations to prepare for a “patch wave” by improving their ability to deploy fixes quickly, frequently and across suppliers. Not every AI-discovered flaw will be exploitable, but delays can give attackers opportunities.

The immediate priorities remain practical: maintain an accurate view of systems, patch exposed services, control account access, protect backups and rehearse incident response. The review also supports wider passkey adoption and better understanding of supplier dependencies. These measures address the access routes responders continue to encounter.

AI can also help defenders identify weaknesses, review alerts, and support faster response. However, automated actions need clear limits and human oversight to avoid disruption. The challenge is turning that potential into reliable protection while replacing aging technology and consistently applying the basic controls that many organizations still lack today.

articles.title: ARES AI Red Team Platform Automates 66 Attack Modules for Active Directory and Cloud Security Testing
articles.description:
A new open-core project called ARES is giving red teams a way to run planned, controlled attack tests against Active Directory and cloud systems. A developer who goes by Mafifrizi released the tool on GitHub. It ships with 66 active modules, with 70 cataloged in total, covering more than 60 techniques mapped to MITRE ATT&CK. […]

The post ARES AI Red Team Platform Automates 66 Attack Modules for Active Directory and Cloud Security Testing appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
A new open-core project called ARES is giving red teams a way to run planned, controlled attack tests against Active Directory and cloud systems. A developer who goes by Mafifrizi released the tool on GitHub.

It ships with 66 active modules, with 70 cataloged in total, covering more than 60 techniques mapped to MITRE ATT&CK. It is aimed at enterprise red teams, managed security providers (MSSPs), and security operations centers.

Mafifrizi publishes the project as an open-core platform, which means the base tool is free to read and test while a sponsorship page supports ongoing work.

The project page lists the repository under the handle “mafifrizi/ares” and describes it as an autonomous red-team engagement platform with MITRE ATT&CK module orchestration, attack-path solving, and reporting. The README does not give a real name, company, or team behind the code, so readers should treat it as an independent project for now.

The author’s pitch is simple. Traditional penetration tests cost a lot, happen rarely, and only show one moment in time, so new misconfigurations can sit unseen for months.

Vulnerability scanners add to the problem by listing thousands of possible CVEs without proving that any of them can be used. ARES tries to fill that gap by running real test steps and showing which ones lead to the most valuable systems, such as domain admin accounts.

The part of ARES that stands out most is how hard it tries to keep tests inside approved limits. Before a module runs, a check called ScopeGuard confirms the target is in scope.

A second layer, the Scope Firewall and Egress Filter, then blocks traffic at two levels. One level uses the operating system firewall, which is Windows Defender Firewall or Linux Netfilter when the tool runs with elevated rights. The other watches network calls inside Python itself. The goal is a “fail-closed” design, where the tool stops instead of sending traffic to an address nobody approved.

The tool also profiles how noisy each action is, so operators can pick quieter steps when they want to test whether the blue team notices. This matters because a careless test can knock over a production server. For the same reason, security teams are shifting toward tools that put a person in charge of each decision.

Active Directory Attack Paths

For Active Directory, ARES can load BloodHound collections or map live domain sessions. Its built-in graph engine then works out the shortest route to Domain Admin, points out chokepoints, and checks whether a sideways move is possible.

BloodHound uses the same graph idea, where a small group membership can open a path that is many steps long. Cyber Security News has explained how BloodHound Community Edition maps these paths across Active Directory and Azure.

Operators can set a goal such as domain_admin, full_compromise, or cloud_audit. The planning engine then builds a multi-step plan from graph rules. It can also use AI agents such as Claude, OpenAI, or a local Ollama model, but only after the operator gives clear permission.

The same planning engine covers cloud checks, and the cloud_audit goal is one of the built-in options. Letting a language model suggest next steps is now common in offensive tools. Cyber Security News recently reported on Decepticon, an open-source agent with 16 specialist roles. ARES keeps the AI optional, which many teams will prefer.

Defenders have a reason to watch this space. Criminals are using similar tools. Cyber Security News covered how hackers used the ARTEX AI agents to map Windows networks, steal service account passwords, and try to spread inside the network. A platform like ARES lets defenders test the same steps first, on their own terms.

Because ARES stores sensitive material, the author added several protections. Sessions live in the database, access tokens are short-lived and kept in memory, and refresh tokens are rotated. ARES stores harvested hashes and client evidence in a local vault protected with AES-256-GCM and PBKDF2-HMAC-SHA256 at 600,000 rounds.

When a test ends, ARES can produce branded reports in PDF, HTML, Markdown, and JSON. The PDF step runs through a headless browser, so it needs no extra GTK libraries on Windows or Linux. For teams that want a deeper guide to the Active Directory side, the Active Directory attack checklist on Cyber Security News is a useful companion.

Only run ARES on systems you own or have written permission to test. Start in a lab, check that the scope rules block out-of-range addresses, and review the code before using it on real networks. Fix any path the tool finds to a domain admin account, then run it again to confirm the fix.

articles.title: Hackers Exploit Adobe Commerce Zero-Day to Deploy PSK Agent RAT and Remotely Control Servers
articles.description:
Attackers are abusing a serious flaw in Adobe Commerce and Magento to install a hidden remote access tool called PSK Agent on online store servers. Once it is running, they can run commands, route traffic through the server, and keep access even after a restart. The flaw, named StyleSmuggler and tracked as CVE-2026-75650, was first […]

The post Hackers Exploit Adobe Commerce Zero-Day to Deploy PSK Agent RAT and Remotely Control Servers appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
Attackers are abusing a serious flaw in Adobe Commerce and Magento to install a hidden remote access tool called PSK Agent on online store servers.

Once it is running, they can run commands, route traffic through the server, and keep access even after a restart. The flaw, named StyleSmuggler and tracked as CVE-2026-75650, was first revealed as a zero-day in early September.

Sansec said it let anyone run code on a store without logging in, and it affected every current version, including 2.4.9. Within days, more than one group was using it to drop different malware.

Researchers at Imperva noted the PSK Agent activity after tracking a coordinated campaign between September 9 and September 13, 2026.

They saw it hit stores in Western Europe, North America and the Asia-Pacific region. The malware had a 0% detection rate on VirusTotal at the time of analysis, so basic file scanning would likely have missed it.

Hackers Exploit Adobe Commerce Zero-Day

The attackers went after one endpoint, /paypal/transparent/response/, which matches the first step of StyleSmuggler. In that step, the attacker places PHP code in the request’s query string.

Magento then logs the error and writes that code into a report file under var/report/. A second request to /graphql uses attacker-controlled styles values to load the poisoned file and run the code.

Imperva tracked five attack clusters coming from a small set of IP addresses. The near-identical payloads point to automated tools that scan for weak stores at scale.

The download link for the first script, psk_agent.sh, showed up 96 times across 12 payload variants, which suggests the attackers kept using one stable delivery path.

The PHP payload tries the shell_exec, system and exec functions in turn. If one is blocked, it quietly moves to the next. It then runs a curl command that pipes the script straight into bash, so the first command never touches the disk.

The 3,313-byte script looks for a folder that is both writable and executable, such as /tmp or /dev/shm. It then downloads the next stage with curl, wget or Python and starts it in the background.

That stage is chi_down, a heavily obfuscated 10.5 MB Go program. It can run shell commands, collect host details and proxy traffic through SOCKS5.

It also talks to its operators over HTTP, HTTPS and encrypted channels. Its launch arguments, -checkagent=false -maintain=true, suggest it is meant to survive restarts.

DNS Beacons, Webshells and Signs of a Chinese-Speaking Operator

Some payloads also told the attackers when an attack worked. The code put the victim’s hostname into a unique subdomain under 0f851bdc9d.ddns.1433.eu.org and then made both an HTTP and a DNS request.

The attackers controlled the DNS servers, so the lookup alone proved success, even if the web request failed. That gave them a quiet, running list of hacked servers.

In some cases, the operators added a second way back in. They downloaded t4.php and saved it as zer4.php in public folders such as pub/media/.

This 910-line file manager and PHP web shells like it let attackers edit files, upload or download data, and run system commands. It uses PHP’s Foreign Function Interface to call libc directly, which can still work when common PHP functions are turned off.

The same hardcoded AES-256-CBC key appeared in every sample, which hints at one operator or a shared toolkit. Imperva found Chinese-language comments in the script, with names such as chinow and chi_down in the infrastructure.

The researchers rate a Chinese-speaking operator as likely, with moderate confidence. They warn that language clues can be planted or copied, and they do not name a specific group.

They also stress that this applies only to PSK Agent, since other attackers have used the same flaw to drop a Rust backdoor and different PHP droppers.

Store owners should apply Adobe’s VULN-39341 hotfix. That only closes the entry point, though. It does not remove a RAT, webshell or stolen credentials that were planted earlier.

A server with any of these signs should be treated as fully compromised. Check for psk_agent.sh, chi_down, zer4.php and fake process names like kworker, fc-cache and chronyd.

Rotate the Magento encryption key, database logins, admin credentials, API tokens and SSH keys. Watch for DNS lookups to the beacon domain and for web servers making unexpected outbound connections.

Zscaler also saw some of the same download infrastructure in Citrix NetScaler attacks, but that overlap is only a lead and does not prove the same actor is behind both.

Magento stores have long been a favorite target. A past campaign showed how fast things can spread, when the CosmicSting flaw hit thousands of stores.

Patching quickly and checking for earlier compromise remain the best defenses. The full technical breakdown is in Imperva’s research blog.

File Hashes

Network Indicators

Note: IP addresses and domains are intentionally Qdefanged (e.g., [.]) to prevent accidental resolution or hyperlinking. Re-fang only within controlled threat intelligence platforms such as MISP, VirusTotal, or your SIEM.

The post Cogent Security Makes the Fortune Cyber 60 for a Second Year, With a Plan to Run Cyber Defense Like a Factory appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
San Francisco, CA, November 3rd, 2026, CyberNewswire

Cogent Security, an applied AI cybersecurity company, reported that the PHP2Shell vulnerability exposed significant gaps in enterprise vulnerability response.

Disclosed on October 21, PHP2Shell involved two critical flaws that had remained in PHP for more than a decade.

AI-assisted research helped identify the vulnerabilities and develop working exploits in approximately one week, with attacks beginning before a patch was available. Cloudflare recorded millions of exploitation attempts that day.

According to Cogent Security’s research, by 5 p.m. Pacific, the average Fortune 500 company had patched fewer than 1% of its 2,266 affected assets.

That gap between how fast attackers move and how fast large companies respond is the problem Cogent was built to close.

The company, an applied AI lab focused on cybersecurity, has been named to the Fortune Cyber 60 for the second consecutive year.

The list, developed by Fortune with Lightspeed Venture Partners and AWS, recognizes 60 of the most important venture-backed cybersecurity startups that have yet to go public, be acquired, or reach another significant exit, grouped by stage.

Selection weighs financial performance, growth, business operations, and cybersecurity market research, and Fortune validates the final list. 

“Attackers already run like a factory. AI is finding the bugs and writing the exploits, and in some cases it’s running most of the attack,” said Vineet Edupuganti, Cogent’s co-founder and CEO.

“Most enterprises are still defending by hand, one ticket and one handoff at a time. Making this list two years in a row tells us security leaders are ready to change how that work gets done.”

The attackers built their factories first

Edupuganti borrows an analogy from manufacturing. Factories replaced the lone skilled worker with a production line, and the most advanced plants now run largely on their own while people design the line and handle the exceptions.

Offense, he argues, has already made that shift.

The data points the same way. Google’s M-Trends 2026 report estimates the mean time to exploit at negative seven days, which means exploitation now routinely begins before a fix exists.

Researchers have shown AI producing working exploits for newly published vulnerabilities in about 15 minutes, at roughly a dollar apiece. In a state-sponsored campaign that Anthropic disrupted, AI agents carried out 80 to 90% of the tactical work.

Enterprise defense still moves at the pace of its slowest handoff. When PHP2Shell landed, security teams had to find every asset running PHP, including base images and forgotten servers, then work out which were internet-facing and which the business depended on.

After that came owners, tickets, change windows, and a rescan to confirm each fix held, with every step falling to a skilled person with a tool.

Building the Defender’s Production Line

Cogent’s answer is what it calls the Cyber Defense Factory, an operating model in which AI agents take over the work that now moves by hand between security tools, while people set the policies those agents follow.

The company sells an enterprise platform for autonomous cyber defense, and its first product applies the model to vulnerability management.

The line starts with an inventory. Agents build one deduplicated record of every asset across cloud, on-premises and endpoint environments, inferring each one’s owner and business importance from systems the company already keeps.

Findings flow in from the scanners and security tools customers already run, and Cogent matches newly published vulnerabilities against its live software inventory so exposure surfaces before scanners catch up.

Agents then check whether the vulnerable software is running and reachable, and they write out the reasoning behind every priority.

Cogent groups remediation work by fix, so one patch can resolve a vulnerability across dozens of servers. Inside the autonomy zones each customer defines, agents carry out supported fixes on their own.

On managed endpoints, for instance, they write the remediation script, push it through the company’s existing endpoint management platform, and read back the results.

Changes outside those zones go to a single owner as a ticket and wait for a person’s approval, and Cogent closes the work only after the next scan confirms the fix held.

The company says the goal is for enterprises to transform their cybersecurity functions with a factory model to do 100 times more work, 100 times faster.

Most customers start with agents in an assistive role and widen their authority as the results earn trust, an approach Cogent calls progressive autonomy.

PHP2Shell gave the model a live test. Cogent’s Zero Day Response processed the advisory and mapped vulnerable assets across customer environments in an average of five minutes, days before scanner signatures were available.

Applied to the average Fortune 500 environment in Cogent’s research, the analysis cut 2,266 affected assets down to 16 that had PHP loaded at runtime, faced the internet, and supported critical business functions.

That shortlist was waiting for security teams when they sat down to start work.

A Lab With Its Own Models

Cogent describes itself as an applied AI lab that just happens to focus on defensive cybersecurity, and the label reflects how the company is built.

It is the only cybersecurity company that trains and deploys its own frontier reasoning models for security use cases.

Its domain-specific model, VR-1, has topped cybersecurity benchmarks, outperforming general-purpose frontier models on security tasks.

The model works alongside Cogent’s Context Engine, which ties each vulnerability to the assets, identities, applications, owners, and dependencies around it.

That context usually sits scattered across asset databases, ticket histories and architecture documents, and pulling it together is what lets agents judge which changes are safe to make.

“A general-purpose AI model knows a little about everything,” Edupuganti said. “When an AI agent is deciding whether a patch is safe to push to a few thousand production servers, it needs a model that has learned how vulnerabilities, exploits and enterprise systems behave, plus deep context on the company it’s protecting. Put those together and you can give agents real responsibility.”

Racing the Exploit Clock

For security leaders, Edupuganti argues, the number that matters now is the time between a vulnerability’s disclosure and a verified fix, and that window has to be shorter than the time an attacker needs to build and launch an exploit.

Cogent is betting that closing it takes a different operating model, one where security work grows with the production line rather than with headcount.

The company’s second straight appearance on the Cyber 60 suggests buyers are warming to that bet, though Edupuganti expects people to stay at the center of it.

“The most advanced factories still have people in them. They decide what the line builds and the standard it holds,” he said. “Security teams are moving into that role. They set the policy and make the judgment calls, and the agents do the work at machine speed.”

About Cogent

Cogent Security is an applied AI lab building the enterprise platform for autonomous cyber defense. Its AI agents find and fix vulnerabilities at machine speed so every enterprise can run its own Cyber Defense Factory.

Starting with autonomous vulnerability management, Cogent carries vulnerabilities from disclosure to a verified fix across cloud, on-premises, and endpoint environments, identifying exposure within minutes and confirming what attackers can reach along the way.

Customers set the policies the agents follow and decide which fixes run autonomously and which wait for approval.

Fortune 500 security teams using Cogent have reduced the exposure window for critical vulnerabilities by 97 percent.

Built by researchers and operators from Google DeepMind, Abnormal Security, and Coinbase, Cogent is backed by Greylock Partners and Bain Capital Ventures. Learn more at cogent.com.

Contact

Ignacio Ramirez

press@cogent.com

The post Cogent Security Makes the Fortune Cyber 60 for a Second Year, With a Plan to Run Cyber Defense Like a Factory appeared first on Cyber Security News.

articles.title: Hackers Hijacked Linux Hosting Server Security Tool cPGuard and Used It as a Backdoor
articles.description:
An unidentified attacker compromised the update channel for cPGuard, a security tool used on Linux hosting servers, to distribute a malicious script that installed a backdoor and collected sensitive files. OPSSHIELD confirmed that the attacker retrieved some stolen data and urged administrators to install version 5.88.25 or later immediately. According to OPSSHIELD’s security advisory, the […]

The post Hackers Hijacked Linux Hosting Server Security Tool cPGuard and Used It as a Backdoor appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
An unidentified attacker compromised the update channel for cPGuard, a security tool used on Linux hosting servers, to distribute a malicious script that installed a backdoor and collected sensitive files. OPSSHIELD confirmed that the attacker retrieved some stolen data and urged administrators to install version 5.88.25 or later immediately.

According to OPSSHIELD’s security advisory, the breach began on November 2, 2026, at 02:06 UTC. The attacker used compromised credentials to access the company’s update distribution infrastructure, or CDN. How those credentials were obtained remains under investigation.

cPGuard Supply Chain Attack

The attacker distributed the script through cPGuard versions 5.88.12 through 5.88.19. OPSSHIELD detected the attack within 12 hours of the affected updates becoming available, secured the compromised account, cleared infrastructure credentials, and stopped further distribution. Because servers check for updates at intervals, some may not have executed the malicious script.

The attack turned a trusted security update into a route for malware delivery. Related Cybersecuritynews coverage of compromised Terraform workflows shows another way attackers have used trusted software processes to deliver backdoors. The cPGuard incident specifically involved stolen access to the vendor’s distribution infrastructure.

The malicious script collected Linux account files, including /etc/shadow and /etc/passwd, root MariaDB or MySQL configuration, root shell history, and root SSH authorization and known-hosts files. OPSSHIELD has not established that every listed file was collected from every affected server.

Collected data went to OPSSHIELD’s own licensing server under a compromised account, where the attacker could retrieve it later. In a November 3 update, the company estimated that the attacker retrieved 32 collected files, each corresponding to one customer server. That preliminary figure measures confirmed retrieval, not the total number of potentially affected servers.

Linux passwords in /etc/shadow are stored as hashes rather than readable passwords. Attackers can test password guesses against stolen hashes offline, making weak or reused passwords particularly risky. Database configuration and shell history may contain other secrets without that protection.

The wider concern is credential reuse beyond the original server. Cybersecuritynews previously covered QLNX credential theft targeting Linux developers, another case highlighting the value of SSH keys and cloud credentials to attackers. No connection between these incidents has been established.

Administrators should review update history with grep 'Successfully updated' /opt/cpguard/logs/install_log. Entries showing versions 5.88.12 through 5.88.19 confirm installation of an affected update, but do not prove script execution or data transfer. Missing or incomplete logs also cannot establish that a server escaped compromise.

Known indicators include the script cpguard-v58812-i91511.sh, backdoor shell /var/tmp/.cpg91511_sh, collection directory /var/tmp/.cpg91511, and staged archive /var/tmp/.cpg91511/loot.tgz. Their absence after cleanup does not rule out earlier execution.

OPSSHIELD instructs every customer to run cpgcli update --start, then check cpgcli --version to confirm version 5.88.25 or later. Administrators whose updates fail should contact OPSSHIELD Support. The corrective update removes the known backdoor and staged files, but cannot invalidate credentials already copied.

Potentially compromised servers require password resets for root and other password-enabled local accounts from a trusted recovery environment. Administrators should rotate affected database passwords, S3 keys, DigitalOcean tokens, and exposed shell-history secrets. They should replace private keys under /root/.ssh and remove corresponding old public keys wherever trusted.

OPSSHIELD is also releasing an update to remove previously added support-access keys. It does not currently recommend routine server rebuilds, but that guidance remains provisional. Additional compromise signs or uncertain server integrity may justify rebuilding after an individual assessment.

The post CrowdStrike and Deloitte Expand AI Security Partnership to Transform How Enterprises Detect Cyber Threats appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
CrowdStrike and Deloitte have expanded their cybersecurity partnership to connect business risk decisions with threat detection and response. Announced on November 2, 2026, at Fal.Con Europe in Barcelona, the agreement brings Falcon IQ into Deloitte Spain’s advisory services, linking security planning with implementation and managed operations.

The expanded alliance focuses on a practical problem: identifying security weaknesses does not automatically lead to fixing them. CrowdStrike supplies its Falcon platform and AI tools, while Deloitte turns findings into investment plans, technology changes, and ongoing security work.

“Finding risk is only half the battle. What matters is how quickly you can act on it and evolve strategy for the future,” said Daniel Bernard, CrowdStrike’s chief business officer.

Falcon IQ Connects Risk Findings

At the center of the expansion is Falcon IQ, which gives Deloitte a measurable view of exploitable risk. Deloitte will use those findings alongside executive Innovation Workshops to build security plans covering immediate fixes, medium-term improvements, and longer-term goals tied to business needs and regulatory priorities.

CrowdStrike introduced Falcon IQ on August 31, 2026, to automate assessment and repair workflows under Project QuiltWorks. The platform combines customer security data, CrowdStrike threat intelligence, and findings from Falcon OverWatch threat hunters to help partners understand exposure and recommend action.

Built on Falcon Foundry and Charlotte AI AgentWorks, Falcon IQ uses more than 50 AI agents across assessment, prioritization, and remediation tasks. NVIDIA’s open Nemotron models power its agent engine. Partners can also map findings to their own services, producing action plans and tracking progress through a customer dashboard.

This work sits alongside broader concerns about AI systems. Cyber Security News previously covered CrowdStrike’s research into prompt injection techniques, showing how malicious instructions can target agents that browse websites, access data, and execute commands.

The implementation stage includes moving customers to Falcon Next-Gen SIEM. SIEM, short for security information and event management, brings security data together for analysis. CrowdStrike’s platform combines that data with AI-based detection, investigation tools, threat intelligence, and automated response workflows.

For analysts, the intended benefit is clearer context across connected systems rather than isolated alerts. Falcon Next-Gen SIEM supports third-party security and IT data, while licensed Falcon modules can contribute endpoint, identity, and cloud activity without additional ingestion charges.

Data handling is also part of this shift. Cyber Security News previously reported on CrowdStrike’s planned acquisition of Onum, whose technology filters and routes security data before analysis. Falcon’s current SIEM offering includes Onum data pipelines.

The operational stage builds on Deloitte’s November 2025 integration of Falcon Next-Gen SIEM into its Managed Extended Detection and Response service, known as MXDR. That service combines continuous monitoring with human investigation, threat intelligence, and response support.

Deloitte’s EMEA Cybersphere Center in Madrid will support delivery under the expanded agreement. Edward James Moore, cybersecurity partner at Deloitte Spain, said the collaboration helps clients connect risk insights with security investments and carry those priorities into implementation and daily operations.

The announcement sets out a service model, not measured customer results. It provides no deployment timelines, pricing, or evidence showing how much the expanded arrangement improves detection or response times.

articles.title: Attackers Started Scanning in the Wild for Linux Kernel RCE Flaw, Ubuntu Releases Fixes
articles.description:
Ubuntu has put early kernel fixes for CVE-2026-98432 in its -proposed pocket for 22.04 LTS and newer releases. The bug is a serious Linux kernel flaw that can let a remote user run commands as root without a login or any user action. The patches are still in testing, so many servers stay open for […]

The post Attackers Started Scanning in the Wild for Linux Kernel RCE Flaw, Ubuntu Releases Fixes appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
Ubuntu has put early kernel fixes for CVE-2026-98432 in its -proposed pocket for 22.04 LTS and newer releases. The bug is a serious Linux kernel flaw that can let a remote user run commands as root without a login or any user action. The patches are still in testing, so many servers stay open for now.

Canonical’s security team says the flaw sits in how the Linux kernel sets up IPv4 TCP connections, and it affects kernel versions 4.4 and later. The fixed builds are 5.15.0-203.213 for Jammy (22.04), 6.8.0-149.149 for Noble (24.04), and 7.0.0-43.43 for Resolute (26.04). Stonking (26.10) is already fixed in 7.3.0-10.10, and Trusty (14.04) is not affected. Fixes for Xenial, Bionic and Focal are still pending.

Canonical runs tests on more than 2,000 certified servers and devices before it moves a kernel to the updates pocket. Teams that run their own acceptance tests can install the early builds today, as described in Canonical’s new SRU strategy for faster CVE fixes.

Ubuntu’s CVE-2026-98432 tracker rates the bug 9.8, which is Critical. Its own blog post calls the same score “High,” so readers may see both labels. The record was published on October 15, 2026.

The bug is a use-after-free. In plain terms, the kernel keeps using a piece of memory after it has already let go of it. One CPU frees the IP options of a new connection. Another CPU, handling a repeated SYN packet, still reads them while building a reply. The upstream fix delays that free with kfree_rcu(), so readers finish first.

Anthropic’s Frontier Red Team shared its research on October 27, 2026. It says an unreleased Claude model wrote a working exploit after one first prompt. The exploit targets Linux servers with a multipath TCP (MPTCP) listener.

It works in two stages. First, it makes the kernel send back extra bytes that may hold a kernel pointer, which defeats KASLR, a defense that hides where kernel code sits. Second, it overwrites a callback pointer so the kernel runs a payload and ends in a shell command as root.

A lost race only fails the handshake and does not crash the machine, so the attacker can retry. In the test, the leak took 48 minutes, and the shell took five more.

Cyber Security News covered this in Claude AI Exploits Linux Kernel Flaw to Execute Root Commands Without User Interaction. Our earlier report on Claude building Chrome and Linux exploit chains shows how this fits a wider pattern. Anthropic’s exploit has not been released. It also says this was a lab test and not a real-world incident.

Signs of Scanning in the Wild

Researcher Marcus Hutchins says his team has seen what looks like threat actors scanning the whole internet for affected systems. In a post on X, he reports that residential proxies and Russia-based VPN servers began probing port 443 with MPTCP connections as of November 2.

Normal scanners do not use MPTCP by default, so he strongly suspects this activity targets CVE-2026-98432. His scan on October 30 found about 2,102,043 servers reachable over MPTCP on port 443.

A deeper TLS scan found about 762,774. He says a valid HTTP request is not needed, so the true exposure is likely closer to 2.1 million. These counts show exposure only and do not prove the kernels are unpatched.

There is no public remote code execution exploit yet. Several denial-of-service proofs-of-concept do exist, and they give attackers a starting point.

Some people assumed MPTCP listeners were rare. Hutchins points out that Debian and several other kernels enable MPTCP by default. Go 1.24 and later also bind MPTCP sockets when the kernel allows it, so tools built on Go, such as Caddy, create the needed listener.

Ubuntu emphasizes that the flaw itself is not tied to MPTCP, and the MPTCP link comes only from the Anthropic exploit. Ubuntu’s security team says updates are the only proper fix. Hutchins adds that setting net.mptcp.enabled=0 does not close sockets that are already open, so those apps must restart. You can list MPTCP listeners with sudo ss -Mlnp.

For Admins

Run uname -r and compare the result with the fixed versions above. Ubuntu’s guide to enabling the -proposed pocket explains how to pull in the new kernel, and a reboot is needed afterward. Packages in -proposed are not chosen for upgrade by default, so you must name the pocket when you install.

For hosts that cannot update yet, Ubuntu’s tracker lists an nftables rule that drops incoming IPv4 TCP packets carrying IP options. It reduces risk but does not fully prevent exploitation, and it breaks any connection that relies on IP options.

Ubuntu 20.04 LTS and older need Ubuntu Pro. Focal and Bionic fall under Expanded Security Maintenance, while Xenial and Trusty need the Legacy add-on. Ubuntu Pro is free for up to five machines.
