articles.description:
Hackers have reportedly targeted refrigeration systems at Swedish supermarkets, leaving stores with spoiled food after freezers reached temperatures as high as 55°C. Several ICA locations and six Coop stores were affected overnight into November 2, forcing staff to clear damaged stock and restore cooling systems. The incidents follow similar attacks against French supermarkets in October, […]

The post Hackers Hijack Swedish Supermarket Fridges and Raise Freezer Temperatures to 55°C appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
Hackers have reportedly targeted refrigeration systems at Swedish supermarkets, leaving stores with spoiled food after freezers reached temperatures as high as 55°C.

Several ICA locations and six Coop stores were affected overnight into November 2, forcing staff to clear damaged stock and restore cooling systems. The incidents follow similar attacks against French supermarkets in October, although no connection has been confirmed.

According to Swedish broadcaster SVT, ICA Nära store manager Mats Olsson found water on the floor when he arrived at his shop in Böda, Öland. He reported a freezer temperature of 55°C, with refrigerators and freezers knocked out and their contents ruined.

Swedish Stores Face Food Losses

Affected ICA stores included locations in Sjöbo, Tomelilla, Brösarp and Sankt Olof in Skåne. Reports also covered Öland, Värmland and Stockholm. Six Coop stores in Gästrikland and Hälsingland were affected, but the full number of Swedish stores involved remained unclear.

The ICA store in Sjöbo temporarily closed after reporting temperatures around 50°C. In Sankt Olof, store manager Dennis Vidal said workers were emptying freezers as cooling began to return, but the food was already ruined. At ICA Baronen in Stockholm, staff reported temperatures rising from 38°C to around 50°C.

ICA press officer Gustaf Nilsson said the company was investigating and helping affected stores. Importantly, ICA said the affected shops had connections outside its central network. That distinction does not establish how attackers gained access, but it means the incident should not automatically be described as a breach of ICA’s central systems.

The Swedish reports have not identified the controller brands, entry point, exploited software flaw or attackers. There is also no confirmed evidence that the same group targeted stores in Sweden and France. Any claim naming a specific vulnerability would therefore be premature.

However, the earlier French incidents show why connected cooling equipment needs close attention. Cybersecurity News previously reported on supermarket refrigerators being remotely manipulated, with attackers reportedly changing settings to keep equipment in defrost mode. This function normally clears ice, but prolonged operation can raise temperatures and destroy stock.

France’s national cyber response team, CERT-FR, confirmed compromises involving Danfoss AK-SM and AK-SC controllers, alongside Copeland xweb and Dixell xweb devices. Its official refrigeration security alert warned against exposing management interfaces directly to the internet. These findings concern the French incidents, not confirmed equipment at Swedish stores.

A related Cybersecurity News report on exposed Danfoss systems highlighted how widely refrigeration management pages could be reached online. Such exposure creates a direct route to equipment that controls physical conditions, rather than only business records or payment systems.

CERT-FR advises operators to remove public internet access, check controller settings, including defrost schedules, and restore remote access through a secure VPN or protected network. It also recommends firmware updates and changing default passwords. Operators should coordinate changes with refrigeration providers, including checking insurance terms before interrupting monitoring connections.

The agency also warns that resetting an unsupported controller is not enough. Without removing exposure and addressing the underlying weakness, the equipment can be compromised again, putting replacement stock at risk once cooling resumes and stores begin restocking their shelves.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
Quick Answer: Linx is the AI-native solution for modern IGA across all identity types; SailPoint remains the IGA benchmark with AI-driven certifications; Saviynt leads cloud-native converged governance; Microsoft Entra ID Governance wins bundled economics in M365 estates; Omada owns the configurable mid-enterprise; One Identity rules AD-heavy shops.

IGA answers the question auditors always ask: who should have access and can you prove it?

Access reviews done in spreadsheets are how audit findings and insider breaches happen. Identity Governance & Administration automates the entitlement lifecycle: joiner-mover-leaver provisioning, access certifications, separation-of-duties enforcement, and the continuous evidence trail that SOX, ISO, and enterprise cybersecurity frameworks now expect on an ongoing basis rather than during annual scrambles.

The 2026 field pairs deep incumbents with cloud-native challengers, while AI-assisted certification (recommend, don’t rubber-stamp) became the real differentiator.

We scored ten tools across five weighted criteria, then detail each features, best fit, pros, cons. Editorial assessment, not a lab test; pricing by model only.

  1. How We Evaluated
  2. The Scorecard

How We Evaluated the Best Identity Governance & Administration (IGA) Tools in 2026

To select the top 10 Identity Governance and Administration (IGA) tools in 2026, we evaluated each solution based on its identity security capabilities, governance features, automation, scalability, and overall business value. Our evaluation focuses on the following 10 key criteria:

1. Identity Lifecycle Management: We assess how effectively each tool automates user provisioning, access modifications, and deprovisioning across employee, contractor, and third-party identities.

2. Access Governance and Certification: We evaluate access reviews, periodic certifications, entitlement management, and approval workflows to determine how well organizations can control user permissions.

3. Role-Based Access Control (RBAC): We examine how each platform supports role management, least-privilege access, role mining, and separation of duties (SoD) to reduce unnecessary access.

4. Automation and AI Capabilities: We assess AI-driven access recommendations, automated identity workflows, risk-based decisions, and intelligent access reviews that reduce manual administrative work.

5. Integration and Compatibility: We examine integration capabilities with Active Directory, Microsoft Entra ID, cloud applications, HR systems, enterprise applications, and existing security infrastructure.

6. Compliance and Audit Readiness: We evaluate built-in reporting, audit trails, access certification records, and support for regulatory requirements such as GDPR, HIPAA, SOX, and ISO 27001.

7. Security and Risk Management: We assess how effectively each solution detects excessive privileges, orphaned accounts, toxic access combinations, and identity-related security risks.

8. Scalability and Deployment Flexibility: We examine whether the platform supports growing enterprise environments, hybrid infrastructures, multi-cloud deployments, and complex organizational structures.

9. Ease of Use and Administration: We evaluate dashboard usability, configuration complexity, workflow customization, deployment effort, and the administrative skills required for ongoing management.

10. Pricing, Support, and Overall Value: We consider licensing models, implementation costs, technical support, documentation, customer feedback, and the overall value delivered to organizations of different sizes.

Our Evaluation Approach: These criteria provide a consistent framework for comparing IGA solutions based on security effectiveness, operational efficiency, and enterprise requirements. The final ranking should also consider verified product documentation, available demonstrations, independent user reviews, and publicly documented capabilities to help organizations identify the most suitable identity governance platform for their needs.

The Scorecard

The 10 Tools in Depth

1. Linx Security

Description. The AI-native leader: Linx is the identity security platform for the agentic era. Linx’s AI-native platform unifies identity discovery, posture management, and access governance to help organizations uncover critical exposures, prioritize what matters most, and enforce least-privilege access.

From employees and service accounts to applications and AI agents, Linx enables organizations to govern every identity and proactively mitigate risk across the enterprise.

Key features: Autonomous agents; identity graph; lifecycle automation; access review campaigns; MCP Gateway; converged IGA+ISPM

Best for: Mid-market and enterprise teams modernizing IGA that don’t want to rely on professional services

Pros: AI-driven review automation; unified governance and posture; native NHI and AI agent coverage; time-to-value.

Cons: Newer vendor with a smaller install base.

2. Saviynt

Description. The cloud-native converger: Enterprise Identity Cloud delivers converged IGA and Cloud Infrastructure Entitlement Management (CIEM) alongside application GRC in a single unified SaaS platform strongest where governance must bridge SaaS applications, multi-cloud control planes, and SAP-grade SoD without deploying three separate products.

Key features: Converged IGA+CIEM+app GRC; fine-grained SoD (SAP/ERP depth); cloud-native SaaS; risk-based certifications; peer analytics.

Best for: Cloud-first enterprises and ERP-heavy compliance.

Pros: Convergence breadth; ERP SoD depth; SaaS delivery.

Cons: Configuration complexity at depth; services-heavy deployments persist.

3. Microsoft (Entra ID Governance)

Description. Governance at bundle economics: native entitlement management, access reviews, lifecycle workflows, and Privileged Identity Management (PIM) integration built directly into Microsoft Entra hardening directories to prevent scenarios where Microsoft Entra ID vulnerabilities let attackers escalate privilegesthrough unmonitored service principals and federated roles.

Key features: Access packages/entitlement management; automated access reviews; lifecycle workflows (JML); PIM synergy; published add-on pricing.

Best for: M365 estates wanting governance without a new platform.

Pros: Price/level of effort unbeatable in-stack; native depth.

Cons: Cross-platform/legacy connector breadth trails specialists; deep SoD lighter than SailPoint/Saviynt.

4. One Identity (Identity Manager)

Description. The Active Directory and SAP workhorse: Identity Manager delivers granular lifecycle provisioning, access certification, and SoD policy enforcement, supported by active vendor patches that remediate One Identity Manager privilege escalation vulnerabilities
across on-premises enterprise environments.

Key features: Deep AD/SAP connectors; granular lifecycle; certification/SoD; data governance extension; on-prem/hybrid deployment.

Best for: AD/SAP-centric enterprises modernizing deliberately.

Pros: AD/SAP depth benchmark; deployment control.

Cons: Cloud-native polish trails SaaS rivals; interface utilitarian.

5. IBM (Verify Governance)

Description. Governance with services scale: IBM Verify Governance handles access certification, automated provisioning, and role and risk modeling, supported by security updates addressing vulnerabilities in the IBM Security Verify platform typically deployed inside larger IBM identity or GRC transformations where consulting delivery matters as much as software.

Key features: Certifications; provisioning; role/risk modeling; SAP integration; IBM services ecosystem.

Best for: IBM-aligned enterprises and services-led programs.

Pros: Enterprise credibility; services muscle.

Cons: Product momentum trails leaders; ecosystem-dependent value.

6. Omada

Description. The configurable mid-enterprise champion: Omada Identity Cloud incorporates standard IGA process frameworks (IdentityPROCESS+) that deploy in weeks rather than years, aligned with essential criteria for choosing the right enterprise IAM and IGA solutions to deliver European-grade governance globally.

Key features: Templated best-practice processes; certification/SoD; lifecycle automation; SaaS delivery; strong European compliance fit.

Best for: Mid-to-large enterprises wanting depth without SailPoint-scale programs.

Pros: Time-to-value with real depth; process templates.

Cons: Connector breadth and AI trail the top two; NA brand still building.

7. Oracle (Access Governance)

Description. Oracle-estate governance modernized: the cloud-native Access Governance service brings AI-assisted access reviews and continuous lifecycle automation across Oracle applications, OCI, and databases, protecting against configuration gaps that expose vulnerabilities in Oracle E-Business Suite and ERP applications.

Key features: AI-assisted access reviews; OCI-native service; Oracle app/DB connector depth; lifecycle; usage-based cloud pricing.

Best for: Oracle-centric enterprises.

Pros: Oracle-stack integration; modernized SaaS delivery.

Cons: Limited pull beyond Oracle estates; ecosystem breadth narrow.

8. Okta (Identity Governance)

Description. Governance unified where access lives: Okta Identity Governance (OIG) adds access requests, periodic certifications, and lifecycle workflows natively to Okta’s core platform, evaluated in our top identity and access management solutions roundup for SaaS-centric businesses.

Key features: Access requests/certifications in Okta; workflow automation; lifecycle synergy with Okta provisioning; per-user add-on pricing.

Best for: Okta estates needing pragmatic governance fast.

Pros: Zero-friction adoption; unified admin.

Cons: SoD/analytics depth trails specialists; Okta-tenant scope.

9. RSA (Governance & Lifecycle)

Description. The installed-base stalwart: RSA Governance & Lifecycle (formerly Aveksa) serves long-standing enterprise deployments with access certification, request management, and identity tracking, evaluated among enterprise user access management and governance tools
for high-assurance compliance.

Key features: Certifications; lifecycle; violation management; on-prem strength; RSA Unified Identity platform alignment.

Best for: Existing RSA governance estates optimizing continuity.

Pros: Proven at scale; incumbent stability.

Cons: New-selection momentum low; modernization diligence needed.

10. Ping Identity (incl. ForgeRock)

Description. Scope note: Ping Identity (with ForgeRock unified under its umbrella) is primarily an access management and CIAM platform; its governance capabilities focus on identity orchestration and relationship modeling aligned with NIST Zero Trust Architecture guidelines
, typically pairing with a specialist like SailPoint or Saviynt for full SoD programs.

Key features: Identity lifecycle (ForgeRock lineage); relationship/role modeling; orchestration hooks to IGA partners; unified Ping platform.

Best for: Ping-anchored estates with light governance needs or as the access layer beside specialist IGA.

Pros: Orchestration strength; platform consolidation.

Cons: Not a certification/SoD specialist; pair for full IGA.

Full Comparison Table

Buyer’s Guide

Match program appetite to platform weight. Full-scale regulated governance → SailPoint (depth/AI) or Saviynt (convergence/ERP). Weeks-not-years with real depth → Omada.

M365-centric → Entra ID Governance first; add a specialist only where its SoD/connector gaps bite. Okta-centric SaaS estates → OIG for pragmatic coverage. AD/SAP-on-prem truth → One Identity. Oracle estates → Access Governance.

AI is the certification cure: recommendation engines (SailPoint’s benchmark) are what stop reviewers from approve-all fatigue demand live demos on your entitlement data.

Secure on-premises truth: Where Active Directory and legacy on-premises systems remain authoritative, One Identity provides direct operational control ensure environments are audited against an Active Directory security checklist to eliminate stale privileged accounts.

Key takeaways: per-identity quoting dominates (Entra’s published add-on is the price anchor); machine and non-employee identities are the growth audit surface verify coverage; convergence (Saviynt IGA+CIEM) saves platforms but adds configuration; and certification evidence must export cleanly auditors, not dashboards, are the customer.

FAQ

What are the best IGA tools in 2026?

SailPoint (benchmark depth/AI), Saviynt (cloud-native convergence), Entra ID Governance (bundled economics), Omada (configurable time-to-value), One Identity (AD/SAP depth) with Okta OIG, Oracle, IBM, and RSA serving their ecosystems.

What does IGA do that IAM doesn’t?

IAM authenticates and connects users; IGA governs entitlements automated joiner-mover-leaver provisioning, access certifications, SoD enforcement, and audit evidence. IAM is the door; IGA decides who deserves keys.

How is IGA priced?

Per governed identity per year, almost universally by quote SailPoint/Saviynt/Omada at premium tiers, with Microsoft’s published Entra ID Governance add-on the market’s transparent price anchor, and Okta OIG a per-user add-on.

Why is IGA critical for preventing privilege abuse?

Unmonitored entitlement creep leaves orphaned accounts and dormant permissions open for attackers. Understanding how attackers exploit privileged access highlights why continuous access certifications and automated deprovisioning are necessary to starve lateral movement.

SailPoint or Saviynt?

SailPoint for the deepest certifications, AI, and connector maturity; Saviynt for converged IGA+CIEM+ERP GRC in one SaaS. ERP-heavy SoD leans Saviynt; broadest governance depth leans SailPoint. Both are program commitments.

Is Entra ID Governance enough?

For M365-centric estates with moderate SoD needs often yes, at unbeatable economics. Cross-platform connector depth, ERP SoD, and advanced role mining remain the specialist’s territory.

Why did AI become the IGA differentiator?

Certification fatigue: reviewers rubber-stamp bulk approvals. AI recommendations, peer-group outliers, and role mining turn reviews into risk decisions measurably reducing inappropriate access instead of documenting it.

Conclusion

IGA turns “who has access” from an audit scramble into an automated, evidenced process. SailPoint sets the depth-and-AI benchmark; Saviynt converges governance with cloud entitlements; Entra ID Governance makes M365 estates governance-credible at add-on pricing; Omada compresses time-to-value; One Identity, Oracle, IBM, RSA, and Okta serve their strongholds; and Ping (ForgeRock) plays the access layer beside true specialists.

Demand AI recommendations on your own data, verify machine-identity coverage, and buy the platform your program appetite can actually feed.

There’s ahigh change AI has already entered your workflow the question is whether it has entered on your terms oryour employee’s personal […]

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
Every penetration testing firm is facing the same pressure right now. AI tools are faster, cheaper, andincreasingly capable, and testers are using them whether the company has a policy on it or not.

There’s ahigh change AI has already entered your workflow the question is whether it has entered on your terms oryour employee’s personal Claude account.And in this industry, that distinction really matters.

The Cloud AI Problem No One Wants to Talk About

When a developer pastes code into ChatGPT, the worst case is a licensing headache. When a penetration tester does the same thing with a client’s findings, you’ve just uploaded a detailed map of a company’s vulnerabilities to a third-party cloud infrastructure you have no control over.

Besides a policy violation, that’s a potential breach of client confidentiality, NDA, and in regulated industries, compliance frameworks like GDPR or HIPAA.

The major AI providers (OpenAI, Anthropic, Google) are excellent products. But their cloud-hosted models were not designed with the data sensitivity of offensive security work in mind.

Client scope documents, discovered vulnerabilities, network diagrams, hardcoded credentials found during testing. None of that should be leaving your infrastructure, and none of it should be in a training pipeline you didn’t consent to.

The truth is that if your firm doesn’t give testers a sanctioned AI workflow, they will build their own. And it’s not likely they’ll be thinking about your client contracts when they do.

The Right Architecture Exists

The answer isn’t to ban AI. That ship has sailed, and the firms that try will just end up with testers using it covertly while competitors who embrace it properly pull ahead on speed and output quality.

The answer is to bring AI in-house, on infrastructure you control, with client data that never leaves your network.

Self-hosted AI models have matured significantly. Running a capable model locally is no longer just a research project, but an operational choice.

And when you combine a self-hosted model with an orchestration layer built specifically for security workflows, you get the productivity benefits of AI without handing your clients’ attack surface to a third party.

AI specifically designed for cybersecurity companies

PentestPad is a pentest reporting tool that reduces the time security teams spend turning raw notes into a client-ready report, while keeping the project organised around it.

The teams using it are not all in the same business. Some deliver security testing to clients. Some test their own systems in-house.

Others coordinate several external providers at once, and use the platform to keep the findings in one place.

Day to day that means project management, collaboration, retesting and report generation. Much of the tooling that usually surrounds a pentest sits inside it as well: notes, evidence and attachments, comments on findings, proposals and scope import.

Less of the work needs a scratch file, a shared drive or a spreadsheet.

Almost none of it is fixed. Reports generate from your own template rather than a generic one, the client portal carries your branding on your own domain, and the fields, layouts and statuses behind a finding are defined by your team rather than inherited.

The instructions the AI assistant writes to are yours as well, so a draft comes back in your methodology and your wording rather than a generic house style.

The same holds for where it all runs. PentestPad is available as a managed cloud service or fully self-hosted on your own infrastructure, including air-gapped, and the writing assistant can be pointed at a self-hosted model inside your own network rather than a vendor’s.

That last choice is the one pentest teams get stuck on. A finding is a client’s unremediated vulnerability, and handing it to OpenAI or Anthropic’s API sends it to a company your client never agreed to.

Most client contracts list which outside companies are allowed to handle their data, and a model vendor is not on that list.

Adding one means telling every client and usually asking them to sign off, while the data sits somewhere you did not choose for as long as someone else decides. Running the model yourself removes the question instead of answering it.

The platform exposes itself over MCP, so an agent can work against your real findings, fields and templates instead of guessing at them.

Built for agents as well as people

PentestPad is built to be driven by software as well as by a person at a keyboard, and the model doing the driving can sit inside your own network.

That is the whole answer to the problem above: the assistant is pointed at a self-hosted LLM, and client content never crosses your perimeter.

The writing assistant works from what a tester already has. Hand it scanner output, a Burp finding, a screenshot or a log file, attach the evidence, and it returns a structured finding written to the instructions your organisation has defined, so the draft arrives in your format rather than a generic one.

Underneath, PentestPad exposes itself over MCP. Methodology, past findings, templates, finding fields and the rules for writing them live in the platform, and the MCP server exposes fourteen typed tools over them, from searching projects and findings to filing a new one from a template, updating remediation after a retest, or adding a comment.

The platform stays the source of truth and the agent holds no state of its own.

Run end to end the stack is three parts, all on hardware you control. PentestPad is the knowledge base, a local model does the reasoning, and a terminal harness is wired to both.

PentestPad’s own team uses Qwen3 Coder through Ollama, with OpenCode or Claude Code as the harness.

For teams that would rather not assemble one, there is a command-line agent for macOS, Linux and Windows, carrying six customisable specialists across web, network, reconnaissance, API and mobile testing, plus a general one for methodology and tool selection.

How the report gets built

A project holds the client, the assessment type, the scope, the testers assigned to it and the timeline.

Findings attach to it as testing progresses, so what is in scope, who is working on it and what has been found so far sit together rather than across a folder, a chat thread and a spreadsheet.

Each finding carries a title and description, the affected assets, severity, remediation, references and the supporting evidence.

Severity is set with a built-in CVSS calculator, and where a team hides its own impact and probability fields the risk rating derives from the CVSS score instead.

Findings do not have to start empty. A library of reusable vulnerability templates sits alongside the projects, searchable by name and filterable by assessment domain, and importing one fills every field of a new finding with your own house description, remediation text and CVSS vector, leaving only the engagement-specific detail to write. Executive summaries work the same way.

Findings move through statuses your team defines, from draft to ready. Comments attach to individual vulnerabilities rather than to the document, and revision history shows what changed between drafts.

The report itself is built from your own file, with placeholders dropped in where the data belongs, and the PentestPad team does the conversion at no cost. For teams starting from scratch there is a free penetration test report template to work from.

Generation pulls the structured data through it. Tables of contents regenerate on every build, charts and tables populate from the findings, and cross-references resolve through a dynamic link system so they stay correct when content moves.

Reusable field templates cover report-level and finding fields, and a live preview renders the document in the browser before anything is exported.

What comes out covers executive summary, scope, methodology, findings, technical detail, remediation recommendations and supporting information.

A single project can span more than one assessment domain, with each finding tagged to the domain it came from, so a web application test and a network test for the same client arrive as one report with the findings grouped rather than as two separate deliverables.

A library of template functions ships with the platform, from parsing a CVSS vector and deriving a risk rating to counting findings by severity or filtering scope down to just the IPs or just the URLs.

You can define your own JavaScript functions and call them from the template. Reports generate over the API, so a pipeline can produce one without a human opening the platform, and a finished PDF can be encrypted with a password you supply.

Individual DOCX or PDF files can be swapped inside an existing report without rebuilding it.

Branding, access and retention

Whitelabeling covers the logo, the colours and the domain, so someone logging in to check progress arrives at your brand rather than the vendor’s, down to the 2FA challenge screen, and exported reports carry the same identity.

Access control is granular rather than role-shaped. Pentester, Manager and Admin ship as defaults, but you can define your own roles from a permission set covering projects, findings, reports and clients, assign more than one role to a single user, and override individual permissions on top of a role where it does not quite fit.

Role administration is itself a separate permission, so team administration can be granted without also handing over the ability to edit roles. Client accounts are created and invited over the API, and client API keys are restricted separately from your team’s.

Uploads are scanned for malware and flagged files rejected, though anyone with the permission can override that and upload a known sample anyway. Scanning is always on for the managed service and optional when self-hosted.

The data lifecycle is configurable in the same way. Inactive projects archive automatically, and archived reports can be deleted on a schedule you set rather than accumulating until someone remembers them.

Deployment, compliance and pricing

Self-hosting is available on every tier, which matters when a client contract or an internal policy restricts where report data may live.

Self-hosted instances check a version endpoint and raise update notifications, so an isolated deployment knows when it has fallen behind.

Project data, evidence, the finding library, penetration test report template and user configuration export in DOCX, PDF, XLSX or over the API.

Quotes

Available if useful. Use either, both or neither.

“Where a client’s findings are allowed to live is decided by the team holding them, and for many that means nowhere outside their own infrastructure. That is the requirement we built the AI around, so the model runs wherever a team needs it to, including entirely inside their own network.”

Luka Šikić, CEO, PentestPad, Secure Block.

“Most teams reshape the fields, the layout and the statuses to match how they already work, set which parts a client can see, put their own branding on the portal and write their own instructions for how the AI should fill a finding in. That was the point of building it that way.”

Mirna Novak, Director, PentestPad

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
A retainer converts breach-day chaos into a phone number with obligations attached: guaranteed response times, pre-negotiated rates, privilege structure already standing, and in the modern form unused hours flexing into proactive work so the contract pays for itself in quiet years.

Rosters overlap with our DFIR-capability ranking by nature; this piece ranks the contracts: SLA teeth, credit flexibility, and terms that reward rather than punish an uneventful year. Google (Mandiant) takes 1; CrowdStrike and Unit 42 complete the podium.

Key Takeaways

• 1 overall: Mandiant the retainer that guarantees the bench everyone wants mid-crisis.

• Podium: Mandiant, CrowdStrike (speed-SLA strength), Unit 42 (the most flexible credit model).

• Contract lens: this ranking scores retainer mechanics response SLAs, credit conversion, zero-dollar options on top of bench quality, not instead of it.

• Roster note: BlackBerry’s Cylance endpoint business moved to Arctic Wolf; its retainer-relevant arm is the BlackBerry/Cylance IR services lineage confirm current structure before contracting.

How We Scored (Methodology)

Research-based evaluation; no lab testing, no paid placement; editorial scores excluded from structured data.

Criteria: response-time SLA strength, credit/hour flexibility (proactive conversion), bench quality behind the contract, privilege/insurer integration, global activation reach, and commercial accessibility (including zero-dollar retainers).

Weights: SLA strength 25%, credit flexibility 25%, bench quality 20%, insurer/privilege fit 15%, reach 15%.

The 2026 IR Retainer Power Rankings

*Editorial research-based scores, not lab results.

1. Google (Mandiant) — Best Guaranteed-Bench Retainer

Snapshot: Tiered retainers, proactive-conversion options | Priority access to the reference bench | Expertise-on-demand model

Why it earns 1: The scarcest resource in a mega-incident week is Mandiant’s calendar, and the retainer is how you reserve it: contracted response SLAs, pre-standing terms, and unused hours convertible into tabletops, threat assessments, and hunt engagements.

The contract’s core value is queue priority on the bench everyone calls scarcity economics, formalized.

Pros: Priority on the reference bench; proactive conversion breadth; privilege maturity.

Cons: Premium pricing; convert-or-lose terms need attention.

Bottom line: Reserving the firm everyone else is dialing.

2. CrowdStrike — Best Response-Speed SLAs

Snapshot: Retainer tiers with rapid-engagement terms | Falcon-deployment speed built into method | Services+platform bundling

Why it ranks here: CrowdStrike’s retainer sells minutes: aggressive engagement SLAs backed by a method Falcon pushed estate-wide in hours that makes the speed promise structural rather than aspirational. Bundling options alongside platform subscriptions tighten the economics for existing Falcon estates.

Pros: Engagement-speed terms; telemetry-backed method; platform bundling.

Cons: Method leans on Falcon deployment acceptance.

Bottom line: The stopwatch retainer.

3. Palo Alto (Unit 42) — Best Credit Flexibility

Snapshot: Credit-based retainers, broad service catalog | Credits span reactive and proactive catalogs | Platform-adjacent pricing leverage

Why it ranks here: Unit 42 modernized the retainer wallet: credits purchasable in blocks, spendable across a wide catalog IR, tabletops, purple teams, cloud compromise assessments, BEC investigations so an incident-free year converts fully into posture work.

For CFO-friendly retainer design, it’s the flexibility benchmark.

Pros: Widest credit catalog; no-waste economics; scale bench behind it.

Cons: Credit pricing details vary by bundle model carefully.

Bottom line: The retainer that refuses to expire quietly.

4. Kroll — Best Insurer-Integrated Retainer

Snapshot: Panel-aligned retainers, zero-dollar options | Breach-counsel ecosystem native | Notification machinery attached

Why it ranks here: Kroll’s retainer fits the way mid-market breaches actually unfold through insurers and counsel: panel-approved rates, privilege structure standing by design, zero-dollar retainer options that pre-position terms without annual spend, and the breach-logistics machine (notification, call centers, regulatory filings) one signature away.

Pros: Panel alignment; zero-dollar entry; end-to-end breach logistics.

Cons: Elite-APT bench depth sits with the firms above.

Bottom line: The retainer your insurer already recognizes.

5. Secureworks — Best Platform-Paired Retainer

Snapshot: Retainer + Taegis pairing | CTU-fed response | Sophos-family integration underway

Why it ranks here: Secureworks’ retainer compounds with its platform: Taegis-covered estates give responders instant telemetry , cutting the first forensic days to hours, with CTU intelligence behind the casework.

The acquisition-era question which entity, which service lines, what continuity belongs in the contract conversation.

Pros: Telemetry-accelerated activation; research-fed bench; co-managed synergy.

Cons: Post-acquisition structure diligence.

Bottom line: Strongest where Taegis already watches.

6. Sygnia — Best Boutique-Access Guarantee

Snapshot: Retainer-first engagement model | Senior-operator bench reservation | Active-adversary specialization

Why it ranks here: Boutique capacity makes the retainer the product: Sygnia’s bench is small, senior, and heavily booked, so the contract is effectively the only reliable path to its operators in a live-adversary crisis.

If its eviction craft is your worst-case answer, pre-contracting isn’t optional it’s the mechanism.

Pros: Guaranteed access to scarce operators; senior-density bench.

Cons: Capacity math is the point book or miss.

Bottom line: A reservation at the smallest, hardest table.

7. Cisco Talos — Best Network-Estate Retainer

Snapshot: Retainer tiers with proactive options | Talos intel integration | Network/OT response fluency

Why it ranks here: Talos IR retainers suit estates whose incidents live in infrastructure: network-forensics depth, OT fluency, and intel from backbone-scale visibility, with proactive options (tabletops, readiness reviews) burning unused hours.

Cisco-estate buyers add procurement simplicity through existing agreements.

Pros: Network/OT depth; intel integration; procurement ease for Cisco shops.

Cons: Endpoint-lane gravity sits with the EDR-native firms.

Bottom line: The infrastructure estate’s standing card.

8. Arete — Best Ransomware-Ready Retainer

Snapshot: Insurer-aligned retainers | Extortion-caseload machinery | Recovery-to-restoration pipeline

Why it ranks here: Arete’s retainer pre-positions the exact machinery a ransomware event consumes: negotiation support, decryption logistics, restoration management, insurer-fluent reporting.

For organizations whose realistic worst case is extortion most of the mid-market it’s a specialist contract matched to the probable incident.

Pros: Extortion-pipeline readiness; insurer fluency; caseload-honed process.

Cons: Narrower fit for non-ransomware worst cases.

Bottom line: Pre-signed for the most likely bad day.

9. NCC Group — Best UK/EU Retainer Coverage

Snapshot: Regional retainer structures | UK/EU jurisdiction fluency | Assurance-heritage bench

Why it ranks here: NCC’s retainers carry European weight: UK/EU response presence, GDPR-era regulatory fluency, and an offense-informed bench from its assurance heritage.

For estates whose incidents will unfold under European jurisdiction and notification clocks, regional standing is a contract feature, not a footnote.

Pros: EU jurisdiction fit; offense-informed responders; regional SLAs.

Cons: Global activation breadth versus the majors.

Bottom line: The European-clock retainer.

10. BlackBerry (Cylance Lineage) — Verify the Structure First

Snapshot: IR services retainer lineage | Corporate restructuring reshaped the portfolio | Cylance endpoint assets sold to Arctic Wolf

Why it ranks here diligence first: The sheet lists BlackBerry (Cylance), and honesty requires the update: BlackBerry sold its Cylance endpoint business to Arctic Wolf and has refocused the company, so the IR-retainer offering’s current shape, bench, and continuity need direct verification before any contract.

Rank it as a legacy lineage requiring structural due diligence, not a settled offering.

Pros: Historical IR-services lineage; government-sector relationships.

Cons: Post-divestiture offering clarity is the threshold question.

Bottom line: Confirm what exists before negotiating what it costs.

Full Comparison Table

Yes/No Capability Table

Buying Advice: Negotiate the Quiet-Year Clause

Retainers are judged in two scenarios, and most buyers only negotiate one. For the loud year: response SLA in hours with remedies attached, named regional team, activation path that doesn’t route through sales, and privilege structured through counsel from day one test it all with an annual no-notice activation drill, because an untested retainer is a hope.

For the quiet year: full credit conversion into a proactive catalog you’d actually buy (tabletops, compromise assessments, hunt time), no silent expiry, and rollover terms in writing.

Align panel status with your insurer at policy-writing time so your chosen firm is pre-approved, not argued about at 2 a.m.

Price zero-dollar options honestly they pre-position terms but guarantee no queue priority, which is precisely what you’re buying in a paid tier.

And run the structural diligence this roster demands in 2026: the Secureworks–Sophos and BlackBerry post-divestiture questions answered in the contract, not the pitch deck.

FAQs

What are the best IR retainer services in 2026? Mandiant for guaranteed bench priority, CrowdStrike for speed SLAs, Unit 42 for credit flexibility, Kroll and Arete for insurer alignment, with Secureworks, Sygnia, Talos, NCC, and the BlackBerry lineage pending structural verification.

What should an IR retainer SLA actually guarantee? Remote engagement in contracted hours with remedies, a named regional team, and an activation path independent of business hours plus the drill rights to test it.

Are zero-dollar retainers worth it? As term pre-positioning, yes; as capacity guarantee, no queue priority is what paid tiers buy, and in a mega-event week it’s the only thing that matters.

How do credits work in modern retainers? Prepaid hours or credit blocks spendable on reactive response or a proactive catalog negotiate full conversion and rollover so quiet years still return value.

Should the retainer match our insurance panel? Ideally both: name your preferred firm in the policy as a pre-approved exception, or choose from the panel deliberately deciding during the incident is the failure mode.

Verdict

Ten contracts, two scenarios, one discipline: negotiate the breach and the quiet year. Mandiant’s priority, CrowdStrike’s stopwatch, Unit 42’s wallet, Kroll’s insurance rail, Sygnia’s reservation, Arete’s ransomware pipeline, Secureworks and Talos and NCC by estate, the BlackBerry lineage behind a verification gate contract the hours, drill the activation, convert the quiet, and never meet your responder for the first time on the worst day.

The post Top 10 Best Digital Forensics & Incident Response (DFIR) Companies in 2026 [Ranked & Scored] appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
DFIR is the one security purchase evaluated under the worst possible conditions: mid-breach, counsel on the line, adversary still inside.

What separates firms then isn’t marketing it’s responder bench depth, forensic rigor that survives litigation, and how fast a qualified human reaches your keyboard. This ranking scores the capability itself; its sibling piece on IR retainers covers the contract vehicles.

Google (Mandiant) takes 1; CrowdStrike and Unit 42 complete the podium.

Key Takeaways

• 1 overall: Mandiant the deepest nation-state and APT response bench in commercial practice.

• Podium: Mandiant (APT depth), CrowdStrike (telemetry-accelerated response), Unit 42 (scale with platform reach).

• Capability lens: this ranking rates investigation muscle forensic rigor, eradication discipline, litigation survivability not retainer pricing (see the retainer-services ranking for contract strategy).

• 2026 theme: extortion economics the firms with ransomware-negotiation fluency and recovery discipline carry the caseload reality.

How We Scored (Methodology)

Research-based evaluation; no lab testing, no paid placement; editorial scores excluded from structured data.

Criteria: responder bench depth, forensic/litigation rigor, threat-actor knowledge currency, eradication-and-recovery discipline, global reach, and insurer/counsel ecosystem standing.

Weights: bench depth 25%, forensic rigor 20%, actor knowledge 20%, recovery discipline 20%, reach/ecosystem 15%.

The 2026 DFIR Power Rankings

*Editorial research-based scores, not lab results.

1. Google (Mandiant) — Best APT/Nation-State Response Bench

Snapshot: Engagement + retainer structures | Two decades of frontline APT work | Google-scale intel fusion

Why it earns 1: When the intrusion is sophisticated enough to make the news, Mandiant is usually already in the building.

The bench has worked more nation-state casework than any commercial rival, the actor knowledge updates from live engagements, and Google’s acquisition added telemetry and analytics scale without diluting the responder culture.

For the worst day imaginable, it remains the reference call.

Pros: APT casework depth; actor-attribution authority; intel-fused investigation.

Cons: Premium rates; demand queue at major-event peaks.

Bottom line: The firm the other firms cite in their reports.

2. CrowdStrike — Best Telemetry-Accelerated Response

Snapshot: Services + retainer tiers | Falcon-deployed investigation speed | eCrime fluency

Why it ranks here: CrowdStrike’s responders arrive with a weapon others lack: Falcon deployed across the estate in hours, turning forensic collection from weeks of disk imaging into days of telemetry.

The services arm pairs that speed with deep eCrime fluency ransomware operators tracked by its own intel. Fastest time-to-visibility in the ranking; platform deployment is part of the method.

Pros: Deployment-speed advantage; eCrime depth; intel-services fusion.

Cons: Method assumes Falcon rollout; premium economics.

Bottom line: Speed as a forensic strategy.

3. Palo Alto (Unit 42) — Best Platform-Scaled Response

Snapshot: Engagement + retainer credits | Large global responder bench | Cortex/XSIAM-era tooling

Why it ranks here: Unit 42 built response at portfolio scale: a large global bench, methodology sharpened across a heavy caseload, threat intel from Palo Alto’s telemetry base, and investigation tooling riding Cortex.

Retainer credits flexing into proactive work make it a program partner, not just an emergency number.

Pros: Bench scale; caseload breadth; flexible retainer credits.

Cons: Platform-coupled tooling preferences.

Bottom line: Enterprise response with a platform engine behind it.

4. Kroll — Best Insurer/Counsel-Channel Response

Snapshot: Panel-based engagements | Breach-counsel ecosystem fluency | Notification/regulatory machinery

Why it ranks here: Kroll dominates the lane where most mid-market breaches actually route: cyber-insurance panels and breach counsel.

The machinery around the forensics privileged-investigation discipline, notification logistics, regulatory filings, litigation support is as developed as the investigation itself. If your incident starts with an insurer’s phone tree, Kroll is likely on the list.

Pros: Panel ubiquity; legal-process fluency; end-to-end breach logistics.

Cons: Elite-APT depth concentrated in the firms above.

Bottom line: The breach-counsel ecosystem’s workhorse.

5. Sygnia — Best Hands-On-Keyboard Containment

Snapshot: Engagement-based | Elite operator culture | Active-adversary specialization

Why it ranks here: Sygnia’s reputation grew from engagements where the adversary was still typing: live containment, adversary eviction under fire, and post-incident hardening delivered by a deliberately senior bench.

Boutique scale is the trade for operator density fewer bodies, each one you’d want in the room.

Pros: Senior-operator density; live-eviction craft; hardening follow-through.

Cons: Boutique capacity; book early via retainer.

Bottom line: The special-forces call for active intrusions.

6. Secureworks — Best Research-Fed Response

Snapshot: Services + Taegis-era delivery | CTU intel lineage | Sophos-family integration underway

Why it ranks here: Secureworks’ IR arm draws on Counter Threat Unit research and two decades of casework, with Taegis telemetry accelerating investigations in covered estates.

The Sophos acquisition folds the bench into a larger family service-line continuity is the diligence question while the responder quality lineage stands.

Pros: Research-fed methods; platform-accelerated collection; tenure depth.

Cons: Acquisition-era structure clarity.

Bottom line: Proven bench confirm the post-acquisition shape.

7. Cisco (Talos IR) — Best Network-Depth Response

Snapshot: Retainer + engagement tiers | Talos intel at backbone scale | Network-forensics strength

Why it ranks here: Talos IR brings the network operator’s eye: packet-level forensics, infrastructure-scale intel from Cisco’s visibility, and particular strength where the investigation lives in routers, VPNs, and traffic the lanes endpoint-first firms under-weight.

For network-centric estates and OT-adjacent incidents, the fit is structural.

Pros: Network-forensic depth; Talos intel; infrastructure fluency.

Cons: Brand gravity in pure-endpoint casework.

Bottom line: The responders who read packets natively.

8. Arete — Best Ransomware-Caseload Specialization

Snapshot: Insurer-panel engagements | High-volume extortion casework | Recovery+negotiation machinery

Why it ranks here: Arete built its practice where the caseload actually is: ransomware triage, negotiation support, decryption logistics, restoratio executed at a volume that compounds into pattern knowledge of specific extortion crews.

For the mid-market ransomware event routed through insurance, it’s a specialist with the reps.

Pros: Extortion-case volume; recovery machinery; insurer integration.

Cons: Scope concentrated on the ransomware lane.

Bottom line: Ransomware reps, by the thousand.

9. NCC Group — Best Technical-Assurance-Adjacent DFIR

Snapshot: Engagement + retainer | Pentest-heritage technical depth | UK/EU response strength

Why it ranks here: NCC’s response arm inherits its assurance DNA: responders who think like the attackers its testers emulate, strong malware-analysis craft, and UK/European response presence with regulatory fluency.

A technically serious mid-ranking pick, strongest where European jurisdiction and offensive-informed analysis matter.

Pros: Offense-informed forensics; EU presence; malware-analysis depth.

Cons: Global bench scale versus the majors.

Bottom line: The tester’s eye applied to the breach.

10. Booz Allen — Best Government-Grade Response

Snapshot: Contract vehicles + commercial engagements | Cleared-personnel depth | Critical-infrastructure fluency

Why it ranks here: Booz Allen’s DFIR strength is the government lane: cleared responders, national-security-grade process, and critical-infrastructure incident fluency that commercial boutiques can’t staff. Commercial enterprises in defense-adjacent or regulated-infrastructure sectors get a bench shaped for their constraints.

Pros: Clearance depth; CI/OT fluency; federal-grade process.

Cons: Commercial-market agility versus pure-plays.

Bottom line: When the incident needs a clearance.

Full Comparison Table

Yes/No Capability Table

Buying Advice: Choose the Bench Before the Breach Chooses For You

DFIR bought mid-incident is bought at maximum price and minimum leverage the insurer’s panel decides, the queue decides, the first available team decides.

Pre-select instead: match the firm’s signature lane to your realistic worst case (nation-state exposure → Mandiant/CrowdStrike-tier; ransomware probability → Arete/Kroll’s insurer machinery; active-adversary fear → Sygnia’s operators; OT estate → Talos/Booz Allen fluency), then meet the actual regional team bench quality is a people question, and “who exactly responds to us, from where, in how many hours” belongs in writing.

Align the choice with counsel and insurer early so privilege structure and panel approval exist before the clock starts, and run one tabletop with the chosen firm annually; a team that has seen your network map investigates measurably faster.

The retainer mechanics credits, response-time SLAs, proactive-use terms are the sibling ranking’s subject, but one rule crosses both: the firm you’d want is the firm you’ve already met.

FAQs

Who are the best DFIR companies in 2026? Mandiant for APT depth, CrowdStrike for telemetry speed, Unit 42 for scale, Kroll for the insurer/counsel channel, Sygnia for live containment, with Secureworks, Talos IR, Arete, NCC, and Booz Allen by lane.

DFIR firm versus IR retainer same decision? Related but distinct: this ranking rates investigation capability; the retainer decision adds contract mechanics (SLAs, credits, panel status) ideally you pre-contract the capability you want.

How fast should response start? Remote responder engagement within hours under retainer; meaningful on-estate visibility inside twenty-four to forty-eight ask each firm for their actual medians, not their marketing.

Does our cyber insurance choose our firm? Panels constrain the list, but pre-approved exceptions are negotiable at policy-writing time name your preferred firm in the policy, not during the incident.

What makes forensics litigation-grade? Chain-of-custody discipline, privileged-engagement structure through counsel, and reporting that survives deposition ask for redacted sample reports and their courtroom track record.

Verdict

Ten firms, one buying truth: breach-day quality is decided before breach day. Mandiant for the nation-state call, CrowdStrike for speed, Unit 42 for scale, Kroll and Arete for the insurance-rail reality, Sygnia for the live fight, Secureworks and Talos and NCC and Booz Allen for their lanes pick the bench that matches your worst case, meet the humans, structure the privilege, and rehearse once a year.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
The dirty secret of SIEM ownership: the license is half the cost, and the unstaffed half tuning, content, triage is where programs quietly die. Managed SIEM rents that discipline, in flavors that matter more than brands: vendors managing their own platform, operators managing yours, and services where ownership is genuinely shared.

The ranking scores ten providers on tuning quality, model flexibility, and cost honesty. Splunk takes 1 on managed-platform depth; Rapid7 and Secureworks complete the podium.

Key Takeaways

• 1 overall: Splunk the deepest managed bench for the market’s most powerful platform.

• Podium: Splunk (platform depth), Rapid7 (turnkey bundle value), Secureworks (Taegis-transparent co-management).

• Model question first: vendor-managed (Splunk, Sumo, Devo), operator-managed-yours (deepwatch, ReliaQuest, BlueVoyant), or platform-bundled (Rapid7, Arctic Wolf) the model decides your lock-in and exit math.

• Brand note: LogRhythm’s managed lane now ships from the merged Exabeam company confirm entity and roadmap in contracting.

How We Scored (Methodology)

Research-based evaluation; no lab testing, no paid placement; editorial scores excluded from structured data.

Criteria: tuning/detection-content quality, ownership-model flexibility, transparency (console and case access), platform expertise depth, escalation maturity, and cost predictability.

Weights: tuning quality 25%, model flexibility 20%, transparency 20%, platform depth 20%, cost predictability 15%.

The 2026 Managed SIEM Power Rankings

*Editorial research-based scores, not lab results.

1. Splunk — Best Managed Depth on the Deepest Platform

Snapshot: License + managed-service contracts | Splunk-delivered and partner-delivered tiers | ES content mastery

Why it earns 1: Splunk’s managed lane answers Splunk’s own complexity: vendor and certified-partner services that run ingestion, tuning, and Enterprise Security content at the depth the platform rewards.

If you’ve committed to Splunk’s ceiling, managed delivery from inside the ecosystem extracts it at pricing that reflects both halves of the commitment under the Cisco portfolio.

Pros: Platform mastery; content depth; ecosystem bench.

Cons: Total-cost stacking (license + service); Cisco-era packaging watch.

Bottom line: Maximum Splunk, rented.

2. Rapid7 — Best Turnkey Managed Bundle

Snapshot: Per-asset managed tiers | InsightIDR + MDR analysts | VM-context fusion

Why it ranks here: Rapid7 collapses the managed SIEM question into one bill: InsightIDR as the platform, Rapid7 analysts as the staff, vulnerability context in the same pane, per-asset pricing a budget meeting can approve.

The mid-market reality check it’s the fastest route from no-SIEM to monitored outweighs the single-vendor telemetry ceiling for its buyers.

Pros: One-bill simplicity; fast time-to-monitored; accessible pricing.

Cons: Platform lock; enterprise-custom ceilings.

Bottom line: The managed SIEM most mid-market teams actually finish deploying.

3. Secureworks — Best Transparent Co-Management

Snapshot: Taegis subscriptions + managed tiers | Shared-console co-management | CTU detection content

Why it ranks here: Secureworks built co-management as a first principle: your analysts and theirs working the same Taegis console, detection content from CTU research, and graduated ownership so internal capability can grow without re-platforming.

The Sophos acquisition folds it into a larger ecosystem whose roadmap deserves written confirmation; the co-managed model remains the category’s reference.

Pros: True shared-console model; research-fed content; capability-growth path.

Cons: Taegis-platform coupling; acquisition-era diligence.

Bottom line: Co-management done as architecture, not marketing.

4. deepwatch — Best Managed-Splunk Specialization

Snapshot: Managed tiers | Named squads on your Splunk | Maturity scoring

Why it ranks here: deepwatch does one thing at depth: run enterprise Splunk estates with named squads, detection engineering, and hygiene scoring that tells you how your deployment ranks.

For the large Splunk-committed estate that doesn’t want vendor-delivered services, it’s the specialist alternative with continuity baked into the model.

Pros: Splunk-specialist depth; squad continuity; benchmarking.

Cons: Single-platform focus by design.

Bottom line: Your Splunk, their obsession.

5. ReliaQuest — Best Manage-Your-SIEM Operations

Snapshot: GreyMatter platform | Operates across your SIEM/EDR/cloud | Detection unification

Why it ranks here: ReliaQuest manages the SIEM you own Splunk, Sentinel, QRadar through GreyMatter’s unification layer, adding detection-as-code discipline across the whole stack rather than one console.

It’s the anti-lock-in managed answer: your licenses, your data, their operating rigor.

Pros: SIEM-agnostic operations; unified detection layer; sunk-cost respect.

Cons: Enterprise-weight platform and pricing.

Bottom line: Keep your SIEM; rent the discipline.

6. Arctic Wolf — Best Concierge-Wrapped SIEM Function

Snapshot: Per-user/asset subscription | Aurora platform ingestion | Concierge team delivery

Why it ranks here: Arctic Wolf delivers the SIEM function broad telemetry ingestion, correlation, retention, triage without selling you a SIEM at all: Aurora ingests, the Concierge team interprets, and the customer never touches a query language.

For teams that want outcomes rather than consoles, the abstraction is the product.

Pros: Zero-console burden; named-team continuity; broad ingestion.

Cons: Not your SIEM portability and query freedom traded away.

Bottom line: The SIEM you never have to see.

7. BlueVoyant — Best Microsoft-Estate Managed SIEM

Snapshot: Managed service tiers | Sentinel-specialist operations | MXDR for Microsoft lineage

Why it ranks here: BlueVoyant concentrated where the market moved: managed Sentinel at specialist depth data-connector hygiene, analytics-rule engineering, cost-tier tuning that keeps consumption honest plus Defender-stack response.

For E5-committed estates, it’s the focused alternative to generalist MSSPs running Sentinel as one of many.

Pros: Sentinel depth; consumption-cost tuning; Microsoft-stack response.

Cons: Microsoft-centric by design.

Bottom line: Sentinel estates’ specialist bench.

8. Sumo Logic — Best Vendor-Managed Cloud-Native Option

Snapshot: Credits/consumption | Vendor-operated SaaS + managed add-ons | Dual-use analytics

Why it ranks here: Sumo’s cloud-native SaaS already removes infrastructure ownership; its managed and partner layers add content and monitoring atop.

For teams whose logs serve both security and observability, the dual-use consolidation keeps total spend saner than running parallel stacks.

Pros: No-infrastructure baseline; dual-use economics; consumption flexibility.

Cons: Managed-service depth varies by partner.

Bottom line: The cloud-native path of least ownership.

9. Devo — Best High-Velocity Data Managed Service

Snapshot: Platform + services | Hot-data architecture | SOC-services layer

Why it ranks here: Devo’s always-hot architecture query years without rehydration pairs with managed SOC services for estates whose defining problem is data velocity and uncompromised cloud logging : telecoms, large retail, high-event-rate operations.

It’s a performance-first pick with a services layer, strongest where speed-at-volume is the purchase driver.

Pros: Hot-retention performance; velocity economics; services layer.

Cons: Brand gravity and content ecosystem versus leaders.

Bottom line: For estates that measure ingest in terabytes per day.

10. LogRhythm (Exabeam) — Best Mid-Market Managed Lineage

Snapshot: Platform + partner-managed tiers | Merged-company mid-market base | Partner delivery network

Why it ranks here: LogRhythm’s large mid-market install base carries a mature partner-managed ecosystem, now operating under the merged Exabeam behavioral analytics portfolio.

Existing estates get continuity economics; new buyers should ask the merged-roadmap question directly which platform line, which managed partners, what investment trajectory.

Pros: Install-base continuity; partner network; mid-market pricing.

Cons: Post-merger roadmap clarity is the homework.

Bottom line: Continuity pick for existing estates; diligence pick for new ones.

Yes/No Capability Table

Buying Advice: Decide Whose SIEM Dies If You Leave

The managed SIEM decision is an exit-math decision wearing a service contract. Vendor-managed and bundled models (Splunk-delivered, Rapid7, Arctic Wolf) are fastest to value and hardest to leave the detections, dashboards, and history live in their world.

Operator models (deepwatch, ReliaQuest, BlueVoyant) cost more coordination but leave you owning the platform, content, and data when the contract ends.

Price both paths across three years including the exit scenario: data export, detection-rule portability, and historical-retention transfer.

In the pilot, audit tuning honestly ask for the before/after alert-volume numbers on their last three onboardings and the detection-content changelog they’d commit to monthly.

Confirm the two merged-entity roadmaps here (Secureworks–Sophos, LogRhythm–Exabeam) in writing. And measure the metric the category exists for: analyst-confirmed true-positive rate per hundred alerts escalated to you, quarter over quarter.

FAQs

What are the best managed SIEM services in 2026? Splunk for vendor-managed depth, Rapid7 for turnkey bundles, Secureworks for co-management, deepwatch and ReliaQuest and BlueVoyant for operating your own SIEM, with Arctic Wolf, Sumo Logic, Devo, and LogRhythm/Exabeam by model fit.

Managed SIEM versus SOCaaS? Managed SIEM scopes to the platform (ingestion, tuning, content, triage); SOCaaS wraps broader SOC function around it many contracts blend both, so scope beats label.

Should we keep owning the SIEM license? Yes if exit optionality or data sovereignty matters: operator models preserve ownership; bundled models trade it for speed.

What does good tuning look like? Falling alert volume with rising true-positive rate, a monthly detection-content changelog, and consumption costs that trend flat as telemetry grows.

What’s the hidden cost in managed SIEM? Exit: unexportable detections and historical data re-ingestion write portability into the original contract, not the renewal.

Verdict

Ten providers, three ownership models, one math problem: entry speed versus exit freedom. Splunk’s depth, Rapid7’s bundle, Secureworks’ shared console, deepwatch and ReliaQuest and BlueVoyant running what you own, Arctic Wolf hiding the console entirely, Sumo and Devo as cloud-native lanes, the LogRhythm lineage under Exabeam model the three-year total with the breakup included, demand the tuning changelog, and sign the version of the contract your future self can leave.

The post Top 10 Best SOC-as-a-Service Providers in 2026 [Ranked & Scored] appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
Building a 24/7 SOC takes roughly a dozen analysts before vacation math works which is why SOC-as-a-Service became the mid-market’s default answer and the enterprise’s pressure valve.

The 2026 field divides by philosophy: concierge models that assign you named humans, platform models that sell detection engineering at scale, and bring-your-own-stack operators who run the tools you already own.

Arctic Wolf takes 1; Expel and eSentire complete the podium.

Key Takeaways

• 1 overall: Arctic Wolf the concierge model at category-defining scale.

• Podium: Arctic Wolf (concierge scale), Expel (transparency and automation ethos), eSentire (response authority).

• Philosophy split: concierge (Arctic Wolf, eSentire), platform-transparent (Expel, Rapid7), BYO-stack (ReliaQuest, deepwatch, Proficio, Novacoast) decide whether they bring the stack or run yours.

• 2026 theme: response authority the providers willing to contain, not just notify, separate from the alert-forwarders.

How We Scored (Methodology)

Research-based evaluation; no lab testing, no paid placement; editorial scores excluded from structured data.

Criteria: detection/response outcomes, response authority (containment actions, not just alerts), stack flexibility, transparency (console/case visibility), named-team continuity, and commercial accessibility.

Weights: outcomes 25%, response authority 20%, transparency 20%, stack flexibility 20%, continuity 15%.

The 2026 SOCaaS Power Rankings

*Editorial research-based scores, not lab results.

1. Arctic Wolf — Best Concierge Security Operations

Snapshot: Per-user/asset subscription | Concierge Security Team model | Aurora platform telemetry

Why it earns 1: Arctic Wolf productized the thing small teams actually lack: a named squad that knows your environment.

The Concierge Security Team owns your account’s triage, tuning, and quarterly posture work atop the Aurora platform’s telemetry breadth security operations as a relationship, not a ticket queue, delivered at a scale no other concierge model matches.

Pros: Named-team continuity; posture work included; telemetry breadth.

Cons: Platform lock to Aurora; enterprise-custom depth versus BYO operators.

Bottom line: The strongest “we’ve got you” in the category.

2. Expel — Best Transparent, Automation-Led SOC

Snapshot: Tech-stack-based pricing | Workbench transparency | Automation-heavy triage

Why it ranks here: Expel runs the glass-walled SOC: every investigation visible in Workbench as it happens, findings written in plain English, and automation (their bots) doing the repetitive triage so analysts spend minutes on judgment.

It runs atop your existing stack EDR, cloud, SIEM scoring it for signal quality and telling you honestly what to fix.

Pros: Investigation transparency; automation efficiency; BYO-stack respect.

Cons: Wants a decent existing stack to shine.

Bottom line: The SOC that shows its work.

3. eSentire — Best Response Authority

Snapshot: Service tiers | Atlas platform | 24/7 threat response unit

Why it ranks here: eSentire’s pitch is verbs: isolate, kill, contain authority written into the service, with its own threat response unit executing within minutes rather than emailing you at 3 a.m.

Atlas-platform telemetry plus original threat research back the muscle. For buyers whose nightmare is the un-actioned alert, this is the design center.

Pros: Containment authority; response speed culture; original research.

Cons: Full value needs you granting real response permissions.

Bottom line: Hire it to act, not to notify.

4. ReliaQuest — Best Bring-Your-Own-Stack Operations

Snapshot: GreyMatter platform subscription | Stack-agnostic unification | Detection-as-code ethos

Why it ranks here: ReliaQuest’s GreyMatter sits above whatever you already bought SIEM, EDR, cloud, identity unifying detection and response across it without rip-and-replace.

The model respects sunk investment and kills the single-vendor telemetry tax; its ceiling is that unification quality tracks the quality of what you feed it.

Pros: True stack agnosticism; unified detection layer; enterprise fit.

Cons: Garbage-in constraint; enterprise-weight platform.

Bottom line: The SOC layer for estates that refuse lock-in.

5. Rapid7 — Best Platform-Bundled SOC Service

Snapshot: Per-asset MDR tiers | Insight platform native | D&R + VM fusion

Why it ranks here: Rapid7’s managed SOC rides its own platform: InsightIDR detection, managed by Rapid7 analysts, with vulnerability context from InsightVM in the same pane.

The bundle economics are the argument detection, response, and exposure management in one per-asset bill a mid-market CFO can parse.

Pros: Bundle value; VM-context fusion; accessible packaging.

Cons: Single-platform telemetry view.

Bottom line: The tidy all-Rapid7 answer at mid-market price.

6. deepwatch — Best Splunk-Centric Managed SOC

Snapshot: Managed service tiers | Splunk-native operations | Squad-based delivery

Why it ranks here: deepwatch built its service as Splunk operations perfected: your Splunk (or theirs), run by named squads with detection engineering, hygiene scoring, and maturity benchmarking layered on.

For the large Splunk-committed estate that wants the platform’s ceiling without staffing it, the specialization is the value.

Pros: Splunk mastery; squad continuity; maturity benchmarking.

Cons: Splunk-centric by design.

Bottom line: Splunk estates’ outsourcing shortcut.

7. Huntress — Best Affordable Managed SOC for SMBs

Snapshot: Predictable endpoint-based pricing | 24/7 SOC monitoring | Managed EDR with active threat remediation

Why it ranks here: Huntress stands out for making managed security operations accessible to small and mid-sized businesses. Its 24/7 Security Operations Center combines managed endpoint detection, threat hunting, and automated response to identify and stop attacks before they spread.

The platform focuses on ransomware, persistent threats, and suspicious endpoint activity, helping organizations strengthen security without building an expensive in-house SOC.

Pros: Affordable and predictable pricing; 24/7 human-led SOC; strong ransomware protection; automated threat containment.

Cons: More endpoint-focused than full-scale enterprise SOC platforms; advanced SIEM and custom detection capabilities are limited compared with larger providers.

Bottom line: The practical, cost-effective managed SOC choice for SMBs that need reliable threat detection and response without enterprise-level complexity.

8. Sophos MDR — Best AI-Powered Managed Detection and Response

Snapshot: MDR Essentials and Complete tiers | 24/7 expert-led SOC | AI-assisted threat detection and response

Why it ranks here: Sophos MDR combines AI-powered detection with round-the-clock human expertise to identify, investigate, and contain threats across endpoints, networks, cloud environments, and identity systems.

Its flexible service tiers, broad third-party integrations, and incident response capabilities make it a strong choice for organizations seeking enterprise-grade security operations without building an in-house SOC.

Pros: 24/7 threat monitoring; AI-assisted investigations; broad security integrations; active threat containment.

Cons: Advanced response capabilities depend on service tier; full value may require deeper Sophos ecosystem integration.

Bottom line: The AI-powered managed SOC choice for organizations seeking continuous protection and expert-led response.

9. Proficio — Best Co-Managed Flexibility

Snapshot: Co-managed/full-managed tiers | ProSOC model | SIEM-flexible delivery

Why it ranks here: Proficio built its niche on meeting you where you are: co-managed SIEM (yours or theirs), graduated response authority via ActiveDefense, and healthcare/mid-enterprise vertical depth.

It’s the flexible mid-tier operator for teams that want partnership gradients, not binary outsourcing.

Pros: Co-managed gradient; vertical focus; SIEM flexibility.

Cons: Scale and research depth versus majors.

Bottom line: Outsource exactly as much as you want.

10. Novacoast — Best Services-Depth Boutique

Snapshot: Custom service engagements | Identity+security services lineage | novaSOC operations

Why it ranks here: Novacoast pairs its SOC service with unusual bench depth in identity and security engineering the boutique that can also fix what monitoring finds.

For buyers wanting a services partner with a SOC rather than a SOC with upsells, the shape fits; brand reach is the honest constraint.

Pros: Engineering bench; identity depth; partnership posture.

Cons: Boutique scale; regional gravity.

Bottom line: The engineer’s SOCaaS pick.

Full Comparison Table

Yes/No Capability Table

Buying Advice: Grant the Verbs or Keep the Pager

The SOCaaS value cliff sits at response authority: a provider allowed only to email you is a very expensive smoke detector.

Decide before procurement which actions you’ll delegate host isolation, account disable, token revocation under what guardrails, and shortlist only providers contractually comfortable executing them; then test with an unannounced drill in the pilot and measure minutes-to-containment, not minutes-to-email.

Choose the philosophy honestly: strong existing stack → BYO operators (Expel, ReliaQuest, deepwatch); thin stack and thin team → concierge platforms (Arctic Wolf, eSentire); somewhere between → co-managed gradients (Proficio).

Interrogate continuity who exactly works your account, their tenure, and what happens when they leave and write telemetry sovereignty into the contract: your logs, exportable, with exit assistance.

The provider’s own metrics deserve audit too: ask for their median containment times across clients, and how they’re measured.

FAQs

Who are the best SOC-as-a-Service providers in 2026? Arctic Wolf leads the concierge model, Expel for transparency, eSentire for response authority, ReliaQuest and deepwatch for BYO-stack operations, with Rapid7, Alert Logic, Cybereason, Proficio, and Novacoast by fit.

SOCaaS versus MDR versus MSSP? Heavily overlapping labels: MDR is the detect-respond core, SOCaaS wraps it in full SOC function (triage, tuning, posture), MSSP is the widest umbrella including device management contract scope matters more than the acronym.

Should the provider run our stack or theirs? Good existing telemetry favors BYO operators; greenfield or thin stacks favor platform-native providers switching stacks mid-contract is the expensive mistake.

What response authority should we grant? Host isolation and account disable under written guardrails is the common baseline; start with after-hours authority if full delegation feels early.

How big must we be before building our own SOC? The usual arithmetic says roughly a dozen security FTEs before 24/7 in-house coverage beats renting most organizations below a few thousand employees rent.

Verdict

Ten providers, three philosophies, one cliff: authority. Arctic Wolf’s concierge squads, Expel’s glass walls, eSentire’s containment verbs, ReliaQuest and deepwatch running your stack, Rapid7’s tidy bundle, Alert Logic’s value tiers, Cybereason’s operation lens, Proficio’s gradient, Novacoast’s bench pick who may act at 3 a.m., write it down, and drill it before the adversary does.

articles.title: Critical ChatGPT Flaw Allowed Attackers to Hijack Accounts and Steal Private Conversations With One Link
articles.description:
A critical ChatGPT flaw that let a malicious shared conversation run attacker-controlled JavaScript in another user’s signed-in session. The attack could list private chats, read conversations never shared with the attacker, and send stolen data to an outside server. Opening one crafted link was enough in the final demonstration. OpenAI fixed the issue on October […]

The post Critical ChatGPT Flaw Allowed Attackers to Hijack Accounts and Steal Private Conversations With One Link appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
A critical ChatGPT flaw that let a malicious shared conversation run attacker-controlled JavaScript in another user’s signed-in session. The attack could list private chats, read conversations never shared with the attacker, and send stolen data to an outside server. Opening one crafted link was enough in the final demonstration.

OpenAI fixed the issue on October 26, 2026, according to Parameter’s technical disclosure, published by Mukul Goyal on October 28. The company classified the report as P1 and awarded a $5,000 bounty. The demonstrated account access came through the victim’s active browser session, rather than a stolen password.

The exploit combined an interactive graph with ChatGPT’s HTML Preview feature. Preview normally runs code inside a restricted frame on a separate web address, preventing it from directly reading the main ChatGPT page. That boundary initially worked as intended.

ChatGPT Flaw Exploited With One Link

The graph, however, loaded MathLive, a math library that added a message listener to the main page for its virtual keyboard. Through the browser’s postMessage interface, the isolated Preview could send instructions to that listener. MathLive accepted keyboard changes without properly checking the sender’s origin or requiring an approved source window.

One message supplied a keyboard layout containing attacker-controlled HTML. Another opened the keyboard, placing that HTML into the real ChatGPT page through innerHTML. A helper called createHTML passed the content through without removing unsafe markup.

This differs from the previously reported ChatGPT sandbox flaw that exposed Gmail data, which used shared internal storage. Here, the escape crossed a browser boundary through messages trusted by a privileged page component.

HTML injection alone did not immediately execute JavaScript. The researchers inserted an iframe using srcdoc, which stores an embedded page’s HTML directly in an attribute. Because this new frame lacked sandbox restrictions, it inherited ChatGPT’s web origin and could access the parent page.

ChatGPT’s Content Security Policy blocked inline scripts but allowed scripts from YouTube. The researchers found that YouTube’s oEmbed endpoint returned an attacker-supplied JSONP callback as JavaScript, even when reporting an invalid callback. Loading that response provided the final step needed to run code as chatgpt.com.

The researchers then placed both the graph and HTML Preview inside a public conversation. An earlier version required clicking Preview. The final version opened it automatically and was reproduced three times in a separate account, with execution appearing after roughly 4.5 seconds.

Private Chat Theft and OpenAI’s Fix

The payload read session details already available to ChatGPT’s frontend and called authenticated conversation APIs. It retrieved a private conversation unrelated to the shared link, then sent a small selected value to a research server through an image request.

Unlike the separately reported ChatGPT GitHub connector flaw, this attack did not depend on repository instructions or connected tools. Its access came directly from JavaScript running within the trusted website.

Parameter submitted the report on October 18. OpenAI reproduced the issue and raised its priority on October 21. By October 26, both affected web frontend versions rejected the reported MathLive messages. The case highlights why cross-frame receivers must verify both sender origin and source window, while untrusted HTML must remain sandboxed throughout rendering.

Give your SOC the alert context to stops incidents quickly. Integrate Threat Intel from 16K SOCs.
